Et huic laudatissimo studio totum incubuisse, ab annis compluribus, pro iis quibus succendebatur pietatis et charitatis ignibus, Germaniae illum Mavortem vere Christianum, Libertatis juxta et Religionis Statorem, FRIDERICUM WILHELMUM, S. R. I. Electorem, animo juxta et armis Invictissimum, ut testis est Europa, sic nos quoque et olim, et non diu ante fata, in tanti Principis Sacrarium et colloquium admissi.
english: III. As to the Article concerning the Person of Christ, both sides agreed (pp. 13–16): 1. That the Divine and Human Nature are truly and personally united, so that Christ is God and Man in the unity of Person; and that that Union was made ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως — without confusion, without change, indivisibly, and inseparably. 2. That the Names of the Natures are truly predicated of each other, and in the proper signification of the words: God is Man, Man is God; and that the Properties also of each united Nature are truly and really predicated of the whole Person in the concrete, but according to that Nature to which those Properties or Attributes truly belong — which the Theologians have been pleased to call the Communication of Properties (Communicatio Idiomatum). 3. That the Human Nature is not intrinsically omnipotent, nor omniscient; thus in the Union the united Natures remained distinct, and the essential Properties of each safe; that the Principle which acts is the Person, the Principle by which, each Nature, and so on. 4. That the Human Nature has truly been raised to the highest glory, sitting also itself at the Right Hand of God. 5. That on both sides the Heresies of Nestorius, Eutyches, Marcion, Arius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Socinus (they place them in this order), and the like, are rejected.

There remained a dissent, and one not acknowledged as essential by those Men: 1. Whether to the Human Nature in the abstract there was communicated the divine Majesty, or All power, which it would exercise through the Omnipotence everywhere present and hypostatically joined to it? 2. Whether of the same Human Nature, in the abstract, there could be predicated the divine Properties that are fitted for operating — Omnipotence, and so on.

IV. As to the Article concerning Holy Baptism, both sides consented to this (pp. 17–18): That Infants are to be baptized; that the end of Baptism is that they be grafted into Christ and spiritually regenerated; that Baptism is necessary, yet not absolutely, so that only contempt of Baptism damns; that Infants are capable of regenerating grace: and both Parties established that these things belong to the essentials of that Sacrament. Controversies remained, yet acknowledged on both sides as not essential: 1. Whether Infants are at last grafted into Christ and regenerated through Baptism by the necessity of a means — namely an ordinary means? 2. Whether, because of the danger from neglect of Baptism, in a case of necessity, even a Layman may administer Baptism if a Minister's supply is denied?

V. As to Ceremonies — for example Exorcism in the Baptismal formula — there was consent on both sides: 1. That it is not to be thought the infant is corporally possessed by Satan. 2. That that rite can be employed no otherwise than to signify the habitual inherence of Original Sin. 3. That those formulas of Exorcism can be omitted and changed into express Prayers.

And according to the norm of this Agreement, the said Theologians judged that the Academies and Churches of Germany — especially (as nearer) the Brandenburg and Brunswick ones — ought to be invited into the same fellowship. And that truly Christian Mars of Germany, Assertor of Liberty as well as of Religion, FREDERICK WILLIAM, Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, most Invincible alike in mind and in arms — as Europe is witness, and as we too once were, and not long before his death, admitted into so great a Prince's sanctuary and conversation — had for many years wholly devoted himself to this most praiseworthy zeal, according to those fires of piety and charity with which he was kindled.

source_text:
Ibant quo poterant! Piorum certe quorumcunque Theologorum est, ministram operam adhibere, neque dictis tantum, aut scriptis, sed et factis; scilicet vera charitate accensis et cordibus, et linguis, et calamis, compositisque domesticis dissidiis, inter consortes ejusdem Fidei, atque Tesserae. Quod posterius, de universis aut plerisque, optandum magis est quam sperandum, donec erit humanis affectibus atque infirmitatibus locus.

Sint jam in Protestantium Virorum ordine, qui Errorem quemvis in Haeresin, aut Dissensum quemvis in Fundamentalem vel Essentialem, pro libidine vertant! Nihilominus persaepe verbalis ea dissensio fuerit, et circa phrasim vel enunciandi modum; ex. gr. in vocibus realiter, oraliter, sufficienter, efficaciter, &c. Saepe circa rei modum, puta rationem praesentiae vel adessentiae in Eucharistia. Aut circa rei circumstantias, puta Latitudinem Redemptionis — an et pro reprobis — manente re et substantia immotis. Saepe etiam dissensus non in vere traditis, sed in affictis, per consequentias non innatas, sed illatas, certe rejectas; v. gr. de negata a Reformatis Dei Omnipotentia, de Deo auctore Peccati, de Stoica necessitate asserta, &c. Denique dissidium privatum Theologorum magis, quam publicum Confessionum, in non una quaestione, Fratres distraxit: Qualiter in quaestione Supralapsaria, fere sopita, aliisque id genus quam plurimis.
english: They went as far as they could! It belongs to pious Theologians of every sort to lend a helping hand — not by words or writings only, but also by deeds; that is, with hearts and tongues and pens kindled by true charity, and with domestic discords composed among the partners of the same Faith and of the same Token. That latter point, as concerns all or most, is more to be wished than hoped for, so long as there is still room for human affections and infirmities.

There are already in the rank of Protestant Men those who turn any Error into Heresy, or any Dissent into something Fundamental or Essential, as their passion wills! Nevertheless that dissent has very often been merely verbal, and has turned on phrasing or on the manner of stating a thing — for example in the words realiter, oraliter, sufficienter, efficaciter, and so on. Often it has turned on the mode of the thing — for instance the manner of presence or of being-present in the Eucharist. Or on the circumstances of the thing — for instance the Breadth of Redemption, whether also for the reprobate, while the thing itself and its substance remain unmoved. Often too the dissent is not in what was truly handed down, but in things fastened on by consequences not born in the teaching but brought in from outside — and certainly rejected; for example, that the Reformed deny God's Omnipotence, that they make God the author of Sin, that they assert a Stoic necessity, and so on. Finally, the private quarrel of Theologians more than the public quarrel of Confessions has pulled Brethren apart in more than one question: as in the Supralapsarian question, now nearly laid to sleep, and in very many others of that kind.

source_text: Addam et in illa de Potestate Majestatis circa Sacra, ab his magis restricta, ab aliis in Architectonicam versa: Vel etiam de limitibus Regiae Potestatis, et passivae obedientiae; Quo in argumento Theologus Hafniensis nuperus toti Reformatorum Ecclesiae, ex nonnullorum forte dictis vel assertis, in sensum quemcunque voluit, inflexis, hanc notam inussit parum verecunde, esse illam adversam et infestam Regum ac Principum juribus, vel etiam divinae istorum origini, imo et securitati: Nec alio instituto, quam ut Exules Gallos, in gremium Potentissimi Regis profugos, si non tecto, certe Templo, et libertate Sacrorum prohiberet. Procul a mea tuus sit furor omnis Domo! Ita sint nonnunquam Viri fratres, qui dicta saepe in disputationis aestu, saepe titubanter vel opinative, saepe sensu commodo, sed locutione incommoda, qualia primaevae Ecclesiae Scriptoribus et Patribus innumera exciderunt, parum Christiane in contentionis argumentum et λογομαχιῶν, avidissime rapiant! Sint qui in cogitatis quibusdam suis, aut sensu suo abundent, in praejudicium Ecclesiasticae tranquillitatis, et contra prudentiae Christianae leges! Sint qui privatorum naevos in publicos Ecclesiarum transformant: sic dicta quaedam, v. gr. Zwinglii, Calvini, Martyris, Bezae, &c. in sententiam Eccl. Reformatae, et duriore quidem sensu intellecta!
english: I will add also that dispute concerning the Power of Majesty about Sacred things — more restricted by some, turned by others into an Architectonic power; or even concerning the limits of Royal Power and of passive obedience. On that argument a recent Theologian of Copenhagen has, with little modesty, branded the whole Reformed Church — twisting certain sayings or assertions of a few into whatever sense he wished — as adverse and hostile to the rights of Kings and Princes, and even to their divine origin, and indeed to their security: and with no other design than that he might shut out the French Exiles, fled into the bosom of the Most Powerful King, if not from a roof, at least from the Temple and from the liberty of Sacred things. Far be all your fury from my House! So there are sometimes brother Men who, with little Christian spirit, most eagerly snatch sayings — often spoken in the heat of disputation, often hesitatingly or as opinion, often sound in sense but awkward in wording, such as fell in countless numbers from the Writers and Fathers of the early Church — into matter for contention and for battles about words (λογομαχίαι)! There are those who abound in certain private thoughts of their own, or in their own sense, to the prejudice of Ecclesiastical tranquillity and against the laws of Christian prudence! There are those who transform the blemishes of private men into public marks of the Churches: thus taking certain sayings, for example of Zwingli, Calvin, Martyr, Beza, and others, as the judgment of the Reformed Church, and understood in a harsher sense!

source_text:
Sint qui ex se ἀδιάφορα in necessaria, aut quae ad rationem externae disciplinae, vel ordinis, variam utique pro varietate Locorum, Gentium, Consuetudinum, in ipsam Christianismi substantiam, et quasi animam, abire jubeant! Sint qui fundamentalis quidem erroris (ut ἐπιεικῶς judicare prompti sumus) theoretice immunes, practico semet et graviori longe distinguant, charitatis nempe defectu, Matth. v. 23. 24. 1 Cor. xiii. 1. &c.! Certum jam fieri ista omnia, posthabito Servatoris nostri mandato, exemplo, charactere, ultimis verbis, Joh. xiv. 27. ac spretis divi Gentium Apostoli regulis monitisque Eph. iv. 2. 3. Phil. iii. 16. 1 Tim. vi. 4. &c. Neglecto etiam Ordinis sui decore et Officii; susque deque habitis sive piis Maximorum Principum studiis, sive ardentissimis Theologorum Partis utriusque votis, sive Bonorum omnium gemitibus ac suspiriis, nec attento Pacis Evangelicae instaurandae momento.

Nos sane haud intermittimus, seu lugere animo atque indolescere iniquissimis hominum affectibus, tanto cum veritatis Evangelicae dispendio, Ecclesiae damno, Hostium gaudio, Piorum offendiculo, Antichristianae tyrannidis incremento; seu etiam cum iis jungere dextras, quibus de meliore luto finxit praecordia Divinum Numen, qui de nobis nostrisque Ecclesiis sentiunt aequius ac moderatius, ac fundamentalem consensum intelligunt. Quales sunt, Dei beneficio, hinc inde varii per Germaniam pene omnem, et Arcticum Orbem; cumprimis luctosissimis temporibus, oppressa jam a communi Hoste Ecclesia, et deinceps opprimenda, nisi conjunctis et viribus et animis, sub auspiciis summarum Potestatum, furorem ista represserit. Jamque accipimus laetabundi, in amplissimis Ditionibus Potentissimi Brandenburgici, coalescere sensim studia, odia facessere, eristica arceri, in commune consuli, revocarique ad animos, ante concitatiores, quae hanc in rem suasere superiore et nostro Seculo Viri spectatae pietatis, moderationis prudentiaeque — Capitones, Buceri, Melanchthones, Strigelii, Peuceri, Pierii, Himmelii, Palladii, Donaweri, Chytraei, Pelargi, Osiandri, Calixti, Meyffarti, Matthiae, Dilheri, Drejeri, Conringii, Musaei, Heinichii, Helmstadienses, &c.
english: There are those who of themselves order things indifferent (ἀδιάφορα) to become necessary, or order what belongs to the pattern of external discipline or of order — variable of course with the variety of Places, Nations, and Customs — to pass over into the very substance of Christianity, and as it were its soul! There are those who, theoretically immune from fundamental error (as we are ready to judge gently, ἐπιεικῶς), yet distinguish themselves practically by something far heavier: namely by a defect of charity (Matthew 5:23-24; 1 Corinthians 13:1, and so on)! It is already certain that all these things are done when our Savior's mandate, example, character, and last words are set aside (John 14:27), and when the rules and warnings of the holy Apostle of the Gentiles are despised (Ephesians 4:2-3; Philippians 3:16; 1 Timothy 6:4, and so on). The dignity and Office of their own Order are neglected as well; the pious efforts of the Greatest Princes, the most ardent vows of Theologians of either Party, and the groans and sighs of all the Good are tossed up and down as of no account; and no attention is paid to the weight of restoring Evangelical Peace.

We for our part do not cease either to lament in spirit and to grow sick at heart over the most unjust affections of men — with so great a loss to Evangelical truth, harm to the Church, joy to Enemies, offense to the Pious, and increase of Antichristian tyranny — or also to join right hands with those for whom the Divine Majesty has shaped the heart of better clay, who think more fairly and moderately of us and of our Churches, and who understand the fundamental consensus. Such men there are, by God's kindness, here and there through nearly all Germany and the Northern world; especially in these most mournful times, when the Church is already oppressed by the common Enemy and will be oppressed still further unless, with forces and minds joined under the auspices of the highest Powers, she has repressed that fury. And already we hear with joy that in the ample Dominions of the Most Powerful Brandenburg Elector studies are gradually coalescing, hatreds are departing, eristic strife is being barred, common counsel is being taken, and there are being recalled to minds formerly more stirred what men of proven piety, moderation, and prudence urged in this matter in the last century and in ours — Capito, Bucer, Melanchthon, Strigelius, Peucer, Pierius, Himmel, Palladius, Donauer, Chytraeus, Pelargus, Osiander, Calixtus, Meyfart, Matthias, Dilher, Dreier, Conring, Musaeus, Heinich, the Helmstedt men, and others.

source_text: Atque utinam iretur ad primas dissensionum Origines, prolixe intellectas ex Historia Diffidii primum Sacramentarii, nati Anno 1524. inter Lutherum et Carolostadium, qui alias Bodenstein ex Carlstadt, mox Huldr. Zwinglio in mediam sententiam ituro: Scilicet Carolostadio, τὸ Hoc (τοῦτο) in verbis Institutionis referente non ad Panem, sed ad Corpus Christi, atque ita praesentiam omnem Corporis in Pane Eucharistico tollente; Luthero contra corporalem asserente, specie τοῦ ῥητοῦ; Zwinglio autem et Oecolampadio Sacramentalem, sub figura Panis et Vini. Intelligenda praecipue dissidiorum origine, ex illorum ingeniis qui horum certaminum pars magna fuere. Lutherus nempe fervidus, nec parem doctrina vel auctoritate satis ferens; Carolostadius minus prudens, impetu magis quam doctrina et judicio ductus; Zwinglius in sententia constans nec cedens Lutheri imperiis, vel nomini; Oecolampadius immotus, auctoritate Augustini, totiusque primae Antiquitatis; Melanchthon mitissimi ingenii, sic asserturus proprietatem Verborum institutionis, ut a Luthero discesserit, non agnita locali coexistentia, vel inclusione Corporis, nec hujus orali manducatione. Sed exceperunt mox Bellonae filii, acerba et eristica ingenia, lites auctura, et Controversias:
english: And would that men went back to the first Origins of the dissensions, understood at length from the History of the Diffidence — first the Sacramentarian schism, born in the year 1524 between Luther and Carolostadius, otherwise Bodenstein of Carlstadt, with Huldrych Zwingli soon about to move into a middle opinion: namely, Carolostadius referring the This (τοῦτο) in the words of Institution not to the Bread but to the Body of Christ, and so removing every presence of the Body in the Eucharistic Bread; Luther on the contrary asserting a corporal presence, by the letter of the text (τοῦ ῥητοῦ); but Zwingli and Oecolampadius a Sacramental presence, under the figure of Bread and Wine. The origin of the discords is to be understood especially from the temperaments of those who were a great part of these contests. Luther, to be sure, was fervid, and did not easily bear an equal in doctrine or authority; Carolostadius was less prudent, led by impulse more than by doctrine and judgment; Zwingli was constant in his opinion and yielded neither to Luther's commands nor to his name; Oecolampadius was unmoved, by the authority of Augustine and of the whole early Antiquity; Melanchthon, of the gentlest temper, would so assert the proper sense of the words of Institution that he departed from Luther, not acknowledging a local coexistence or inclusion of the Body, nor an oral manducation of it. But soon there came after them the sons of Bellona — bitter and eristic tempers — that would enlarge the suits and the Controversies:

source_text:
Quales Joh. Brentius Ubiquitariorum pater; Jac. Andrea, a fabrili arte Schmidlinus, superadditurus multa Brentianis; Tim. Heshusius tot turbarum fax flammarumque; Joh. Marbachius, novis portentis ac calumniis in Pezelium, Zanchium, Tossanum &c. insignis; Samuel Huberus, et Aegidius Hunnius, irrequieta ingenia, novis, etiam de Praedestinatione, feturis turgida: Cumprimis vero Flaccius Illyricus cum suis, iniquissimus insectator Philippi, ac emendatae ab eo Confessionis Augustanae, licet ipso cohortante Luthero, a quo Flacciani, et Flaccio-Brentiani, furoribus notissimi: Tandem Auctores Libri Concordiae, seu Formulae Bergensis, primipilis Jac. Andreae, Selneccero, Chytreo, Chemnitio, &c. De cujus Auctoribus, Scriptione, Scopo, Articulis, Reprobatione, Approbatione, Apologia, Sequelis, &c. fuse Hospinianus, in Opere Concordia Discors, et Palatini in Admonitione Neostad.; Henr. Altingius, in Historia MS. Reformat. Palatinae, &c.

Ex istis facile constabit, esse hujusmodi Schisma inter Evangelicos natum, cui occasionem initio praebuit aemulatio Lutherum inter et Carolostadium, mox Lutherum inter et Zwinglium, pares hos eruditione, ac reformandi studio, in uno forte praesentiae Eucharisticae modo, discordes. Hinc genuit primo infelix Schisma, levius in suis primordiis de S. Coena dissidium; levius dico, vel ex Colloquio Marpurgensi, in quo silentium Lutherus addixerat, tum ex collatione Articuli x. Confessionis Augustanae, cum addita Phil. Melanchthonis deinceps Elucidatione, atque in hac praetermissa improbatione secus docentium. Sed fovit mox animorum sententiarumque divortium, ὀξυχολία quorundam et vehementia, ut fuere hominum ingenia, non postremis hoc ordine Jac. Andreae, vero Smidlino seu fabro contentionum; Tilem. Heshusio, fortunam Superintendentis Generalis totius Palatinatus, anno aetatis XXXII. ferre nescio; dein notis Joh. Marbachio, Fl. Illyrico, &c. Parturivit mox Ubiquitatis dogma, quod assertum quidem primo occasione Controv. Eucharisticae, sed tacitum postea Luthero ac missum omnino, ut et in Augustana Confess. Recruduit autem post Lutheri fata, propinatur Brentio, sed interpolaturis ac promoturis J. Andreae, Flaccianis, Bergensibus, &c. Unde illorum divortium ab Augustana Confessione qualem recognoverat et emendarat Melanchthon, cumprimis ad Artic. x. et discrimen per eos natum inter Confess. variatam et invariatam. Accesserunt odia, furor, vis, exacerbatio hinc inde.
english: Such were Johann Brenz, father of the Ubiquitarians; Jakob Andreae, from the carpenter's craft called Schmidlin, who would add much to the Brentians; Tilemann Heshusius, fire and flame of so many tumults; Johann Marbach, marked by new portents and calumnies against Pezel, Zanchi, Tossanus, and others; Samuel Huber and Aegidius Hunnius, restless tempers, swollen with new births even concerning Predestination: and above all Flacius Illyricus with his party, the most unjust persecutor of Philip and of the Augsburg Confession as Melanchthon had emended it — though Luther himself had encouraged that work — from whom the Flaccians, and the Flaccio-Brentians, are most noted for their furies: and at last the Authors of the Book of Concord, or Bergen Formula, with Jakob Andreae, Selnecker, Chytraeus, Chemnitz, and others as chief captains. Concerning its Authors, Writing, Scope, Articles, Reprobation, Approbation, Apology, Sequels, and so on, Hospinian treats at length in his work Concordia Discors, and the Palatines in the Neustadt Admonition; also Heinrich Alting in his manuscript History of the Palatine Reformation, and others.

From these things it will easily be plain that a Schism of this kind was born among Evangelicals, to which rivalry between Luther and Carolostadius first gave occasion, and soon rivalry between Luther and Zwingli — men equal in learning and in zeal for reform, yet discordant in one point, the mode of Eucharistic presence. Hence first arose the unhappy Schism, a dissent about the Holy Supper lighter in its beginnings; lighter, I say, both from the Marburg Colloquy, in which Luther had enjoined silence, and from comparing Article X of the Augsburg Confession with the Elucidation Melanchthon afterward added, in which the disapproval of those who teach otherwise was omitted. But soon the sharp anger (ὀξυχολία) and vehemence of certain men fostered the divorce of minds and opinions — such as men's tempers were — and not last in that order Jakob Andreae, truly a Schmidlin or smith of contentions; Tilemann Heshusius, who somehow could not bear the fortune of General Superintendent of the whole Palatinate at the age of thirty-two; then the notorious Johann Marbach, Flacius Illyricus, and others. Soon the dogma of Ubiquity was brought to birth — asserted indeed at first on the occasion of the Eucharistic Controversy, but afterward left silent by Luther and dropped altogether, as also in the Augsburg Confession. Yet it broke out again after Luther's death, poured out by Brenz, but interpolated and promoted by Jakob Andreae, the Flaccians, the Bergen men, and others. Hence came their divorce from the Augsburg Confession as Melanchthon had reviewed and emended it, especially at Article X, and the distinction they produced between the Confession as varied and as unvaried. Hatreds, fury, force, and exacerbation followed on every side.

source_text: per Germaniam; adeo ut etiam in optimos pientissimosque Principes insurgerent, qualiter in Fridericum III. Palatinum atrox tempestas excitata, incentoribus praecipue J. Andreae, Heshusio, Bidenbachio, ut scilicet Fridericum Pium Pace Religionis, & Societate Augustanae Confess. excluderent, frustra futuri in Comitiis Augustanis A. 1566. Absolvit ultimo Formula Concordiae primo Torgensis, Bergensis postea, de qua modo dictum, re vera Discordiae Formula, & duraturi Schismatis Complementum; reclamaturis statim, Ludovico Elect. Palatino, Lutheranis quanquam addictissimo, aliisque Principibus, sed & Theologis gravissimis, ut fuse laudati Hospinianus, Altingius, &c. Sed diduxit ulcus in majus ac insanabile reddidit infelix Controversia de Praedestinatione, & annexis Capitibus nata praecipue, per Sam. Huberum, tum per Aegid. Hunnium Wittenbergensem, circa A. 1580. vel teste infra Georgio Calixto ad Confessionem Thorunensem, p. 14. Ac tandem obfirmarunt in hunc usque diem Evangelicor. istud dissidium, Satanae κακοτεχνία; occultae Jesuitarum artes τῶν πολυμηχάνων; Politicorum rationes Romae servientium, aut commodis suis; ac Theologorum plerumque κακοζηλία, typhus, odia, calumniae, praejudicia, scripta eristica & virulenta, ac privata in plurimis studia, ut accidit, nec habitura finem, donec Serenissimorum Principum auctoritate, ac vi majore, si interveniat unquam, coerceantur.
english: through Germany — so far that they rose even against the best and most pious Princes: as when a fierce tempest was stirred against Frederick III of the Palatinate, with Jakob Andreae, Heshusius, and Bidenbach as chief firebrands, that they might shut pious Frederick out of the Peace of Religion and the Society of the Augsburg Confession — though they would fail at the Augsburg Diet of 1566. At last the Formula of Concord finished the work — first the Torgau Formula, afterward the Bergen — of which we have just spoken: in truth a Formula of Discord, and the complement of a lasting Schism. Elector Ludwig of the Palatinate protested at once, though most devoted to the Lutherans, and other Princes with him, and also the weightiest Theologians — Hospinian, Alting, and the rest already praised at length. But the unhappy Controversy concerning Predestination and its annexed Heads, born chiefly through Samuel Huber and then through Aegidius Hunnius of Wittenberg around the year 1580 — or so Georg Calixtus testifies below on the Confession of Thorn, p. 14 — drew the ulcer wider and rendered it incurable.

And at last they have hardened that Evangelical dissent down to this very day: Satan's malign craft (κακοτεχνία); the hidden arts of the many-scheming Jesuits (τῶν πολυμηχάνων); the calculations of Politicians who serve Rome or their own advantage; and among Theologians for the most part a spiteful rivalry (κακοζηλία), pride, hatreds, calumnies, prejudices, eristic and virulent writings, and private ambitions in very many cases — as it happens — and it will have no end until, by the authority of the Most Serene Princes and by a greater force if one ever intervenes, they are coerced.

source_text: Caeterum in materia Tolerantiae mutuae, fraternaeque Concordiae, quaesitae inter Protestantium Ecclesias, non confundenda est (ut vellent) Lutheranorum, qui sic vocantur causa, cum illa hodiernorum Remonstrantium, de quorum Schismate non par Reformatis judicium fuit, & quorum Dogmata prolixe ante recensita. Minus conferenda Augustanorum Fratrum causa, in negotio Irenico, cum Pontificiorum altera, componant licet utramque Methodistae hodierni Romanenses. Unde nos utrique, & Remonstrantes & Pontificii, pridem ad Syncretismum in Religione sollicitarunt, intuitu oblatae communionis fratribus Confessionis Augustanae. Ac fecerunt Pontificii quidem, in ea Methodo quam Richelianam vocant, & quam revocavit nuper Clerus Gallicanus, in Methodo 1. inducendis nobis per Missionarios suos ad Communionem cum Rom. Ecclesia; In specie quoque urfit idem Condomiensis, nunc Meldensis Episcopus, Expositionis Catholicae seu Tridentinae, Cap. II.
english: But in the matter of mutual Tolerance and of fraternal Concord sought among the Churches of Protestants, the cause of those called Lutherans must not be confused — as some would wish — with that of today's Remonstrants, concerning whose Schism the Reformed judgment was not the same, and whose Dogmas were reviewed at length above. Still less is the cause of the Augsburg Brethren, in the irenic business, to be set beside that of the Pontiffs, though today's Roman Methodists may try to compose both. Hence both parties — Remonstrants and Pontiffs alike — have long solicited us toward Syncretism in Religion, with an eye to the communion offered to the brethren of the Augsburg Confession. And the Pontiffs have done so in that Method they call Richelian, which the Gallican Clergy lately revived, as Method 1: leading us by their Missionaries into Communion with the Roman Church. In particular the same Bishop of Condom, now of Meaux, pressed it in Chapter II of his Catholic or Tridentine Exposition.

source_text: Obtentus est, 1. Lutheranos defendere Praesentiam realem (ut vocant) Corporis Christi in Eucharistia; unde sequatur, quam tantopere refugimus, praesentis in Eucharistia Corporis adoratio. 2. Defendere eosdem dogma Ubiquitatis, ex quo sequatur omnino, Humanitatis Christi destructio: Et tamen paratos esse Reformatos illis communionem suam offerre, quia hoc destructae Humanitatis Consectarium negant; quidni & Pontificiis, Consequentias quae ex Doctrina Tridentina inferuntur, pariter refpuentibus? Sed huic vanissimae Methodo fuse, & ex professo, ivimus obviam in Stricturis nostris adversus Condomiensem tum Episcopum; editis A. 1681. Ubi nos pluribus, 1. De ratione tolerantiae & communionis qualis Fratribus Augustanae Confessionis oblata est; retorsione facta in Pontificios, tolerantiae imo humanitatis nescios, dum tamen dissensum a Rom. Ecclesia esse Fundamentalem negant. 2. Ibidem nos de dogmate Ubiquitatis, quatenus censetur convellere, aut non convellere fundamentum; facta collatione cum dogmatibus Pontificiorum controversis, eorumque praxi, longe alia ratione Christianismi essentiam perimentibus. 3. Ibi & nos de Praesentia reali ex mente Lutheranorum, & adoratione qualem probant in Eucharistia; enarrato longa serie discrimine, a dogmate Transubstantiationis, & Sacrificii Missatici, & Latriae Hostiae exhibitae, etiam extra usum Sacramenti; Praeter actus alios Idololatricos, & impense superstitiosos, in Missaticis Pontificiorum Sacris. 4. Tandem de Consequentis, quas causatur Meldensis Episcopus Reformatos non sine calumniae labe elicere ex doctrina Tridentina, pluribus nos in praefatis Stricturis.
english: The pretense was, first, that the Lutherans defend the so-called real Presence of Christ's Body in the Eucharist, from which would follow the Adoration of the Body present in the Eucharist — which we so greatly flee. Second, that they defend the dogma of Ubiquity, from which would follow altogether the destruction of Christ's Humanity: and yet the Reformed are ready to offer them their communion, because they deny that consequence of a destroyed Humanity — why then not also to Pontiffs who equally refuse the Consequences drawn from Tridentine Doctrine? But we went openly and at length against this vainest Method in our Strictures against the then Bishop of Condom, published in 1681.

There we treat at length: (1) of the reason of tolerance and of the communion offered to the brethren of the Augsburg Confession — with a retort upon Pontiffs who know nothing of tolerance, indeed of humanity, while they still deny that dissent from the Roman Church is Fundamental; (2) of the dogma of Ubiquity, how far it is held to overthrow the foundation or not — compared with the contested dogmas of the Pontiffs and with their practice, which destroy the essence of Christianity by a far other reason; (3) of real Presence in the Lutheran sense, and of the adoration they approve in the Eucharist — narrating in a long series the difference from the dogma of Transubstantiation, from the Mass Sacrifice, and from Latria of the Host shown even outside the use of the Sacrament, besides other idolatrous and intensely superstitious acts in the Pontiffs' Mass rites; (4) finally of the Consequences which the Bishop of Meaux charges the Reformed with eliciting from Tridentine doctrine not without the stain of calumny — treated by us at length in those Strictures.

source_text: Nec par sane ratio est causae Remonstranticae & Lutheranae, etiam in negotio Praedestinationis, annexorumve Capitum. Docent vel superiora, ubi suam suorumque mentem Rintelenfes Theologi explicuerunt, defensam ab iisdem postea in Apologia sua. Et appellamus in hac causa Lipsiacos, Gerhardum, Calixtum, imo Calovium in Considerat. Arminianismi, &c. sed ante omnia Lutherum ipsum. Nec enim ulla de Praedestinatione, vel de totali Impotentia servi Arbitrii, vel de Providentia Dei circa actiones malas, cum Luthero controversia fuit, doctrinam Augustini, quae & Pauli, fortiter asserente Libro de Servo Arbitrio, quem emisit contra Erasmum sub finem A. 1525. Nam in eo etiam occurrere horridiora de Decretis Divinis, & de peccandi necessitate, quam in Calvino ipso, fassi omnes ingenui, quaecunque effugia Lutheri nepotes captave-
english: Nor indeed is the Remonstrant cause and the Lutheran on equal footing, even in the business of Predestination and its annexed Heads. The points above already teach as much, where the Rinteln Theologians explained their own mind and their party's, afterward defended by them in their Apology. And in this cause we appeal to the Leipzig men, to Gerhard, to Calixtus, even to Calov in his Consideration of Arminianism, and others — but before all to Luther himself. For there was no controversy with Luther concerning Predestination, or the total Impotence of the bound Will, or God's Providence about evil actions: he strongly asserted Augustine's doctrine — which is also Paul's — in the Book on the Bondage of the Will, issued against Erasmus toward the end of 1525. For in it there occur even more dreadful things concerning the Divine Decrees and the necessity of sinning than in Calvin himself — as all candid men confess, whatever escapes Luther's grandsons may have tried to seize.

source_text: rint. Ac confirmavit postea Lutherus, luculenta Praefat. in Epist. ad Romanos, & scriptis aliis, etiam Germanicis. Nulla etiam hoc de argumento Controversia Reformatis mota, vel in Formula Torgensi, seu Libro Concordiae A. 1577. vel in Colloquio Montis-Belligartensi, vulgato A. 1587. Quin notati in Formula Concordiae Synergistae; nempe qui statuerent συνεργίαν quandam Lib. Arbitrii, & Causas Conversionis esse Spiritum S. Verbum, & Voluntatem Hominis, qui imputatus error fuit Melanchthoni. Sic exorta inter Joh. Marbachium & Hieron. Zanchium contentione, Argentinae A. 1562. & hujus doctrina acerbissime exagitata, nulla gravis expostulatio fuit in argumento de Praedestinat. In qua doctrina judicarunt Arbitri, quos inter Schmidlinus, Tubinga evocatus, non magnam diversitatem esse. Nec ante Aegid. Hunnium Wittenbergae tum docentem, A. 1580. & Georg. Mylium Jenensem, diversam sententiam a recepta illa Augustini, (cui adhaesissent Invariatae Augustanae Confess. Theologi) in Ecclesias Scholasque reductam, monuit ipse Calixtus, Animadvers. ad Confess. Thorunens.
english: And afterward Luther confirmed it in a lucid Preface to the Epistle to the Romans and in other writings, even German ones. Nor was any Controversy on this argument moved against the Reformed — neither in the Torgau Formula or Book of Concord of 1577, nor in the Montbeliard Colloquy published in 1587. On the contrary, Synergists were marked in the Formula of Concord: namely those who set a certain synergy (συνεργία) of Free Will, and held the Causes of Conversion to be the Holy Spirit, the Word, and Man's Will — which error was imputed to Melanchthon. So when contention arose at Strasbourg in 1562 between Johann Marbach and Jerome Zanchi, and Zanchi's doctrine was most bitterly harassed, there was no serious remonstrance on the Predestination argument. In that doctrine the Arbiters — among them Schmidlin summoned from Tubingen — judged there was no great diversity.

Nor, Calixtus himself warns in his Animadversions on the Thorn Confession, was a sentence different from that received Augustinian view — to which the Theologians of the Unaltered Augsburg Confession had clung — brought back into Churches and Schools before Aegidius Hunnius, then teaching at Wittenberg in 1580, and Georg Mylius of Jena.

source_text: Igitur etiamnum hodie fatentur Theologi qui a Luthero denominantur, 1. Eligi certas personas ab aeterno, non propter praevisam fidem, sed eligi in fide, seu per fidem in Christum. 2. Electionis nullam esse causam impulsivam in nobis, sed totum salutis negotium a Deo suspendi. 3. Praevideri fidem in quibusdam, sed ut ex gratia Spiritus S. ut donum Dei, quoad ejus initium, progressum, perseverantiam. 4. Mortuos nos esse in peccatis, nec ullas esse residuas vires in homine lapso ad bonum spirituale, ad actus supernaturales Conversionis. 5. Gratiam Dei re vera praevenire omnem operationem hominis, nec in hoc ullas esse vires ad Conversionem, nisi a Gratia praeventas, excitatas, & motas; ut ad primam Gratiae acceptionem, se non habeant nisi passive, quod diserte Calixtus. 6. Non dari illam nisi ex decreto, de danda Gratia efficaci ad credendum; nec Deum quicquam praevidere, nisi dependenter a se ut causa prima, minus praevidere bonum spirituale in nobis. 7. Fidem esse fiduciam divinae gratiae, seu remissionis peccatorum, per & propter Christum, contradistinctam jam operibus, in negotio Justificationis; darique salutis subjectivam certitudinem. 8. Electionem certarum Personarum esse aeternam, & immutabilem, adeoque Electos κατὰ πρόγνωσιν finaliter excidere non posse, ex hypothesi divinae Praescientiae, quae sit infallibilis. 9. Quoad Reprobationem, quanquam haud aliam velint, quam secundum praescientiam finalis Impoenitentiae, tamen non negant hoc modo aeternam eam esse; Aeternam adeo discretionem esse electorum a reprobis, hujus discretionis comparativae causam, esse Dei beneplacitum; Praescientiam etiam reproborum esse infallibilem. 10. Denique omnem se damnare Pelagianismum, Semi-Pelagianismum. Ut a scopo & mente Remonstrantium longe abfuisse appareant genuini Lutheri nepotes.
english: Therefore even now today the Theologians named from Luther confess: (1) that certain persons are elected from eternity, not because of foreseen faith, but elected in faith, or through faith in Christ; (2) that Election has no impulsive cause in us, but the whole business of salvation hangs upon God; (3) that faith is foreseen in some, yet as from the grace of the Holy Spirit, as God's gift, as to its beginning, progress, and perseverance; (4) that we are dead in sins, and that there are no residual powers in fallen man toward spiritual good, toward the supernatural acts of Conversion; (5) that God's Grace truly precedes every operation of man, and that in him there are no powers toward Conversion except those prevented, excited, and moved by Grace — so that toward the first reception of Grace they have themselves only passively, as Calixtus expressly says;

(6) that that grace is not given except from a decree of giving efficacious Grace for believing; nor does God foresee anything except dependently on Himself as first cause, still less foresee spiritual good in us; (7) that Faith is trust in divine grace, or in the remission of sins, through and on account of Christ, already contradistinguished from works in the business of Justification; and that a subjective certainty of salvation is given; (8) that the Election of certain Persons is eternal and immutable, and so the Elect according to foreknowledge (κατὰ πρόγνωσιν) cannot finally fall away, on the hypothesis of divine Foreknowledge, which is infallible; (9) as to Reprobation, although they want no other than according to foresight of final Impenitence, yet they do not deny that in this way it is eternal — that the distinction of elect from reprobate is eternal, that the cause of this comparative distinction is God's good pleasure, and that Foreknowledge of the reprobate also is infallible; (10) finally that they condemn every Pelagianism and Semi-Pelagianism. So genuine grandsons of Luther appear to have stood far from the aim and mind of the Remonstrants.

source_text: Ex quibus planum fit, quam nulla inter se necessitate colligentur Augustanae Confessionis Theologi cum Remonstrantibus, & quam nihil Dordracenis negotii fuerit cum hujusmodi Fratribus, dum recoctum hi Pelagianismum nobiscum arcerent. Planum etiam, quam proclive foret fraterne conspirare Lutheranos vulgo cum Reformatis, si pro suggestu, missis litigiis, missis etiam apud Principes & Magistratus iniquis delationibus, istos intra terminos consisterent. Accedit, dissensum in causa Praedestinationis nullam dedisse causam Schismati, nec ea de re contentionem cum Luthero fuisse, ex modo dictis. Cumprimis vero nullum cum Socinianis commercium est Fratribus Augustanae Societatis, uti est hodiernis Remonstrantibus ex superiore historia, a pag. 242. Sic nulla apud Lutheranos, qui dicuntur, Fundamentalium palliatio errorum, vel excusatio, aut imminutio, in Capitibus de S. Trinitate, aeterna Divinitate & Generatione Filii, adoratione Spiritus S. Peccato Originis, Satisfactione Christi, Justificatione per fidem solam, &c.
english: From which things it is plain how no necessity binds together the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession with the Remonstrants, and how the men of Dordrecht had nothing to do with brethren of that sort, while these latter barred recocted Pelagianism together with us. It is also plain how ready it would be for Lutherans in the common sense to conspire fraternally with the Reformed, if from the pulpit — dropping quarrels, and dropping also unjust delations before Princes and Magistrates — those men would keep within bounds. Add that dissent in the cause of Predestination gave no cause to the Schism, nor was there contention with Luther on that matter, from what has just been said. And above all, the Brethren of the Augsburg Society have no commerce with the Socinians, as today's Remonstrants do from the history above, from page 242.

So likewise among those called Lutherans there is no palliation of Fundamental errors, nor excuse, nor diminution, in the Heads concerning the Holy Trinity, the eternal Divinity and Generation of the Son, the adoration of the Holy Spirit, Original Sin, the Satisfaction of Christ, Justification by faith alone, and so on.

source_text: Ut si quis remanet Fratrum consensus cum Quinquarticulanis Theologis, dissensus vero a Dordracenis, praecipue in his consistat, 1. In phrasi, ubi de electione vel reprobatione loquuntur Lutherani, (nec ex Luthero tamen) tanquam ex praevisione fidei, vel ex praescientia incredulitatis. Πρόγνωσιν licet a προορισμῳ non distingueret Concordiae Formula, ut Peucero pridem observatum, in Confessione exhibita ab Hospiniano. 2. In ordine Decretorum recensendo; praeposito scilicet Decreto conditionato; de omnium salute, redemptione, vocatione ad fidem, &c. modo huic non desint. 3. In objecto Mortis Christi, qui sint omnes & singuli homines, tam electi quam reprobi. 4. In modo operationis Gratiae asserendo, quae respectu omnium sit etiam interna, & efficax ex parte Dei, sed cui homines resistant, & obicem ponant; licet aliis impotentiam Lib. Arbitrii ad Conversionis opus fateantur. 5. In asserta possibili apostasia sanctorum, quam nec negant Reformati, si sancti in se ipsis considerentur: Negant vero ex altera parte iidem Fratres, si considerentur electi secundum praescientiam Dei infallibilem. 6. Denique in detorta subinde vel sinistre accepta sententia Reformatorum, & afficta Praedestinatiana Haeresi, qualis olim afficta Augustino, Godeschalco, & ὁμοδόξοις fuit. Sed judiciorum ac suspicionum hac iniquitate deinceps valere jussa, in caeteris quae relinquunt discrimen vel in phrasi, vel in methodo concipiendi Decreta, vel in rei modo, aut extensione, aut circumstantiis, salva utrobique substantia (puta Mortis Christi, aut Gratiae praevenientis & confirmantis, aut Fidei justificantis, aut S. Baptismi) per communes Protestantium Adversarios eversa, facilis consociatio fuerit: Nec ad votorum utriusque partis complementum deerit quicquam, praeterquam optatam pacem ἵνα τελέσῃ ὁ πάντων τελειωτὴς Θεὸς, qui quotidie πληροῖ etiam τὰ παρ' ὅρκον, καὶ παρ' ἐλπίδα, ut cum Lyrico loquar.
english: So that if any consensus of the Brethren with the Quinquarticularian Theologians remains, the dissent from the men of Dordrecht consists chiefly in these: (1) In phrase, where Lutherans speak of election or reprobation (yet not from Luther) as from foresight of faith, or from foresight of unbelief — although the Formula of Concord did not distinguish πρόγνωσις from προορισμός, as Peucer long ago observed in the Confession set out by Hospinian. (2) In reviewing the order of the Decrees; namely with a conditional Decree set first — concerning the salvation of all, redemption, calling to faith, and so on — provided they are not wanting to it. (3) In the object of Christ's Death, which is all and every human being, elect as well as reprobate. (4) In asserting the mode of the operation of Grace, which with respect to all is even internal, and efficacious from God's side, yet which men resist and against which they set an obstacle — although elsewhere they confess the impotence of Free Will for the work of Conversion.

(5) In the asserted possible apostasy of the saints, which the Reformed also do not deny if the saints are considered in themselves: yet the same Brethren deny it if they are considered elect according to God's infallible foresight. (6) Finally in the Reformed sentence now and then twisted or taken in a sinister sense, and in the Predestinarian Heresy affixed to them — such as was once affixed to Augustine, to Gottschalk, and to those of like mind (ὁμοδόξοις). But once that inequity of judgments and suspicions is hereafter ordered to be of no force, in the remaining things that leave a difference either in phrase, or in the method of conceiving the Decrees, or in the mode of the matter, or its extent, or its circumstances — the substance being safe on both sides (for example Christ's Death, or preventing and confirming Grace, or justifying Faith, or Holy Baptism), overturned by the common Adversaries of Protestants — easy association will follow. Nor will anything be wanting to the complement of either party's vows, except the longed-for peace, that God the perfecter of all may complete it — who daily also fills even what is beyond oath and beyond hope, as I may speak with the Lyric poet.

source_text: Controversiarum cum Augustanae Confessionis Theologis variae constituendae Classes duae. Quaedam enim sunt cum genuinis Lutheri Discipulis, ac professis Augustanam Confessionem, etiam ut a Melanchthone recognita fuit, post Concordiam Wittenbergensem, ac saepius explicata, in specie quoad Artic. x. Ac jam solum fere caput controversum remanet de Cena Domini; praesentiam Corporis Christi efferente his verbis Melanchthone, in posteriori Confessione, quam alii Variatam dicunt privata auctoritate Philippi: Quod cum pane & vino vere exhibeantur Corpus & Sanguis Christi vescentibus in Cena Domini. Habuerat editio prior, Anni 1530. Quod Corpus & Sanguis Christi vere adsint, & distribuantur vescentibus in Cena Domini, addita improbatione secus sentientium. Quod unum vivo Luthero fuit μῆλον ἔριδος, primo cum Carolostadio, ex ante dictis, deinde & cum Helvetiis, Zwinglio, Oecolampadio, ac qui his accesserunt in Reformatorum ordine. Aliae intercedunt cum discipulis J. Brentii, Jac. Andreae, M. Flaccii Illyrici, Aegid. Hunnii, &c. & quotquot subscripsere Torgensibus Articulis, scriptis primo A. 1576. Praecipuo horum architecto Jacobo Andreae Tubingensi Theologo, mox (paucis mutatis) referendorum in Librum Concordiae, seu Formulam Bergensem, A. 1577. vulgatam A. 1580. post exortas subscriptiones. Et in hac jam dogma de Ubiquitate, seu Majestate Naturae Hum. Christi in arce collocatum; admissaque etiam sola Confessio Augustana prior, Anni 1530. quam invariatam vocant! Sed & aliae sententiae definitivae in eo Libro expressae, de Controversiis, ut inter ipsos Lutheranos tum agitatis, puta Flaccianos, Wittenbergenses, Osiandristas, &c. sic & cum Calvinianis quos vocant. Quas inter illa de Praedestinatione, sed sic ibi explicata, ut sola salutis causa adeoque & electionis ponatur in Deo, non in nobis.
english: Of the Controversies with the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession, two various Classes are to be set up. For some are with the genuine Disciples of Luther, and with those who profess the Augsburg Confession even as Melanchthon recognized it after the Wittenberg Concord, and as it was often explained, especially as to Article X. And now almost the only contested head remaining is the Lord's Supper — Melanchthon expressing the presence of Christ's Body in these words in the later Confession, which others call the Variata by Philip's private authority: That with the bread and wine the Body and Blood of Christ are truly exhibited to those who eat in the Lord's Supper. The prior edition, of the year 1530, had: That the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat in the Lord's Supper, with the disapproval of those who think otherwise added. That one thing was, while Luther lived, an apple of discord (μῆλον ἔριδος) — first with Carolostadius, from what was said before, and then also with the Swiss, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, and those who joined them in the order of the Reformers.

Others intervene with the disciples of Johann Brenz, Jakob Andreae, Matthias Flacius Illyricus, Aegidius Hunnius, and others, and as many as subscribed the Torgau Articles, first written in the year 1576 — Jakob Andreae, the Tübingen Theologian, being their chief architect — soon to be referred (with few changes) into the Book of Concord, or Bergen Formula, of 1577, published in 1580 after the subscriptions had arisen. And in this the dogma of Ubiquity, or the Majesty of Christ's Human Nature, is already set in the citadel; and only the prior Augsburg Confession of the year 1530 is admitted, which they call the Unaltered! But other definitive sentences also are expressed in that Book concerning Controversies then agitated among the Lutherans themselves — for example Flaccians, Wittenbergers, Osiandrists, and so on — and likewise with those they call Calvinists. Among which is that concerning Predestination, yet explained there so that the sole cause of salvation, and therefore also of election, is placed in God, not in us.

source_text: Reclamasse adversus hanc temeritatem Electores, Principes, Theologos per Germaniam Lutheranam plurimos, in confesso est, ipsumque Danorum Regem, in specie Electorem Palatinum Ludovicum, ut nuper observatum. Et hunc in Hist. MS. Palatina notat H. Altingius, quinque reprehendisse in ea Bergensi Formula; 1. Quod Augustanam Confessionem restrinxisset ad primum Exemplar, oblatum Caesari A. 1530, exclusis Editionibus, in quibus mutatio seu variatio aliqua accesserat, majoris evidentiae causa. 2. Quod inductis nominibus Flaccianorum, Osiandristarum, Antinomorum, reliquissent alia, uti Synergistarum nomen, minus candide explicata sententia Melanchthonis. 3. Quod doctrinae de Coena Domini & Praesentia Christi in eadem Coena, subjecissent doctrinam de Ubiquitate, quam nec probasset Lutherus, nec putasset adhibendam in hac de Coena Controversia. 4. Quod phrases multas, & abstractivas voces, extra & praeter Scripturam, nec aedificationi Ecclesiae inservientes, in eam Formulam intulissent. 5. Quod Zwinglianos & Calvinianos, non sine specie tyrannidis Pontificiae, damnarent, hac dura voce adhibita, etiam non auditos, minus convictos errore. Sed vicit tandem illinc facilitas Principum, hinc adhibita a Theologis istis industria, qua, Praefatione scripta a Schmidlino & Chemnitio, cothurnis constante & captionibus, (sic judicatum) ad subscribendum illos induxerunt. Nec diu post Apologiam hujus Libri Erfordiae concinnarunt, antesignano M. Chemnitio, censendam per Academias Ecclesiasque, & edendam A. 1583. Dum in Palatinis Zach. Ursinus jussus est a Joh. Casimiro, Fratre Ludovici Elect. dare refutationem Libri, quae inter Acta Neostadiana est, & qua nihil plenius, nihil accuratius, nihil doctius, contra hos Lutheranos, unquam Scriptum editumque esse, laudatus Altingius in MS. ea Historia, quam Heidelbergae olim usurpare nobis licuit.
english: It is confessed that Electors, Princes, and very many Theologians throughout Lutheran Germany protested against this temerity — and the King of the Danes himself — especially Elector Ludwig of the Palatinate, as was lately noted. And Heinrich Alting notes him in the manuscript Palatine History as having reprehended five things in that Bergen Formula: (1) That it had restricted the Augsburg Confession to the first Exemplar offered to the Emperor in 1530, excluding Editions in which some change or variation had entered for the sake of greater evidence. (2) That after introducing the names of Flaccians, Osiandrists, and Antinomians, they had left other names — such as that of the Synergists — with Melanchthon's sentence less candidly explained. (3) That to the doctrine of the Lord's Supper and of Christ's Presence in that same Supper they had subjected the doctrine of Ubiquity, which Luther had neither approved nor thought fit to be employed in this Controversy concerning the Supper. (4) That they had brought into that Formula many phrases and abstract terms outside and beyond Scripture, and not serving the edification of the Church. (5) That they condemned Zwinglians and Calvinists — not without the appearance of Pontifical tyranny — using this hard voice, even those not heard, and still less convicted of error.

Yet at length the facility of the Princes on that side, and the industry employed by those Theologians on this, won out — by which, with a Prefation written by Schmidlin and Chemnitz, consisting of tragic buskins and captious turns (so it was judged), they induced those men to subscribe. And not long afterward they composed an Apology of this Book at Erfurt, with Martin Chemnitz as standard-bearer, to be censured through the Academies and Churches, and to be published in 1583. Meanwhile among the Palatines Zacharias Ursinus was ordered by Johann Casimir, brother of Elector Ludwig, to give a refutation of the Book, which is among the Neustadt Acts — and than which, the praised Alting says in that manuscript History which we were once permitted to use at Heidelberg, nothing fuller, nothing more accurate, nothing more learned was ever written and published against these Lutherans.

source_text: Ab eo tempore fuerunt Controversiae cum Flaccianis, & Bergensibus, horumque nepotibus, in triplici fere differentia; praeter priorem illam de Coena Domini, seu de modo percipiendi Corporis Christi in Eucharistia. I. Aliae Controversiae non ex doctrina Reformatorum natae, sed extorsionibus illius, non ex traditis, sed ex affictis, quae adeo non juris quaestiones sunt, sed facti. V. gr. An Reformati Rationem naturalem faciant Judicem sententiarum fidei; vel Philosophiam principium conclusionum Theologicarum? An statuant necessitatem absolutam actionum humanarum, fatum Stoicum, Haeresim Manichaeam, vel Praedestinatianam? An Deum adeo faciant auctorem vel causam, seu physicam, seu moralem Peccati? An negent Dei Omnipotentiam, in Cap. praesentiae Corporalis, vel Misericordiam, in altero Gratiae Universalis? Sic an dividant Naturas Christi, aut cum Nestorio sentiant, quia Naturas in unitate Personae distinguunt? An vim & efficaciam Mortis Christi tollant? An Sacramenta sint ipsis nuda signa, nudae tesserae? An praesentiam Christi in Eucharistia omnem negent, oppugnent? An negent gratiam omnem Infantibus, aut semen fidei, gratiae, regenerationis, &c. Et hae Controversiae ut calumniosae, sic re ipsa sunt nullae, circa quas tamen operosi sunt ac fere toti Eckhardus, Meisnerus, Musaeus, Gerhardus, Hutterus, Mentzerus, Calovius, Dorschaus, Danhawerus, Schlüsselburgius, &c. II. Aliae quaedam minus principales aut momentosae sunt, puta, de Ritibus quibusdam & Ceremoniis Adiaphoris, circa Baptismum, Eucharistiam, Confessionem, Genuflexionem ad nomen Jesu, vel ornatum Templorum, usum Imaginum, Festorum, &c. Quos Ritus nec ab omnibus Lutheranis perinde adhiberi constat, ortos partim ex Lutheri in Carolostadium animis, in causa Imaginum, &c. III. Aliae denique Controversiae magis reales sunt, seu principales, de Doctrinae capitibus, quae sunt post Lutherum exorta: Puta de Persona Christi, & Omnipraesentia Naturae Humanae; de Praedestinatione & annexis; tandemque de Baptismo. Et has potissimum hoc in loco attendimus, ut & Controversiam Eucharisticam, quo de Statu Controversiae nostris Auditoribus constet. Videndae plenius apud Ursinum, Polanum, Zanchium, Sadeelem, Bezam, Danaeum, Pareum, Wendelinum, Altingium, Massonium, J. Crocium, Maresium, Hoornbekium, Hottingerum, Arnoldum, Heideggerum, &c.
english: From that time there have been Controversies with the Flaccians, and with the Bergen men, and with their grandsons, in nearly a threefold difference — besides that prior one concerning the Lord's Supper, or the mode of receiving Christ's Body in the Eucharist. I. Other Controversies not born from the doctrine of the Reformers, but from extortions of it — not from things handed down, but from things affixed — which are therefore not questions of right, but of fact. For example: Whether the Reformed make natural Reason the Judge of sentences of faith; or Philosophy the principle of Theological conclusions? Whether they assert an absolute necessity of human actions, a Stoic fate, a Manichaean or Predestinarian Heresy? Whether they so make God the author or cause — physical or moral — of Sin? Whether they deny God's Omnipotence, in the Chapter of Corporal presence, or His Mercy, in the other Chapter of Universal Grace? Likewise whether they divide the Natures of Christ, or think with Nestorius, because they distinguish the Natures in the unity of the Person? Whether they take away the force and efficacy of Christ's Death? Whether the Sacraments are to them bare signs, bare tokens? Whether they deny and assail every presence of Christ in the Eucharist? Whether they deny all grace to Infants, or the seed of faith, of grace, of regeneration, and so on? And these Controversies, as they are calumnious, so in the matter itself they are null — about which nevertheless Eckhard, Meisner, Musaeus, Gerhard, Hutter, Mentzer, Calov, Dorsch, Danhauer, Schlüsselburg, and others are laborious and almost wholly occupied.

II. Certain others are less principal or weighty — for example, concerning certain Adiaphorous Rites and Ceremonies around Baptism, the Eucharist, Confession, kneeling at the name of Jesus, or the adornment of Temples, the use of Images, of Feasts, and so on. Which Rites it is agreed are not equally employed by all Lutherans, having arisen partly from Luther's temper against Carolostadius in the cause of Images, and so on. III. Finally other Controversies are more real, or principal, concerning Heads of Doctrine that arose after Luther: for example concerning the Person of Christ, and the Omnipresence of the Human Nature; concerning Predestination and its annexed heads; and at last concerning Baptism. And these we chiefly attend to in this place, as also the Eucharistic Controversy, so that the State of the Controversy may be clear to our Hearers. They are to be seen more fully in Ursinus, Polanus, Zanchi, Sadeel, Beza, Danaeus, Pareus, Wendelin, Alting, Masson, Johann Crocius, Maresius, Hoornbeek, Hottinger, Arnold, Heidegger, and others.

source_text: COENA DOMINI, Unde initium Schismatis. 1. An verba institutionis Eucharisticae, Hoc est Corpus meum, &c. Hoc est Sanguis meus, uti seria sunt, & verissima, & verba Testamenti Christi, ita sint proprie & literaliter intelligenda, plane κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν? Non vero in sensu metonymico & sacramentali, eodemque in Scriptura S. & in locutionibus Sacramentalibus, imo & extra Sacramenta, familiari, Gen. XVII. 10, XLI. 26. Ex. XII. 11. XXXI. 13. 16. quo scilicet rerum signatarum nomina, puta Corpus & Sanguis, signis ipsis ac sigillis tribuuntur, Pani & Vino? An adeo sensus verborum sit iste: Hoc quod vobis do, est vere ac substantialiter Corpus meum, naturale illud quod pro vobis traditur; Vel, in, cum, sub hoc Pane est Corpus meum, ἀδιαστάτως secundum indistantiam loci, atque essentialiter seu corporaliter ibi praesens; Ut adeo Panis dicatur esse Corpus Christi, non quidem Transsubstantiatione, non etiam sola Significatione vel Obsignatione; sed Consubstantiatione, quadam, seu reali & occulta inclusione? Affirm. Luth. Negant Reform.
english: THE LORD’S SUPPER — Where the schism took its start.

1. Should the words of Eucharistic institution — "This is my Body," and so on; "This is my Blood" — because they are serious, entirely true, and the words of Christ’s Testament, be taken properly and literally, plainly according to the letter? Or should they rather be taken in a metonymic and sacramental sense — the sense Holy Scripture already uses in sacramental speech and even outside the Sacraments (Genesis 17:10; 41:26; Exodus 12:11; 31:13, 16) — so that the names of the things signified (Body and Blood) are given to the signs and seals themselves (bread and wine)?

Or does the sense run this way instead: what I give you is truly and substantially my Body, that natural Body delivered for you; or else, in, with, and under this bread my Body is present without spatial distance, essentially or bodily there — so that bread is called Christ’s Body neither by Transsubstantiation nor by signification or sealing alone, but by a kind of Consubstantiation, a real and hidden inclusion?
Lutherans say yes; the Reformed say no.

source_text: HYPOTHESES Virorum fratrum, quas enarrasse hoc loco suffecerit, prolixe a Theologis expensas, fuere, ex. gr. Sensum figuratum evertere scilicet veritatem verborum: Illud, est Corpus, necessario innuere esse reale, substantiale: Christum in prima Coena fuisse corporaliter praesentem, Ergo & in Pane & Vino, qui tamen Christus erat extra Panem; Ergo corporaliter praesentem post ascens. in Caelos: Corpus Christi manducari in Coena, ergo ut ἀδιαστάτως praesens, nec Corpus posse esse praesens spirituali modo: Manducationem sacramentalem plus dicere quam spiritualem; E. dicere manducat. oralem Corporis veri & naturalis: Tutius esse adhaerere sensui literali, a quo scil. recedant Reformati, & temere quidem: Institutum quoque his verbis Testamentum, vel Pactum, Ergo verbis propriis, quia haec sola clara sint; quasi non institutum signum Foederis vel Testamenti, ut nos ex Matth. XXVI. 28. Luc. XXII. 20. Ita supponunt τὸ κρινόμενον, nempe explicari a se verba Institutionis (Hoc est Corpus meum) in sensu literali, nativo, proprio, perspicuo, dum ita reddunt: In vel sub hoc, scil. composito, complexo (Panis & Corporis) continetur Corpus meum, hoc ipsum Corpus quod vobis adest, sed illocale, &c.
english: Our brethren’s hypotheses — enough to list them here; theologians have weighed them at length — include claims such as these: a figurative sense destroys the truth of the words; "is Body" must mean something real and substantial; Christ was bodily present at the first Supper, and therefore also in the bread and wine even while he stood outside the bread, and therefore remains bodily present after the ascension into the heavens; Christ’s Body is eaten in the Supper and so must be present without spatial distance, since a body cannot be present in a spiritual mode; sacramental eating means more than spiritual eating and therefore means oral eating of the true and natural Body; clinging to the literal sense is safer, and the Reformed leave it rashly; what these words institute is a Testament or Covenant and therefore must use proper words alone, as if clarity belonged only to proper speech — as though no sign of the Covenant or Testament were instituted, which is how we read Matthew 26:28 and Luke 22:20.

In that way they beg the question under judgment. They treat the Institution words ("This is my Body") as self-explanatory in a literal, native, proper, and clear sense, yet they paraphrase them as: in or under this — namely the composed complex of bread and Body — my Body is contained, this very Body present to you, yet illocal, and so forth.

source_text: Licet Lutherani negent 1. Panem esse ipsum Corpus Christi, quod sonat sensus literalis. 2. Itidem negent Hoc referri ad Panem, ad id quod Christus monstrabat, quod vult litera. 3. To Est, sit illis inest, subest, continetur, &c. contra literam. 4. Corpus intelligant invisibile, illocale, invita rursum litera. 5. Mutent subjectum in locum praedicati, v. gr. Corpus meum est in vel sub hoc pane, &c. 6. Fateantur locutionem esse Synecdochicam, per Synecdochen contenti, vel totius, &c. sed quae amittat (ajunt) nomen figurae; alii inusitatam locutionem esse, &c. 7. Plurimum a se invicem discesserint in reddendis his verbis; dum alii hoc de pane; alii complexe de pane & Corpore; alii adverbialiter, Ecce Corpus meum; alii active, haec tota actio, &c.
english: Yet the Lutherans deny (1) that the Bread is itself Christ's Body. Which is what the literal sense sounds. (2) likewise that This refers to the Bread, to what Christ was showing. Which is what the letter wants. (3) for them the word is becomes is in, is under, is contained, and so on. Against the letter. (4) they take Body as invisible and illocal. Again against the letter's will. (5) they shift the subject into the place of the predicate, for example My Body is in or under this bread, and so on. (6) they confess the way of speaking is synecdochic, by synecdoche of the contained or of the whole, and so on. Yet a figure which (they say) loses the name of figure; others call it an unusual locution, and so on. (7) they have parted far from one another in rendering these words: some take this of the bread; others complexly of bread and Body; others adverbially, Behold my Body; others actively, this whole action, and so on.

source_text: Caeterum non de re ipsa, praesentia Corporis Christi in S. Coena aut manducatione illius, sed de modo utriusque, controversia est. Inclusio vero Corporis Christi, manente panis substantia, ut ἀδιαστάτως praesentis, dicta Consubstantiatio, alias Coexistentia, olim Impanatio, a Berengarianis temporibus, nonnullis excogitata fuit, vel ex Lombardo Sentent. L. IV. D. xi. C. 4. & a Petro de Alliaco Cardinali Camerac. probata; quam Transsubstantiationi Lutherus praetulit, licet in semet explicando varius, ut fuse Hospinianus Hist. Sacrament. Parte II. p. 7. & seq. Utinam vero Lutherus adhaesisset sententiae, expressae illi A. 1519. ante certamen Sacramentar. Concione Germ. De Sacramento Veri Corporis Christi, &c. Tomo I. Jen. fol. 201. 202. &c. Sacramentum Corporis Christi tria habet quae sciri debent: Primum est sacramentum, sive signum quod externum & visibile est, in forma Panis & Vini: Alterum, significatio hujus sacramenti, quae debet esse interna & Spiritualis, &c. Tertium, fides quae debet utrumque conjungere in usu sacramenti; Explicata deinceps κοινωνία Paulina. 1. Cor. X. cujus certum signum accipiamus in Sacramento Corporis & Sang. Christi. Adde Artic. XII. Confess. August. Sacramenta instituta esse ut sint signa & testimonia Voluntatis Dei erga nos, proposita ad excitandam & confirmandam fidem, &c. Quae credat promissionibus quae per Sacramenta exhibentur & ostenduntur.
english: What remains of the dispute is not the thing itself — whether Christ’s Body is present in the Holy Supper, or whether it is eaten — but the mode of both.

Some devised an inclusion of Christ’s Body that leaves the substance of the bread intact and treats the Body as present without spatial distance. That teaching goes by Consubstantiation, also Coexistence, and formerly Impanation. It arose in Berengarian times, or was drawn from Lombard’s Sentences, Book IV, Distinction 11, Chapter 4, and Peter of Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, approved it. Luther preferred it to Transsubstantiation, though his own explanations varied — Hospinian’s History of the Sacraments, Part II, from page 7 onward, treats the shifts at length.

How much better if Luther had held to what he himself said in 1519, before the Sacramentarian contest, in the German sermon On the Sacrament of the True Body of Christ (Jena, Volume I, folio 201–202 and following): three things in the Sacrament of Christ’s Body ought to be known. First, the sacrament or sign, external and visible, under the form of bread and wine. Second, the signification of that sacrament, which ought to be internal and spiritual. Third, faith, which ought to join both in the sacrament’s use. He then explains Paul’s κοινωνία in 1 Corinthians 10, of which we receive a sure sign in the Sacrament of Christ’s Body and Blood.

Add Article XII of the Augsburg Confession: the Sacraments were instituted as signs and testimonies of God’s will toward us, set forth to awaken and confirm faith — faith that should believe the promises the Sacraments exhibit and show.

source_text: II. An verum & substantiale Corpus Christi, una cum Pane, & Sanguis una cum Vino in usu Sacramenti, jubente ita Christo in Institutione S. Coenae: ore corporis ab unoquoque, tam fideli quam infideli, revera accipiatur & manducetur; utpote quae unita sint physice, ἀδιαστάτως, & per συνουσίαν, adeoque eodem oris instrumento percipienda? An vero quemadmodum Symbola ipsa, quae dicuntur Corpus & Sanguis Christi metonymice, & figurative (ut calix dicitur Novum Testamentum Luc. XXII. 20.) sane oraliter ac proprie manducantur; ita res iis Symbolis significata, scil. verum Corpus & Sanguis Christi, manducentur nonnisi spiritualiter & improprie, nempe ore fidei (per Sacramentum & Memoriale excitatae) a vere fidelibus percepta & apprehensa? Ut tamen utraque manducatio, tum sacramentalis, ipsius Sacramenti, ipsorum symbolorum Corporis Christi, tum Spiritualis veri Corporis fide apprehensi, sint necessario conjuncta in fidelibus, debito modo manducantibus: Qui dum ore manducant Panem Domini, quod commune est Infidelibus, simul actu verae fidei, accedente virtute vivifica Spiritus S. Joh. VI. 63. manducant Panem Dominum, seu fiunt spiritualiter κοινωνοὶ participes Corporis Christi pro nobis Crucifixi, omniumque quae inde fluunt Beneficiorum, 1. Cor. X. 16? Prius Affirm. Luth. Post. Reform.
english: II. Next: in the use of the Sacrament, when Christ so commands in the Institution of the Holy Supper, is the true and substantial Body of Christ taken together with the Bread, and the Blood together with the Wine, truly received and eaten by the bodily mouth of every communicant — the faithful and the unfaithful alike — because they are joined physically, without spatial distance, and by co-presence, and therefore must be taken by that same instrument of the mouth?

Or is it rather this way: the Symbols themselves, called Christ's Body and Blood by metonymy and figure (as the cup is called the New Testament in Luke 22:20), are eaten orally and in the proper sense; yet the reality those Symbols signify — the true Body and Blood of Christ — is eaten only spiritually and in an improper sense, namely by the mouth of faith awakened through the Sacrament and Memorial, and is perceived and laid hold of by the truly faithful alone?

Still, in those who eat rightly, the two eatings must go together: the sacramental eating of the Sacrament itself (of the symbols of Christ's Body), and the Spiritual eating of the true Body laid hold of by faith. So while they eat with the mouth the Bread of the Lord — something Unbelievers also do — they at the same moment, by a true act of faith and with the life-giving power of the Holy Spirit (John 6:63), eat the Bread who is the Lord, or become spiritual sharers (κοινωνοί) in Christ's Body crucified for us and in every Benefit that flows from it (1 Corinthians 10:16). Lutherans affirm the first alternative; the Reformed affirm the second.

source_text: Precariae Hypotheses prioris afferti fuerunt: 1. Hunc manducationis oralis, etiam ab Infidelibus, modum, in Augustana Confessione, etiam Invariata quam vocant, Philippo primum conscripta & recognita a Principibus & Theologis Wittenbergae A. 1531. fuisse expressum. Imo haec nonnisi indefinite Artic. X. Quod Corpus & Sanguis Christi vere adsint, & cum Pane & Vino distribuantur vescentibus in Coena Domini: Sed modo manducationis non expresso, nec subjecto Infidelium. Quin haud obscure subintellectum, exhiberi Corpus & Sang. Christi vescentibus modo debito, & in fide. 2. Praesens esse Corpus Christi in Eucharistia localiter, ἀδιαστάτως, quod nec Confessio dixit, nec Lutherus, nec Melanchthon, hic alienissimus a dogmate Omnipraesentia vel Ubiquitatis Corporis Christi. 3. Non alium concipi posse manducationis modum respectu essentialis Corporis Christi, nisi qui fiat oraliter, seu ore corporis; contra quam visum est in Statu Controv. Nec sane Christus in Instit. Coenae dixit: ore comedite hoc Corpus quod praesens loquebatur. Sed de pane ita comedendo dixit. Nec ore bibite hunc meum Sanguinem, qui nondum effusus sed adhuc effundendus, non sane tum ore hauriendus, bene Calix. Nec minus spiritualis manducatio vera est, licet figurata, hanc unam probante Christo Joh. VI. 55. 63. argumento etiam ab ascensione sua petito, vers. 62. Nec τὸ edere relate ad objectum fidei, aliud notare potuit quam credendi actum, expressum etiam per videre, induere, venire, &c. Nec Christus talis cibus esse potuit, qui εἰς τὴν κοιλίαν χωρεῖ, &c. Matth. XV. 17. uti nec manducare seipsum, in prima illa Coena. Nec minus spiritualis manducatio concipiatur, quam altera nativitas, Joh. III. 3. 5. visio Abrah. Joh. VIII. 56. scissio cordis, Joel. II. 13. indutio Christi Rom. XIII. 14. &c. unio cum Christo Joh. VI. 56. &c. 4. Supponunt pariter Luther. unionem Corporis & Panis per coexistentiam, qualiter vinum in poculo est, aqua in vase, &c. Quod ἄγραφον, ἀντίγραφον, Corpore sane Christi tum a Pane separato. 5. Supponunt, eodem instrumento manducari rem terrenam & caelestem, Panem & Corpus, signum & signatum; quasi non sit os fidei, uti est os corporis.
english: For that first claim, precarious supporting premises have been advanced. First: that this oral mode of eating — even by Unbelievers — was set down in the Augsburg Confession, and even in the so-called Invariata, which Philip first wrote and the Princes and Theologians recognized at Wittenberg in 1531. In fact Article X speaks only indefinitely: That Christ's Body and Blood are truly present, and with Bread and Wine are distributed to those eating in the Lord's Supper. It does not express the mode of eating, nor name Unbelievers as the eaters. Underneath, rather, it is fairly plain that Christ's Body and Blood are exhibited to those who eat in the due mode and in faith.

Second: that Christ's Body is present in the Eucharist in a local way, without spatial distance. Neither the Confession, nor Luther, nor Melanchthon said that — and Melanchthon here stands farthest from any dogma of the Omnipresence or Ubiquity of Christ's Body. Third: that, for Christ's essential Body, no mode of eating can be conceived except oral eating with the bodily mouth — which cuts against what the State of the Controversy has already shown. Christ in the Institution did not say, Eat this Body with the mouth — the Body that was present and speaking. He spoke of eating the bread that way. He did not say, Drink this my Blood with the mouth — Blood not yet poured out, still to be poured out, and so not then drawn by the mouth; the Cup, rather. Spiritual eating is no less true for being figurative. Christ proves that one eating in John 6:55 and 63, and draws an argument from His ascension in verse 62. Related to the object of faith, eating can mean nothing but the act of believing — also spoken of as seeing, putting on, coming, and the like. Christ could not be food that goes into the belly (Matthew 15:17), any more than He could eat Himself at that first Supper. Spiritual eating is no harder to conceive than the other birth (John 3:3, 5), Abraham's seeing (John 8:56), the rending of the heart (Joel 2:13), putting on Christ (Romans 13:14), and union with Christ (John 6:56), and so on.

Fourth: the Lutherans likewise assume a union of Body and Bread by coexistence, as wine sits in a cup or water in a vessel. That is unwritten, and against what is written — Christ's Body then being separate from the Bread. Fifth: they assume the earthly thing and the heavenly thing are eaten by one and the same instrument — Bread and Body, sign and thing signed — as though there were no mouth of faith beside the mouth of the body.

source_text: CONTROVERSIAE POST LUTHERUM NATAE. De Providentia Dei, Praedestinatione, & Annexis Capitibus. III. I. De Deo auctore scilicet Peccati a Reformatis constituto, nempe 1. Ex voluntate εὐδοκίας seu beneplaciti permissivi, a Luthero tam luculenter asserti, non negantibus Filiis ingenuis; 2. Ex necessitate hypothetica seu futuritionis & eventûs, fluente ex infallibili προγνώσει, tùm & necessitate immutabilitatis quam ursit acerrimè Lutherus, ex immutabili ac imperescrutabili Dei beneplacito, consilio, voluntate, dispositione; etiam in Induratione Pharaonis, Proditione Judae, &c. 3. Ex modo Providentiae ejusdem, minimè otiosae aut inefficacis, (Concursum vocant) circa actiones peccato infectas, ut actiones sunt, necessarias rursum ipsi Luthero, quamvis non necessitate coactionis, Libro de Servo Arbitr. p. 67. 68. &c.
english: CONTROVERSIES BORN AFTER LUTHER. On God's Providence, Predestination, and the heads annexed to them.

III. First: whether the Reformed make God the author of Sin — namely (1) from the will of εὐδοκία, that is of permissive good-pleasure, which Luther asserted so clearly that his own candid sons do not deny it; (2) from a hypothetical necessity, or necessity of futurition and of the event, flowing from infallible foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις), and also from that necessity of immutability which Luther pressed hardest, drawn from God's immutable and unsearchable good-pleasure, counsel, will, and disposition — even in the hardening of Pharaoh, the betrayal of Judas, and the like; (3) from the mode of that same Providence, least idle or ineffective (they call it Concurrence) around actions infected by sin, as actions, which again Luther himself treats as necessary, though not by a necessity of compulsion — On the Bondage of the Will, pages 67–68, and so on.

source_text: Redit non tàm vera aliqua Controversia, quam infelix nonnullorum Calumnia, communis jam istis cum Pontif. & Remonstrantibus. Vide πρῶτα ψεύδη prolixè suprâ ad Controvers. cum Remonstr. VII. XV. XVIII. XIX. XXII.
english: What comes back is not so much any true Controversy as an unhappy Calumny of a few — already shared by these men with the Papal party and with the Remonstrants. See the first falsehoods (πρῶτα ψεύδη) treated at length above in the Controversy with the Remonstrants, heads VII, XV, XVIII, XIX, and XXII.

source_text: Offenderunt Viri ad phrases nonnullas, excerptas ex scriptis Zwinglii, Martyris, Calvini, Bezae, Zanchii, Rennecheri, Piscatoris, &c. quibus illi Theologi cum Scripturâ S. voluerunt 1. Providentiam Dei efficacem circa mala, & malos, ex phrasibus, indurandi, excæcandi, indendi Spiritum mendacii, tradendi in reprobum sensum, callum obducendi, mittendi ἐνέργειαν efficaciam erroris, &c. 2. Motionem causarum peccantium vel impulsionem, non certè moralem, sed physicam, ut qui omnes in Deo movemur, prout misit Josephum, Gen. XLV. 7. L. 20, impulit Simehum ad maledicendum 2. Sam. XVI. 10. Prophetas Achabi ad decipiendum, mentiendum, Reg. XXII. 22. 23. &c. 3. Tandem actus Dei, in hac omni Providentia circa malos, judiciales & penales, seu in poenam delicti proprii in Pharaone, Judaeis incredulis, Juda proditore, &c. seu in poenam delicti alieni, qualis fuit incestus Absalomi, Schisma Jeroboami, spiritus mendax inducturus Achabum, &c.
english: Men took offense at certain phrases drawn from the writings of Zwingli, Martyr, Calvin, Beza, Zanchi, Rennecher, Piscator, and others. By those phrases the Theologians meant, with Holy Scripture, three things.

First: God's efficacious Providence around evils and around the wicked — spoken of in the biblical phrases of hardening, of blinding, of sending a lying spirit, of handing over into a reprobate mind (Romans 1:28), of drawing a callus over, of sending the ἐνέργεια — the working — of error (2 Thessalonians 2:11), and the like.
