Second: a motion, or impulse, of sinning causes — not a merely moral one, but a physical one — seeing that in God we all are moved: as when He sent Joseph (Genesis 45:7; 50:20), drove Shimei to curse (2 Samuel 16:10), and drove Ahab's prophets to deceive and to lie (1 Kings 22:22–23), and so on.

Third: God's acts in this whole Providence around the wicked are judicial and penal — either as penalty for one's own crime, as in Pharaoh, in the unbelieving Jews, in Judas the traitor, and the like; or as penalty for another's crime, such as Absalom's incest, Jeroboam's schism, and the lying spirit that was to lead Ahab on, and so on.

source_text: Sed benè est, praeter Scripturam expressam, tot locis & exemplis, conferri posse phrases nostratium Theologorum, cum illis Lutheri, in Libro de Servo Arbitrio, & in Epistolam ad Romanos, atque alibi; aut cum illis Phil. Melanchthonis in Locis Commun. & in Epistolam ad Romanos, &c. Quarum si accusant fratres Lutherani invidiosam interpretationem, addita emollitione Verborum Lutheri, ut ex. gr. factum a Sebastiano Schmidio, Argentinensi Theol. Notis in Librum de Servo Arbitrio, A. 1664. quidni quod juris sibi statuunt, idem nobis permittunt, in reddendis phrasibus & explicanda mente Zwinglii, Calvini, Martyris, Bezae, &c.? Quod fecere, praeter Massonium, Anatomiae Germanicae Parte I. & II. Pareum in Irenico, p. 249. Wendelinum in Exercitat. Theologicis, Exercit. XXVI. & sequent. Hottingerum, Hist. Eccles. T. VIII. a p. 640. &c. sic in ipsis Lutheranis, Rintelenses nuper Theologi, de quibus suprâ, in Epist. Apologetica ad Doctores Wittenberg. Ubi Calvinum excusant, quòd aeque Deum auctorem peccati fecerint, duris suis verbis, Martinus Lutherus & Philippus Melanchthon, in C. VIII. Ep. ad Romanos, &c.
english: But there is this comfort: beside express Scripture in so many places and examples, the phrases of our Theologians can be set beside Luther's — in On the Bondage of the Will, in his work on the Epistle to the Romans, and elsewhere — or beside Philip Melanchthon's in the Common Places and on Romans, and so on.

If Lutheran brethren charge an invidious reading of those phrases, and then soften Luther's own words — as Sebastian Schmid of Strasbourg did, for example, in his Notes on the Bondage of the Will in 1664 — why should the right they claim for themselves not be allowed to us as well, when we render the phrases and explain the mind of Zwingli, Calvin, Martyr, Beza, and the rest?

That work has been done, besides Masson's German Anatomy, Parts I and II, by Pareus in the Irenicum, page 249; by Wendelin in the Theological Exercises, Exercise XXVI and following; by Hottinger in the Church History, Volume VIII, from page 640 onward; and so on. Even among the Lutherans themselves the recent Rinteln Theologians — already mentioned above — do it in their Apologetic Letter to the Wittenberg Doctors. There they excuse Calvin, because Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon, by their own harsh words on Romans chapter 8, equally made God the author of sin, and so on.

source_text: II. An sit in Deo Voluntas generalis, seu antecedens, servandi omnes & singulos homines; eademque non quae dicitur voluntas signi, verbo suo quibusvis promiscuè viam salutis significans, quosvis sine discrimine invitans ad agnitionem veritatis, 1. Tim. II. 4. sed voluntas propriè dicta Dei, seu beneplaciti, aeterna illa, seria, efficax; Nec absoluta tamen aut immutabilis, sed ordinata & conditionata, sub conditionibus fidei, & perseverantiae ab hominibus praestandae?
english: II. Is there in God a general will, or an antecedent will, to save all human beings and each one — and that not what is called the will of the sign, by which His word promiscuously marks the way of salvation for any, inviting any without distinction to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4), but God's will properly so called, the will of His good-pleasure: that eternal, serious, efficacious will — yet not absolute or immutable, but ordered and conditioned, under the conditions of faith and of perseverance that human beings are to perform?

source_text: Secundum quam nempè voluntatem, 1. Filium suum unigenitum dedit, qui promereretur suâ morte omnibus & singulis justitiam & vitam, universali Redemptione. 2. Offert etiam Gratiam suam omnibus & singulis, nemine excluso, per Vocationem universalem; paratus conferre omnibus eam Gratiam per ordinaria media, seu omnes vocare per Verbum Evangelii, omnes convertere, regenerare, justificare, adoptare, & glorificare, modò homines ipsi non obicem ponant? Affirm. Luth. Neg. Orth.
english: Under that will, then, two claims are put: first, that He gave His only-begotten Son so that by His death the Son would merit righteousness and life for every person, through a universal Redemption; second, that He also offers His grace to every person, excluding none, through a universal vocation, and stands ready to confer that grace on all by the ordinary means — calling all through the Word of the Gospel, and converting, regenerating, justifying, adopting, and glorifying all — if only human beings do not place an obstacle in the way.
Lutherans affirm this; the Orthodox deny it.

source_text: Iniqua accusationes in Reformat. Dissensionem Reformatorum, quoad Universalem Gratiam, Redemptionem, Vocationem, non urserant Saxonici in Colloquio Lipsiensi, Anni 1631. Rintelenses in Colloquio Cassellano (ut visum supra) fassi sunt, inconcussum esse per Reformatos, Gratiae divinae fundamentum, & convenire inter utrosque, 1. In damnandis ex aequo Pelagianis & Semi-Pelagianis dogmatis. 2. In urgendis regulis practicis, quae salutem & Justificationem suspendunt, hanc ab antecedente fide, illam etiam à perseverantia. Et certè impositum Reformatis fuit, quasi voluntatem ullam in Deo asseruerint illusoriam, respectu reproborum, quae semper seria, tùm quoad exactionem officii in Verbo; tùm, quoad propositionem unice ad salutem viae, per fidem in Christum; tum quoad veritatem individui illius nexûs, inter fidem & salutem; In quibus fundatur perpetua veritas illius effati, quicunque crediderit servabitur, &c. Quâ de re in Controv. cum primis Armin. IV. deinceps & Controv. XXXI. & nos in Vind. Bibl. ad locum Matth. XI. 28.
english: Unjust accusations against the Reformed. As for the Reformers' dissent on universal grace, redemption, and vocation: the Saxons at the Leipzig Colloquy of 1631 did not press it. The Rinteln theologians at the Cassel Colloquy (as already seen above) confessed that the foundation of divine grace stands unshaken among the Reformed, and that both sides agree (1) in equally condemning Pelagian and Semi-Pelagian dogmas, and (2) in pressing the practical rules that suspend justification on antecedent faith, and salvation also on perseverance.

And it was certainly laid on the Reformed as if they had asserted some illusory will in God toward the reprobate — whereas that will is always serious: as to the exacting of duty in the Word; as to the proposing of the one way to salvation, through faith in Christ; and as to the truth of that individual bond between faith and salvation. On these the perpetual truth of the saying rests: whoever believes will be saved, and so on.
On this see the Controversy with the early Arminians, IV, and afterward Controv. XXXI; and our own Biblical Vindication at Matthew 11:28.

source_text: Suppositum etiam fuit, quasi Reformati Redemptionis Christi aut sufficientiam negent, aut extensionem etiam ad omnes vel ad totum Mundum; Quod sanè largimur, sed in sensu Scripturae S. quoad omnes in gloriam adducendos, etiam quosvis, per totum Mundum, nullo discrimine sub Oeconomia N. T. Ità nec Vocationem negant Reformati, quae fit per Ministros Evangelii, generalem, promiscuam, nemine excluso; Cæterùm negant voluntatem Dei aeternam servandi & redimendi etiam reprobos (quos Lutherani agnoscunt κατὰ πρόγνωσιν tales) sine speciali efficacique Operatione Spiritus S., praestito ab ipsis impossibili, ex concessis. Quis verò, nisi immitis ille Conservus, aeternum damnet ista hoc sensu negantes?
english: It was also supposed that the Reformed deny either the sufficiency of Christ's redemption, or even its extension to all — or to the whole world. That we freely grant, but in Holy Scripture's sense: as to all who are to be brought into glory, even any at all, throughout the whole world, with no distinction under the New Testament economy.

So the Reformed do not deny the vocation that comes through the ministers of the Gospel — general, promiscuous, no one excluded. But they do deny an eternal will of God to save and redeem even the reprobate (whom the Lutherans themselves acknowledge as such according to foreknowledge) without the Holy Spirit's special and efficacious operation — which, from their own concessions, they have already granted is impossible.
Who then, unless that harsh fellow-servant, would damn forever those who deny these things in this sense?

source_text: Hypotheses verò quibus haec Universalitas Gratiae nititur, quamvis diversa sit ratio & scopus Lutheranorum à Remonstrantium illo, suprâ sunt ex parte indicatae, ad Articulos cum Arminianis controversos I. II. III. IV. &c. Et ex sequentibus quoque intelliguntur. In specie verò confunduntur, Dei mandata, & promissiones in Verbo, à Ministris Euangelii indiscriminatim proponendae; cum voluntate seu beneplacito in Deo omnes & singulos salvandi: Sic confusa universalitas credentium, servandorum, & universalitas hominum; omnes homines collectivè sumpti, indè ab Adamo, & quivis homines distributivè ut prolixè aliàs. Ità vocatio per naturam, quâ Deus manifestatur, ejusque communis bonitas; aut vocatio facta quandoque in majoribus; aut Hebraeorum illa quondam, celebris inter nonnullas sed paucas & viciniores Gentes; aut quae facienda per Apostolos quaquaversum fuit, generatim & promiscuè, &c. Matth. xviii. Marc. xvi. Istae (inquam) vocationes precariè trahuntur ad Vocationem universalem, omnium & singulorum hominum, & ad sufficientem oblationem mediorum salutis, &c. Sed de Vocatione illa communi, & universali etiam antè Christum exhibitum, prolixè suprâ, Controv. cum Remonstr. XXXI.
english: But the hypotheses on which this universality of grace rests — though the Lutherans' reason and aim differ from the Remonstrants' — have already been pointed out in part above, under the articles controversed with the Arminians, I, II, III, IV, and so on. They are also clear from what follows.

In particular, God's commands and the promises in the Word, which gospel ministers are to set out indiscriminately, are confused with a will or good-pleasure in God to save all and each. So the universality of believers — of those who are to be saved — is confused with the universality of human beings: all humans taken collectively from Adam onward, and any humans taken distributively, as is shown at length elsewhere.

Likewise vocation through nature, by which God is manifested, and His common goodness; or vocation given at times in the greater ones; or that former Hebrew vocation, well known among some few neighboring nations; or the vocation the Apostles were to carry out every way, generally and promiscuously, and so on (Matthew 18; Mark 16). These vocations, I say, are precariously dragged into a universal vocation of all human beings and each one, and into a sufficient offering of the means of salvation, and so on.
But of that common and universal vocation even before Christ was exhibited, see at length above, Controv. with the Remonstrants XXXI.

source_text: III. An decretum Electionis divinæ, seu Prædestinationis quorundam hominum ad salutem factum sit secundum præscientiam theoreticam fidei & perseverantiæ, tanquam causæ impulsivæ, vel potiùs conditionis antecedentis; Et hic sit sensus phrasium, electos nos esse in Christo, in fide, per fidem, non sine fide, aut sine fide neminem placere Deo, Hebr. XI. 6.? Quæ tamen ipsa Fides prævisa, sit in solidum ex gratiâ, & Dei donum, quod fatentur; verum illis destinatum quos prævidit Deus certissima præscientia, benè usuros mediis sibi concessis, & facturos quod in se est, nec spreturos gratiam per se, aut in suis majoribus, quorum ob contemptum fiat ut Gratia posteris denegetur? Ut nihilominus hæc Electio, ita facta κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, sit æterna, certa, & immutabilis? Affirm. priora Luther. Negant Reform.
english: III. Has the decree of divine election — or of the predestination of certain human beings to salvation — been made according to a theoretical foresight of faith and perseverance, as of an impulsive cause, or rather of an antecedent condition? And is this the sense of the phrases that we are elect in Christ, in faith, through faith, not without faith — or that without faith no one pleases God (Hebrews 11:6)? Yet that very faith, foreseen, is wholly from grace and is God's gift, which they confess; but it is destined for those whom God foresaw with most certain foresight as going to use well the means granted them, and going to do what lies in them, and not going to spurn grace by themselves or in their greater ones — through whose contempt grace comes to be denied to later generations. So that this election, made thus according to foreknowledge, is nonetheless eternal, certain, and immutable? The Lutherans affirm the earlier points; the Reformed deny.

source_text: Supponuntur plurima, quæ nec Lutherus, nec Melanchthon, nec horum Discipuli tradiderunt antè Ægidium Hunnius Wittenberg. & cum eo Georgium Mylium Jenensem. Undè G. Calixtus antè indicatus, Animadv. ad Confess. Thorunensem, editis A. 1654. P. 14. Nostri Majores, Invariatæ Augustanæ Confessioni adherentes, Augustini doctrinam retinuerunt, & passim docuerunt, usque ad A. MDLXXX. Ægidius Hunnius, ni fallor, primus fuit, vel certè inter primos præcipuus, qui priscám, (sic ille) & ante Augustinum in primitivâ Ecclesiâ receptam sententiam revocavit, &c. Non tamen sine difficultate, contradictione, & insimulatione Pelagianismi. Ex eo apud nostros prævaluit.
english: Many things are assumed which neither Luther, nor Melanchthon, nor their disciples taught before Aegidius Hunnius of Wittenberg and, with him, Georg Mylius of Jena. Hence Georg Calixtus, already cited, in his Animadversions on the Thorun Confession published in 1654, p. 14: "Our fathers, adhering to the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, retained Augustine's doctrine and taught it everywhere up to the year 1580. Aegidius Hunnius, unless I am mistaken, was the first — or certainly among the first the chief — who recalled the ancient opinion (as he calls it), received in the primitive Church before Augustine," and so on. Yet not without difficulty, contradiction, and the charge of Pelagianism. From then on it prevailed among our people.

source_text: ΠΡΩΤΟΝ Hunnianorum ψεῦδος fuit, quasi sequentes doctrinam Augustini velint electionem absolutam à mediis; citra intuitum fidei & perseverantiæ, quæ media sunt congrua ex parte nostri; Sic nec negant hi Electionem fundatam in merito Christi, ut medio executionis, id est, factam intuitu meriti Christi, tanquam causæ meritoriæ Vitæ & salutis; Sed Hunnio cum suis considerata fides fuit ut conditio prærequisita in eligendis, ut causa antecedens, ut qualitas eligendorum; Quæ Augustino & ὁμοψήφοις est conditio requisita in electis, simul iis cum salute decreta, tanquam medium ad salutem, & necessaria qualitas servandorum, undè dicantur servari, justificari per fidem, in Christo, id est, per Christum.
english: The first falsehood of the Hunnians was this: as if those who follow Augustine's doctrine want an election absolute from the means — apart from any regard to faith and perseverance, which are fitting means on our side. In fact these do not deny an election founded on Christ's merit as the means of execution — that is, made with a view to Christ's merit as the meritorious cause of life and salvation. But for Hunnius and his party, faith was treated as a prerequisite condition in those to be elect, as an antecedent cause, as a quality of those to be chosen. For Augustine and those who vote with him, it is a required condition in the elect, decreed for them together with salvation, as a means to salvation and a necessary quality of those who are to be saved — whence they are said to be saved and justified through faith, in Christ, that is, through Christ.

source_text: Ità supponitur, præsciri posse in his & illis fidem, antecedenter ad decretum de dandâ gratiâ fidei, quâ de re in Controv. de Scientia Media, cum Pontific. IX. cum Remonstr. XII. Ità supponunt, hanc gratiam quæ specialissima est electorum, credentium, velle Deum in omnibus operari: Ità, destinari eandem in specie, iis quos prævidet Deus usuros mediis sibi concessis, nec spreturos gratiam, per se aut per majores, &c. Undè sequi videtur, hominem se ipsum discernere, contra Paulum, & in homine esse causam dispositivam ad gratiam, vel dispositiones prævias ad fidem, contrà Lutheri constantem doctrinam, in Libris De Servo Arbitrio, De Origine Fidei, & Præfat. in Epist. ad Romanos, &c.
english: So it is supposed that faith can be foreknown in these and those before the decree to give the grace of faith — on which see the Controversy on Middle Knowledge, with the Pontificals IX and with the Remonstrants XII.

So they suppose that God wills to work in everyone this grace which is most special to the elect, to believers; and that the same grace is destined, as to its kind, to those whom God foresees will use the means granted them and will not spurn grace, by themselves or through their greater ones, and so on.

From this it seems to follow that a human being discerns himself — against Paul — and that in the human being there is a dispositive cause toward grace, or prior dispositions toward faith — against Luther's steady teaching in On the Bondage of the Will, On the Origin of Faith, and the Preface to the Epistle to the Romans, and elsewhere.

source_text: Accedit, non liberari Deum à specie iniquitatis, vel sævitiæ, qui ob spretam fidem à Majoribus, fraudet totam Posteritatem mediis necessariis ad fidem, & salutem, & tamen horum omnium seriò velle salutem, affirmaretur. Et quî in Americanis, Insulanis innumeris, Australibus antè inaccessis, Majores eorum fidem sprevere, aut Euangelium illis nunquam prædicatum? Adde quæ a Lutheranis concessa diximus, in hoc argumento, Protheoriâ pag. 350. 351.
english: Add this: God is not cleared of the appearance of injustice or cruelty if, because the greater ones spurned the faith, He cheats their whole posterity of the means necessary for faith and salvation, and yet is said seriously to will the salvation of all of them.
And how stands it with the Americans, the innumerable island peoples, the southerners formerly out of reach — did their greater ones spurn the faith, or was the Gospel never preached to them at all?
Add what we have already said the Lutherans concede on this argument, in the Protheoria, pages 350 and 351.

source_text: VI. An detur Decretum Reprobationis, seu praeteritionis quorundam quoad gratiam & gloriam, ac praedamnationis divinae, absolutum a priori, seu independens a causâ extra Deum, ejusque beneplacitum: Quô scilicet Deus, (qui omnes, pro liberrimo jure, servare potuit, ac neminem praeterire, illustrareque solam misericordiae gloriam, sufficiente in Deo potentia, & in Christi satisfactione λύτρῳ) in consilio suo aeterno, quô de rebus omnibus extra sese faciendis aut permittendis statuit, Prov. XVI. 4. Lam. III. 37. Matth. XXV. 34. Act. II. 23. XV. 18. eodemque immutabili Rom. IX. 11. 2. Tim. II. 19. Hebr. VI. 17. actu liberrimi beneplaciti κατ' εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος, Matth. XX. 15. Rom. IX. 15. 20. 21. &c. certos homines Rom. IX. 13. 15. 17. & comparatè multos, Matth. VII. 13. XX. 16. in equali cum reliquis conditione positos, Rom. V. 12. IX. 11. 21. Eph. II. 3. voluit relinquere in peccato & miseria, seu non eligere, non misereri ad salutem, Matth. VII. 13. XXIV. 40. Joh. XIII. 18. Rom. VIII. 29. IX. 13. 15. &c. Hinc negare illis gratiam, non quidem omnem, praetextum ne haberent, Joh. XV. 22. Rom. I. 20. (puta invitationis, sollicitationis ad officium, beneficentiae, tolerantiae, praedicationis Verbi Matth. XXIII. 37. Rom. II. 4. &c.) sed tamen negare gratiam salutarem, seu reconciliationis illam per Christum, Joh. X. 15. 26. XVII. 9. seu etiam vocationis efficacis, fidei, justificationis, Matth. XI. 26. XIII. 11. Rom. VIII. 28. 29. Eph. II. 8. &c.? Deinde etiam, Deus eodem Decreto, ut actu severissimi Judicis, Rom. I. 18. 32. IX. 22. eosdem homines suo vitio malos & miseros, miseria ut originali, Rom. V. 12. Eph. II. 3. sic acquisita per peccata actualia, & voluntaria, seu in Legem, Rom. II. 12. seu in Evangelium Marc. XVI. 16. Joh. III. 18. XII. 40. ac finaliter impaenitentes, Deique variis modis contemptores, Rom. II. 4. XI. 7. Matth. X. 15. &c. ac suo quemque judicio convictos, sibique conscios ultroneae rebellionis, Matth. XXVII. 4. Luc. XVI. 24. 28. Rom. II. 15. adjudicarit aeternae morti, propter peccata sua damnandos, Prov. XVI. 4. Hos. XIII. 9. Matth. XXV. 41. 42. Jud. 4. &c. Omnia ad ostensionem suae libertatis, potentiae, irae, justitiae vindicis peccatorum, Prov. XVI. 4. Matt. XX. 15. Rom. IX. 17. 18. 20. 22. &c.
english: VI. Is there a decree of reprobation — or of passing certain people by as to grace and glory — and of divine predamnation, absolute from the first, independent of any cause outside God and His good pleasure?

In that decree God (who by most free right could have saved everyone, passed no one by, and shown only the glory of mercy, power being enough in God and in Christ's satisfaction as ransom) decided, in His eternal counsel about all that would be done or permitted outside Himself (Proverbs 16:4; Lamentations 3:37; Matthew 25:34; Acts 2:23; 15:18) — and that counsel is immutable (Romans 9:11; 2 Timothy 2:19; Hebrews 6:17) — by an act of most free good pleasure according to the good pleasure of His will (Matthew 20:15; Romans 9:15, 20–21, and the like), to leave certain people (Romans 9:13, 15, 17), and comparatively many (Matthew 7:13; 20:16), who stood level with the rest (Romans 5:12; 9:11, 21; Ephesians 2:3), in sin and misery: not electing them, not pitying them for salvation (Matthew 7:13; 24:40; John 13:18; Romans 8:29; 9:13, 15, and the like).

So He withholds grace from them — not every grace, lest they have a pretext (John 15:22; Romans 1:20) (invitation, urging to duty, kindness, forbearance, preaching of the Word — Matthew 23:37; Romans 2:4, and the like) — yet He does withhold saving grace, the grace of reconciliation through Christ (John 10:15, 26; 17:9), and with it effectual calling, faith, and justification (Matthew 11:26; 13:11; Romans 8:28–29; Ephesians 2:8, and the like).

And by the same decree, acting as a most severe Judge (Romans 1:18, 32; 9:22), has He adjudged those same people — evil and miserable by their own fault, under original misery (Romans 5:12; Ephesians 2:3) and misery gained by actual, voluntary sins against the Law (Romans 2:12) or the Gospel (Mark 16:16; John 3:18; 12:40), finally impenitent and in many ways despisers of God (Romans 2:4; 11:7; Matthew 10:15, and the like), each convicted by his own judgment and conscious of willing rebellion (Matthew 27:4; Luke 16:24, 28; Romans 2:15) — to eternal death, condemned for their own sins (Proverbs 16:4; Hosea 13:9; Matthew 25:41–42; Jude 4, and the like)?
All of it displays His liberty, power, wrath, and justice that avenges sins (Proverbs 16:4; Matthew 20:15; Romans 9:17–18, 20, 22, and the like).

source_text: An verò Reprobatio nulla detur, nisi secundùm praescientiam finalis impaenitentiae, & incredulitatis, & hujus tanquam causae unicae Reprobationis consideratae in Decreto; dùm fuerint omnibus ità praescitis sufficientia ad fidem & resipiscentiam, tum & ad salutem concessa media? Prius negant, post. affirm. Luth. Contra Reform.
english: Or is there no reprobation at all except according to foresight of final impenitence and unbelief, treated as the one cause of reprobation inside the decree — while those so foreseen have all been granted means enough for faith and repentance, and for salvation too?
The Lutherans deny the first account and affirm this second one. The Reformed stand against that.

source_text: Cum Luthero rursum, & ὁμοψήφοις, lis de Reprobatione nulla, seu aeternâ Dei ordinatione, dispositione omnium, etiam quoad damnationem reproborum, indurationem Pharaonis, proditionem Judae, &c. Loca ex Luthero, & Melanchthone, vide vel in Apologia Rintelensium, aut apud Calixtum, Consultat. de Tolerantia Reform. p. m. 12. 13. 14. ut nostros taceam. V. gr. Melanchthon; Non minùs Judae proditionem, quàm Pauli conversionem Dei opus esse; Evenire omnia juxta divinam Praedestinationem, secundum quam Universa propter seipsum operatus est Dominus, etiam impium ad diem mali, &c. Lutherus verò; Deus suâ voluntate nos necessariò damnabiles facit; ut videatur delectari cruciatibus miserorum: Deus non vult mortem peccatoris Verbô, vult autem Voluntate imperescrutabili: Frustrà dicitur, quicquid dicitur, pro excusando Deo, &c. ne ipse sit auctor & culpa nostrae Indurationis: Si praescivit Deus Judam fore proditorem, necessariò Judas fiebat proditor, &c. Et quae plura excerpta sunt, vel ex uno Libro de Servo Arbitrio, Tomo II. Ed. I. Wittenb.
english: Again with Luther and those who vote with him, the fight is not over a vacant reprobation, but over God's eternal ordination — His disposal of everything, even the damnation of the reprobate, Pharaoh's hardening, Judas's betrayal, and the rest.
See the passages from Luther and Melanchthon in the Rinteln Apology, or in Calixtus's Consultation on Tolerating the Reformed, around pages 12–14 — not to mention our own writers.

Melanchthon, for example: Judas's betrayal is no less God's work than Paul's conversion; everything falls out by divine predestination, by which the Lord has worked all things for Himself, even the wicked for the day of evil.

Luther, for his part: by His will God necessarily makes us damnable, so that He seems to take pleasure in the torments of the miserable; God does not will the sinner's death by the Word, yet He does will it by an unsearchable will; whatever is said to clear God is said in vain — lest He Himself be made the author and the blame of our hardening; if God foresaw that Judas would betray, Judas necessarily became a traitor.
Still more of this is drawn from the single book On the Bondage of the Will, volume II, first Wittenberg edition.

source_text: ΠΡΩΤΑ ψεύδη novorum Lutheranor. pleraque in affictis consistunt, & intortis violenter dictis Reformatorum, cum Scripturâ ubique loquentium, ut nos modò in Statu Controvers. V. gr. dùm nobis affingunt Fatum Stoïcum, Manichaicam Haeresim, & Praedestinatianam illam vulgò; adeòque Reprobationem absolutam a posteriori, citra respectum peccatorum, vel incredulitatis. Ita dum confundunt peccati permissionem ut medium Dei placitum, & peccati immissionem, efficientiam, &c. Malè etiam inferunt, si peccatum, incredulitas, &c. est causa damnationis, Ergò & causam esse decreti de damnando; quasi sit eadem ratio volitionis divinae cujus nulla extrà Deum causa propriè dicta est, & rerum volitarum quae per media fiunt. Sic εὐδοκίαν gratiae, misericordiae in Christo, Eph. I. 5. 9. &c.
english: Most of the first falsehoods of the newer Lutherans are pinned-on charges and Reformers' words wrenched out of shape — though those Reformers speak with Scripture at every turn, as we have just shown in the State of the Controversy.
They fasten on us Stoic fate, Manichaean heresy, and the so-called Predestinarian heresy — and with them an absolute reprobation after the fact, with no eye to sins or unbelief.
In the same way they confuse God's permission of sin as a means that pleases Him with His sending sin in, with efficient causation, and the like.

They also argue badly: if sin and unbelief are the cause of damnation, then they must also be the cause of the decree to damn — as if God's willing, which has properly no cause outside God, worked by the same account as the things He wills, which come about through means.
So likewise with the good pleasure of grace and mercy in Christ (Ephesians 1:5, 9, and the like).

source_text: Cæterùm concessa utrimque sunt, 1. Nihil fieri in tempore, quod non ex ordinatione Dei, eâque aeterna. 2. Praedestinationis comparatae, horum potius quam illorum, causam esse Dei summum beneplacitum. 3. Praescientiam reproborum esse infallibilem unde saltem necessitas infallibilis eventûs. 4. Intuitum peccatorum, incredulitatis, impaenit. finalis, ingredi decretum Reprobat. nec damnari quemquam nisi propter peccata, ut causam suae perditionis, ex Statu Controv. 5. Deum peccatorum nullo modo causam esse, nec physicam, nec moralem, nec vim ullam ex decreto peccantibus admoveri, neque ullam in reprobis peccandi esse necessitatem destructivam τῷ ἑκουσίῳ, τῷ ἐλευθέρῳ, τῷ προαιρετικῷ, ut nos fusè in superioribus. 6. Reprobationis neminem posse sibi esse conscium, nisi fortè peccantem in Spiritum S. Hinc semper locum esse ut paenitentiae, sic remissioni peccatorum, saluti; Deo singulari misericordiâ operato saepè conversionem in maximè perditis, etiam in extremo agone, horâ ultimâ, in ipsis Orci faucibus, spe omni veniae demum post mortem praereptâ, &c. 7. Reprobis a Deo concedi multiplicem gratiam, puta tolerantiae divinae, beneficentiae, & externae invitationis, ex dictis, etiam interni luminis.
english: Besides this, both sides concede the following.
1. Nothing takes place in time except from God's ordination, and that eternal.
2. In comparative predestination — these rather than those — the cause is God's highest good pleasure.
3. Foresight of the reprobate is infallible, and from it comes at least an infallible necessity of the event.
4. Regard to sins, unbelief, and final impenitence enters the reprobation decree; and no one is damned except for sins as the cause of his own ruin — so the State of the Controversy.

5. God is in no way the cause of sins, neither physical nor moral; no force from the decree is applied to sinners; and in the reprobate there is no necessity of sinning that destroys what is voluntary, free, and of deliberate choice — as we have argued at length above.

6. No one can know himself reprobate, unless perhaps by sinning against the Holy Spirit. So there is always room for repentance, for forgiveness of sins, and for salvation; and God by singular mercy has often worked conversion in the most lost — even in the last agony, in the final hour, in hell's very jaws — when every hope of pardon is finally cut off only after death.
7. God grants the reprobate many kinds of grace: divine forbearance, kindness, and outward invitation, from what we have said, and even inward light.

source_text: VII. De Morte Christi universali pro omnibus & singulis, tam electis quam reprobis, quoad impetrationem remissionis peccatorum, justitiae, & vitae aeternae, modo non ipsi ponant obicem, redit Controv. IV. Vide & Articul. cum Armin. II. de amplitudine, objecto, & efficacia Mortis Christi, ac πρῶτα ibi ψεύδη, p. 250. 251. 252.
english: VII. On Christ's death as universal for all and each — elect and reprobate alike — as to obtaining forgiveness of sins, righteousness, and eternal life, provided they themselves do not put an obstacle in the way: the question returns to Controversy IV.
See also the Articles with the Arminians, II, on the breadth, object, and efficacy of Christ's death, and the first falsehoods there (pp. 250–252).

source_text: Nec tamen ratio eadem Lutheranorum est quae Remonstrant. Illi enim, nec applicationem Mortis Christi & fructum pendere à viribus Lib. Arbitrii, quae nullae sint, asserto Peccato Originis; nec vi Redempt. universalis salvari quemquam posse, sine cognitione Christi.
english: Yet the Lutherans' case is not the Remonstrants' case.
They do not make the application of Christ's death and its fruit hang on the powers of free choice — powers that are none, once original sin is granted.
Nor do they allow that anyone can be saved by the force of a universal redemption without knowing Christ.

source_text: VIII. Excipit Controversia de Gratia convertentis, per Verbum Evangelii, operatione resistibili vel superabili, deque ejus efficacia vel inefficacia, prout homo in virtute Evangelii illi obsequium praestare aut per connatam malitiam Gratiae resistere potest. Quae prima fronte videtur coincidere cum Controversia Armin. Artic. IV. de qua pluribus p. 254. &c.
english: VIII. Next comes the controversy on converting grace through the Word of the Gospel: an operation that can be resisted or overcome, and whether that grace is effective or ineffective, as a person by the Gospel's power can obey it or by inborn malice can resist it.
At first glance this looks like the Arminian Controversy, Article IV — of which more at p. 254 and following.

source_text: Interim tamen discrimen Lutheranorum ab Arminianis rursus non unum est. 1. Nullas supponunt Augustani Fratres in homine corrupto vires Lib. arbitrii; nec hujus volunt συνέργειαν cum Gratia, sensu Pelagiano, aut Semi-Pelagiano, reprobatam in ipso Libro Concordiae. 2. Gratiam praevenientem agnoscunt, quae praeveniat omnem hominis operationem in Conversione, ut supra p. 350. 3. Hominem in primis suae Conversionis momentis se habere mere passive, receptive, in ordine ad Gratiam primam & convertentem nobiscum profitentur. 4. Iidem quoque, Electos κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, ipso eventu Gratiae efficaci nunquam finaliter resistere, atque adeo eos infallibiliter converti, alias implicari contradictionem. 5. Nec etiam Gratiae efficaciam definiunt sola externa & morali suasione, cum Remonstrant, aut quae det tantum credendi potentiam, actu ab hominis voluntate suspenso. Agnoscunt vero Fratres in Electis operationem Spiritus S. internam peculiarem, productricem actus fidei, ac victricem voluntatis, plena lubentia Christum amplexae, & ex rebelli deinceps pronissima ad obsequendum.
english: Still, the Lutherans differ from the Arminians on more than one point.

1. The Augustan brethren suppose no powers of free choice in corrupted man; nor do they want that will's synergy with grace in a Pelagian or Semi-Pelagian sense — which the Book of Concord itself condemns.
2. They acknowledge prevenient grace, which goes before every human doing in conversion — as above at p. 350.
3. They profess with us that in the first moments of conversion a person stands merely passive and receptive toward first, converting grace.
4. They also hold that the elect according to foreknowledge never finally resist effectual grace in the event itself, and so are converted infallibly — otherwise contradiction follows.
5. Nor do they define grace's efficacy by outward moral persuasion alone, with the Remonstrants, or as what only gives a power to believe while the act hangs on the human will.

But they do acknowledge in the elect a peculiar inward work of the Holy Spirit: it produces the act of faith and conquers the will, which with full willingness has embraced Christ and is then most ready, after rebellion, to obey.

source_text: QUICQUID igitur superest Controversiae de resistibilitate vel irresistibilitate Gratiae, hujus efficacia vel inefficacia, nititur fere falsa interpretatione sententiae Reformatae, quae eadem Lutheri fuit, ex ante observatis: Supponunt igitur precario, suntque haec Πρῶτα ψεύδη, 1. Nos velle per Gratiam insuperabilem motionem coactam, violentam, qualis trunci, lapidis, &c. 2. Negare nos resistibilitatem Gratiae respectu naturae corruptae, & carnis Deo inimicae, quae sane quantum in se est nimis resistit; Vel respectu gratiae externe vocantis, seu praevenientis per Verbum Evangelii, cui etiam (& quotidiano usu) resisti largimur, frequentibus & in Scriptura Sacra exemplis; Vel non agnoscere nos resistentiam inchoatam naturae reluctantis, etiam quoad Gratiam internam, & efficacem, qui modo volumus, ultimo & finaliter superari Naturam a Gratia, Carnem a Spiritu, in Electis. 3. Vellent Reprobos, quibus haec efficax Gratia negata est, absque qua converti non possunt, non esse (ex mente Reformatorum) reos ultroneae rebellionis, contumaciae, latae culpae: Aut juxta nos, hujus contumaciae causam in Deo esse, non in reproborum malitia, culpa, voluntate, &c. Loquuntur in contrarium quicquid Confessionum est, quidquid Theologorum, ac Concionatorum, & quae diximus ad Articul. III. & IV. Remonstr. etiam ad Controv. cum R. Pajono, ad Hypoth. ejus v. VI. VII.
english: So whatever is left of the controversy on whether grace can be resisted or not — and whether it is effective or ineffective — rests mostly on a false reading of the Reformed view, which was Luther's view too, from what we noted before.
They therefore assume on a shaky basis, and these are the first falsehoods:
1. That by insurmountable grace we want a forced, violent motion, like a log or a stone.

2. That we deny grace can be resisted as to corrupted nature and flesh hostile to God — which for its part resists all too much; or as to outward calling grace, or prevenient grace through the Gospel Word, which we also grant is resisted (and daily), with many examples even in Holy Scripture; or that we refuse to admit an early resistance of reluctant nature even toward inward effectual grace — we who only want nature finally overcome by grace, and flesh by the Spirit, in the elect.

3. That they would clear the reprobate — to whom this effectual grace is denied, without which they cannot be converted — of willing rebellion, stubbornness, and broad guilt on the Reformers' view; or, against us, put the cause of that stubbornness in God, not in the reprobate's malice, fault, and will.

The Confessions, the theologians, and the preachers all speak the other way — and so do we at Remonstrant Articles III and IV, and in the Controversy with R. Pajon, at his Hypothesis, sections VI and VII.

source_text: IX. De Perseverantia vere justorum, regenitorum (postquam semel justificati per fidem, & in statu Gratiae positi sunt) tanquam non certa aut necessaria, deque possibili eorum defectione a gratia & fide, eademque totali & finali, hinc & salute; videtur redire Controversia cum Arminian. Art. V. pag. 257. 258. Vide & Controv. cum Socinian. LXI. p. 219. 220. Nec tamen Lutheranos Fratres cum istis confundimus.
english: IX. Next comes perseverance of the truly just — regenerate people once justified by faith and already set in grace — treated as if that standing were neither sure nor necessary, and as if the same people could leave grace and faith altogether and for good, and so lose salvation.
At that point the Arminian dispute, Article V (pages 257–258), seems to reappear.
Compare also the Socinian controversy, LXI (pages 219–220).
Even so, we refuse to lump the Lutheran brethren in with those camps.

source_text: Discrimen rursus non unum ab ipsis Remonstrantibus apparet. 1. Fatentur Lutherani, Electos secundum praescientiam Dei, non posse finaliter excidere a fide & gratia, ex hypothesi illius in Deo Praescientiae, quae infallibilis sit. 2. Iidem quoque, dari subjectivam certitudinem, in unoquoque credente, eamque infallibilem, remissionis suorum peccatorum, suaeque salutis; Idque ex natura fidei, seu fiducia de misericordia Dei in Christo, Spiritu Sancto testante cum Spiritu nostro, Rom. VIII. 16. Quae fiducia firmissimum sit animae nostrae columen; arrha quaedam, instar funiculi fili dibaphi, Jos. II. 18. sed cordibus alte condita; & quaedam velut anchora, qua in Deum mediis in fluctibus defixi, ne in extremo etiam discrimine expavescimus; Sed & verus pietatis fomes, & divini amoris incentivum. Quo enim propius portum intuemur, hoc magis, suspiriis & gemitibus enarrari nesciis, ad portum anhelamus. Et quemadmodum haec fiducia nonnisi ex Spiritu regenerante est, ita etiam spiritum accendit, ut nos alibi pluribus.
english: Once more the gap from the Remonstrants is not a single point.
1. Lutherans grant that those elect according to God's foreknowledge cannot make a final exit from faith and grace, because that foreknowledge in God is, by hypothesis, infallible.

2. They likewise grant every believer an inward, infallible assurance that his sins are forgiven and that he will be saved. That assurance rises from what faith is — trust in God's mercy in Christ — while the Holy Spirit testifies with our spirit (Romans 8:16).

Such trust braces the soul more firmly than anything else. It is a pledge like Rahab's cord of twice-dyed thread (Joshua 2:18), buried deep in the heart; an anchor that holds us to God through the waves so that even the last crisis does not make us panic.
It is also real fuel for godliness and a spur to love God. The closer the harbor comes into view, the harder we gasp for it — with sighs and groans no speech can render.
And because this trust is born only of the regenerating Spirit, it in turn sets the spirit on fire; we treat that more fully elsewhere.

source_text: QUOD reliquum est controversiae cum Reformatis, fere in detorta horum sententia consistit. Fatentur enim nostri, ut contra Remonstr. visum, 1. Hominem ex se, & in suis viribus, idest, infirmitatibus consideratum, nimis quam posse deficere a fide, & totaliter quidem. Utpote qui ex se vas fictile, tenellus infans, ovicula imbellis, nonnisi caro & sanguis, fragilis arundo, mobilis arena, semper labilis sine Deo, quin ipsa vanitas ac merum nihil.
english: Whatever quarrel with the Reformed is left turns chiefly on a wrenching of their meaning.
Our side, as already shown against the Remonstrants, concedes this:
1. Take a person by himself and in his own strength — that is, in his frailty — and he can all too easily leave the faith, yes, leave it wholly.

Left to himself he is clay pottery, a soft infant, a defenseless lamb, nothing but flesh and blood, a bruised reed, loose sand, always apt to slide unless God holds him — vanity itself, sheer nothing.

source_text: 2. Fidem quae est πρὸς καιρὸν seu temporariam saepe simillimam esse fidei quae ῥίζαν ἔχει, seu fidei vere justificanti; quemadmodum externa professione vix dignoscitur saepe Irregenitus a Regenito: Certe vestis illa nuptialis festa, γαμική requisita Matth. XXII. 11. in apodosi, non vestis externa, sed interna fidei, charitatis, resipiscentiae, quum induitur Christus Rom. XIII. 14. Certi licet sint characteres, quibus utraque fides, & status Irregeniti hominis a Regeniti illo, distinguitur; Matth. XIII. Rom. VII. Gal. V. &c.
english: 2. Faith that lasts only for a time (πρὸς καιρὸν) often wears almost the same face as faith that has root (ῥίζαν ἔχει) — the faith that truly justifies. Outward profession alone rarely shows who is unregenerate and who is regenerate.

The festive wedding garment (γαμική) required in Matthew 22:11, taken in the saying's closing turn, is not cloth on the body. It is the inward dress of faith, love, and repentance, when a person puts on Christ (Romans 13:14).
Still, sure marks do separate the two faiths and the two states — unregenerate from regenerate: Matthew 13; Romans 7; Galatians 5; and the rest.

source_text: 3. Saepe etiam fidelem actu deficere ad tempus, praevalente seu externo hostium ac tentationum impetu, seu interno Carnis lubrico, Apoc. II. 4. 5. &c. nullo videlicet sensu divinae gratiae, aut exercitio fidei, amissae quasi, in Davide, & aliis. Sed ita ut seminis illius ἀφθάρτου efficacia praepediri possit, nunquam tamen illud emori, & plane suffocari; obturari fons ille gratiae, non tamen prorsus extingui, 1 Thess. V. 19. deficere lumen illud gratiae, obumbratum interpositione quasi terrae, mundi, nube peccatorum, &c. non tamen in totum tolli, & perire, ut in Eclipsibus accidit; vel prout in morbis acutioribus vita periclitatur, pulsu arteriarum quasi nullo, non eo ipso extinguitur. Unde Theologi, effectum & sensum Justificationis posse suspendi, non statum ipsum dissolvi, aut finaliter subverti. Et quamvis peccata sint per se, ratione actus gravissima, ratione meriti aeterna morte ac desertione gratiae dignissima; per accidens tamen talia esse desinunt; Quia Deus non agit cum suis ex jure stricto, ut servis, sed cum paterna ἐπιεικείᾳ ut filiis; Vultu severo saepe, qualis fuit Josephi erga fratres, sed redituro vultu sereniore; quia solidum stat Dei fundamentum, &c. 2. Tim. II. 19.
english: 3. Believers also often slip in act for a season, when either enemies and temptations press from outside or the flesh's slickness works from inside (Revelation 2:4-5 and similar places). Then divine grace is not felt, and faith is not exercised — as if both were gone — the way it was with David and others.

Even then the power of that incorruptible seed (ἀφθάρτου) may be checked, yet the seed never dies or is smothered outright. The spring of grace may be dammed, yet not put out for good (1 Thessalonians 5:19). The light of grace may dim under something like earth's blocking — the world, a cloud of sins, and the like — yet it is not wholly removed and lost, as in an eclipse; or as in a sharp fever life hangs by a thread when the pulse is nearly gone, yet life itself is not thereby extinguished.
Theologians therefore say the fruit and felt sense of justification can pause; the justified state itself is not broken up or finally ruined.

Sins remain, in themselves and by the act, most serious, and by what they deserve most fit for eternal death and for grace's desertion; yet by accident they stop standing as that for God's people. He does not treat his own by bare strict right, as slaves, but with a father's gentleness (ἐπιεικείᾳ), as sons — often with Joseph's hard look toward his brothers, yet with a kinder look ready to return — because God's firm foundation stands, and so on (2 Timothy 2:19).

source_text:
De Persona Christi Θεανθρώπῳ.
I. An vi Unionis hypostaticae Naturarum in Persona Christi Θεανθρώπῳ, (quam fatemur utrimque factam esse ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως) vel etiam vi insecutae Exaltationis, & Sessionis ad dextram Dei, communicatae sint Naturae Humanae in abstracto, communicatione reali & propria, per συνδύασιν vel ἕνωσιν Naturarum, Proprietates Naturae Divinae essentiales, simul cum infinita Dei Majestate, ad communem cum Λόγῳ possessionem, denominationem, operationem? Quae illis est communicatio Majestatis, in abstracto, Naturae ad Naturam in unione; Sive ea jam concipiatur quoad χρῆσιν harum Proprietatum, seu usum, exercitium, ἐνέργειαν communicatam Naturae Humanae, etiam dum in terris esset; sive etiam (ut Suevi) quoad κτῆσιν & communitatem possessionis? Speciatim vero, an communicatae sint illae Proprietates, quae sunt ἐνεργητικαὶ seu operativae per actum secundum, uti Omnipotentia, & vis Vivifica; Tamen (sic illi) citra ἀλλοποίησιν, ἔκπτωσιν, μετέκβασιν, σύγχυσιν, ἐνύπαρξιν, citra multiplicationem, transfusionem, aut confusionem Naturarum, vel etiam Proprietatum utriusque, aut inexistentiam harum per se in Natura humana, subjective, formaliter, habitualiter, ut iidem passim? Affirm. Ubiquitar. nec omnes eodem modo, Negant Reformati.
english: On the person of Christ the God-man (Θεάνθρωπος).

X. First question: by the force of the natures' hypostatic union in Christ's person as God-man — which both sides confess was made without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation (ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως) — or also by the exaltation that followed and by the session at God's right hand, were the essential properties of the divine nature, together with God's infinite majesty, really and properly handed over to the human nature in the abstract, through the natures' pairing (συνδύασις) or union (ἕνωσις), so as to share possession, naming, and working with the Word (Λόγος)?

That is what they call communication of majesty in the abstract — nature to nature inside the union. Take it either as the use (χρῆσις) of those properties — their employment, exercise, and energy (ἐνέργεια) given to the human nature even while it was on earth — or, with the Swabians, as acquisition (κτῆσις) and shared possession.

Ask it more narrowly still: were the operative properties (ἐνεργητικαί) that work by a second act — omnipotence and life-giving power — so communicated, yet without alteration (ἀλλοποίησις), falling away (ἔκπτωσις), transfer (μετέκβασις), confusion (σύγχυσις), or inherence (ἐνύπαρξις), and without multiplying, transfusing, or confusing the natures or either nature's properties, or lodging those properties by themselves in the human nature subjectively, formally, habitually, as the same writers keep saying? The Ubiquitarians say yes — not all by one route. The Reformed say no.

source_text: Benigniorem interpretationem hujus dogmatis, ex mente Rintelensium Theologorum, horumque in fundamento ipso consensum cum Cassellanis, vidimus in Protheoria, p. 319. Summa ejus, confonis aliorum declarationibus, huc redit, 1. Naturam Humanam Christi Θεανθρώπῳ nec subjective, vel intrinsice per ἐνύπαρξιν, nec essentialiter seu proprietate essentiali, nec naturaliter seu actu ipsius Naturae, nec originaliter a se ipsa, nec per conversionem, commixtionem, confusionem cum Natura Divina, esse aut dici Omnisciam, Omnipotentem, Omnipraesentem. 2. Talem vero dici & esse personaliter, in Λόγῳ; Ob Unionem cum eo personalem, actu personae, quo fit Nat. Humana κοινωνὸς καὶ μέτοχος omnium Operationum quae propriae Divinitatis, &c. Quae hinc de ea praedicantur, per denominationem extrinsecam, communicatione tam reali, quam realis est unio Hypostatica utriusque Naturae.
english: We already saw in the Protheoria (p. 319) a kinder reading of this dogma from the Rinteln theologians, and their agreement with the Cassel men at the root of the matter.

Put with other matching declarations, the sum is this: 1. Christ's human nature as God-man is not itself — and is not called — omniscient, omnipotent, or omnipresent, whether subjectively or inwardly by inherence (ἐνύπαρξις), or essentially by an essential property, or naturally by an act of that nature, or originally from itself, or by conversion, mixture, or confusion with the divine nature.

2. Yet it is called — and is — such personally, in the Word (Λόγος), because of the personal union with him. By an act of the person the human nature becomes sharer and partaker (κοινωνὸς καὶ μέτοχος) of every working proper to the divinity, and the like.
What is then said of that nature is said by an outward naming, through a communication as real as the hypostatic union of the two natures itself.

source_text: UNDE patet, quam involutus fuerit ab aliis Status Controversiae, nec uno semper propositus modo a Lutheranis. Suevi enim, Brentius, Schmidlinus, &c. primi autores, effusionem voluerunt Proprietatum Divinar. in Humanam, vi Unionis, jam in Utero: Saxones Communionem Proprietatum Divinarum Omnipot. Omnipraes. &c. in assumpta Carne, vi Exaltationis & Sessionis a Dextris: Hassi, cautiores reliquis visi in Judicio suo de Libro Concordiae, A. 1576. Quae vide sis fuse apud Hospinianum, Ursinum Wendelinum, Massonium Anat. Germ. P. II. &c.
english: So it is plain how tangled others have made the state of this quarrel, and how Lutherans have not always posed it one way.
The Swabians — Brenz, Schmidlin, and the rest who led first — wanted the divine properties poured into the human nature by the union's force, already in the womb.
The Saxons wanted communion of the divine properties of omnipotence, omnipresence, and the like in the assumed flesh, by the exaltation and the session at the right hand.
The Hessians looked more careful than the others in their Judgment on the Book of Concord (1576). Hospinian, Ursinus Wendelinus, Massonius (Anat. Germ. Part II), and others treat this at length.

source_text: Ac post multam inter eos ipsos disceptationem, & vocum ac distinctionum ambages, in ipso Libro Concordiae, tandem iniquiorum in nos Fratrum πρῶτα ψεύδη deprehenduntur in hac Controv. Quasi scil. negent Reformati (quod fecere nunquam) vel Personalem Unionem & indivulsam Naturarum; Vel Communionem earum in Persona Θεανθρώπῳ; Vel communem Proprietatum possessionem; sed quae sit Personae, tanquam subjecti quod, ut loquuntur; Vel Majestatem Christi Hominis, & potestatem Officii Mediatorii illi quoque competentem, Matth. XXVIII. 18.
english: After much debate among themselves, and mazes of words and distinctions, even inside the Book of Concord, the first falsehoods of the harsher brethren against us finally show up in this controversy.

They talk as if the Reformed deny — which they never did — the personal union and the natures' undivided bond; or the natures' communion in the person of the God-man (Θεάνθρωπος); or common possession of the properties, yet as belonging to the person as the subject-which (subjectum quod), in their phrase; or the majesty of Christ the man, and the power of the mediatorial office that is his as well (Matthew 28:18).

source_text: Vel etiam Communicationem (quam vocant) Idiomatum, idest, proprietatum & operationum alterutrius Naturae, in eadem Persona in qua Naturae unitae sunt, eamque reciprocam, κατὰ τρόπον ἀντιδόσεως: Qua scil. Nomina, Proprietates, & Operationes alterutrius Naturae, puta Divinae, praedicantur vere & realiter de tota Persona eaque nonnunquam ab Humanitate denominata, Joh. III. 13. & vicissim ut Act. XX. 28. 1. Cor. II. 8. obviis in Scriptura S. exemplis. Quae Communicatio (ex dictis modo) tam realis est, quam est realis Unio Naturarum; licet modo loquendi ad Synecdochen accedat, qua quod Partis est, tribuitur Toti, secundum illam Partem. Sed haec fuse dicti Theologi.
english: Or even what they call the communication of properties — that is, of either nature's properties and workings in the one person where the natures are united, and that as a two-way exchange (κατὰ τρόπον ἀντιδόσεως).

By it the names, properties, and operations of either nature — say the divine — are truly and really said of the whole person, and that person is sometimes named from the humanity (John 3:13), and the other way round, as in Acts 20:28 and 1 Corinthians 2:8, examples ready in Holy Scripture.

That communication, on the account just given, is as real as the natures' union is real; though the speaking leans toward synecdoche, where what belongs to the part is given to the whole according to that part.
The theologians already named have set this out at length.

source_text: Omnium vero primum ψεῦδος fuit, asserenda Praesentia Corporalis in S. Coena; Unde tandem ad sacram hanc anchoram perfugium, de Communicata realiter Nat. Humanae Omnipraesentia, seu Ubiquitate, ut & Omnipotentia, &c. seu per effusionem, ut Suevi, seu per quandam περιχώρησιν Emmeationem, ut Chemnitius Brunswicensis Theologus, &c. Prudentioribus Hassis, Helmstadiensibus, Anhaltinis, aliisque, qui praesentiam Corporalem fundare voluerunt non in Unione Personali, aut Ubiquitate, sed in Verbis Institut. Hoc est Corpus meum. Adde torquenda a Suevis & Saxonibus loca, Matth. XXVIII. 18. Phil. II. 9. Col. II. 3. 9. &c. & quae alia sunt prolixe a Theologis Palatinis, Anhaltinis, Cassellanis, &c. vindicata.
english: The first falsehood of them all was asserting a bodily presence in the Holy Supper.

From that they finally fled to this sacred anchor: that omnipresence — or ubiquity — and omnipotence too, and the rest, had been really communicated to the human nature, whether by outpouring, as the Swabians say, or by a kind of περιχώρησις / emmeation, as Chemnitz the Brunswick theologian and others say.
The wiser Hessians, Helmstedt men, Anhaltines, and the rest wanted to ground bodily presence not in the personal union or in ubiquity, but in the institution words: This is my body.

Add the places the Swabians and Saxons twist — Matthew 28:18; Philippians 2:9; Colossians 2:3, 9, and so on — and the rest of what the Palatine, Anhaltine, and Cassel theologians have defended at length.

source_text: II. An speciatim Carni vel Corpori Christi, seu vi Unionis cum λόγῳ in Utero Virginis, seu vi Exaltationis ad Dextram Dei, aut saltem vi veritatis Verborum Institutionis, communicata sit Omnipraesentia Majestatica, seu Ubiquitas, secundum quam ea Caro sit Omnipraesens, sed actu personali, ut loquuntur: Unde nihil mirum sit, corporaliter eum praesentem esse in S. Eucharistia, sublata per ejus Omnipotentiam Corporis localitate, hinc tactilitate, visibilitate in actu primo? Ut adeo nec Ascensio Christi fuerit vera aut localis, sed potius disparitio Corporis; Nec Caelum in quod Christus ascendit, sit locus creatus, finitus, corporeus, supra visibiles Caelos; verum Coelum quoddam increatum, immensum, incorporeum, Deus ipse, vel ipsa Dei Majestas, & incomprehensibilis Gloria, ac Potentia? Affirmant Ubiquit. Negant Reformati.
english: Controv. XI. On the ubiquity of Christ's flesh.

II. Was majestic omnipresence — or ubiquity — specially communicated to Christ's flesh or body, whether by the union with the Word (λόγος) in the Virgin's womb, or by the exaltation to God's right hand, or at least by the truth of the institution words, so that that flesh is omnipresent, but by a personal act, as they put it?

On that account it would be no wonder if he were bodily present in the Holy Eucharist, once his omnipotence had taken away the body's locality, and with it its tangibility and visibility in the first act.

Then Christ's ascension would not have been a true local going up, but rather a vanishing of the body; and the heaven he entered would not be a created, finite, bodily place above the visible heavens, but some uncreated, boundless, bodiless heaven — God himself, or God's own majesty, and incomprehensible glory and power.
The Ubiquitarians say yes. The Reformed say no.

source_text: Sed & Ubiquitatem Suevicam Carnis Christi, cum Reformatis, negarunt Melanchthon, Peucerus, Heshusius, ipse Hofmannus, Chemnitius, Chytraeus, Selneccerus, Major, &c. ac pridem Dani, Holsati, Brunswicenses, Helmstadienses, Anhaltini, Hassi, inferioris Saxoniae Theologi, Norimbergenses, &c. Et, Chemnitio praeeunte, substituerunt loco Ubiquitatis, seu πανταχεσίας, Multivoli-praesentiam; Id est, κοινωνίαν vel μετοχὴν realem Divinarum Operationum in Nat. Humana, qua sit ubicunque vult esse, & quandocunque vult; vel qua possit esse ubicunque velit, ut Hassi in Judicio suo de Formula Torgensi, A. 1567.
english: Melanchthon, Peucer, Heshusius, Hofmann himself, Chemnitz, Chytraeus, Selnecker, Major, and others joined the Reformed in denying the Suevic ubiquity of Christ's flesh.
So did the Danes, Holsteiners, Brunswickers, Helmstedt men, Anhaltines, Hessians, the Lower-Saxon theologians, and the Nurembergers, long since.
Chemnitz led the way: instead of ubiquity — or πανταχεσία — they put a multivolitional presence.

That means a real κοινωνία or μετοχή of the divine operations in the human nature, so that it is wherever and whenever it wills to be, or can be wherever it wishes — the Hessian reading in their Judgment on the Torgau Formula (1567).

source_text: Πρῶτα ψεύδη eorum Theologorum qui vulgo Ubiquitarii, & quorum duriores sed & principes Suevi, fuere plurima. Ex. gr. solvi Unionem Hypostaticam Naturarum, si Humana Divinae non sit commensurata, aeque infinita, omnipraesens, &c. Retorsione in promptu; tolli eam Personalem Unionem portento Ubiquitatis: Sic supposuere, Totum Christum, quod dictum de Persona, & subjecto quod, ac Totum Christi, quod de Naturis unitis, vel subjecto quo, unum & idem esse.
english: Those theologians commonly called Ubiquitarians had many first falsehoods. The harsher among them — and their chiefs — were the Swabians.
One sample: they say the hypostatic union of the natures dissolves unless the human nature is stretched to match the divine — equally infinite, equally omnipresent, and so on.
Turn the charge around and it is ready: the marvel of ubiquity is what cancels that personal union.

On that path they collapsed two phrases into one: "the whole Christ," said of the person and of the subject-which (subjectum quod), and "the whole of Christ," said of the united natures or the subject-by-which (subjectum quo).

source_text: Rursus, Sessionem a dextris referendam ad situm, ad ubietatem, & de Carne in abstracto enunciatam esse; aut hanc sedere a dextris Dei ubique, non in Caelo in quod ascendit, qua de illatione nos in Vindic. Marci XVI. 19. Pariter illi, Christum dici, esse nobiscum, Matth. XVIII. 20. XXVIII. 20. praesentia corporis, Locali; & illud, Ego sum vobiscum, idem esse, ac Caro mea est vobiscum ἀδιαστάτως, contra illud Matth. XXVI. 11. Joh. XVII. 11. Dum nos, verius concipi debere Christum nobiscum esse, & fore semper cum suis, nempe Ecclesia sua, praesentia ut Divinitatis, quae communis est, sic speciali altera providentia, virtutis, gratiae, assistentiae, ἐνεργείας, per influxum Spiritus, &c. Qua de re prolixe in Vindic. Biblicis Libr. III. ad Locum Matth. XVIII. 20.
english: Again: that the sitting at the right hand is about place and ubiety, and is said of the flesh in the abstract; or that this flesh sits at God's right hand everywhere, not in the heaven he entered — on that inference see our Vindication of Mark 16:19.

Likewise they take "Christ is with us" (Matthew 18:20; 28:20) as a local presence of the body, and make "I am with you" mean "my flesh is with you without interval (ἀδιαστάτως)," against Matthew 26:11 and John 17:11.

We hold the truer reading: Christ is, and always will be, with his own — that is, with his Church — by the presence of the divinity, which is common to all, and likewise by another, special providence of power, grace, assistance, and ἐνέργεια through the Spirit's influx, and the like.
We have treated that at length in the Biblical Vindications, Book III, on Matthew 18:20.

source_text: Sic illi, Christum dici, implere omnia Eph. IV. 10. respectu Carnis suae, omnia loca implentis; Imo Carnem Paulus ibidem docet evectam, per ascensionem supra coelos visibiles; ut inde non illa Caro omnia impleret, sed Christus exaltatus impleret donis suis, Spiritu, Gratia, &c. omnem suam Ecclesiam. Mittimus Loca alia quibus, ad Ubiquitatem vel Illocalitatem, aut Invisibilitatem &c. Carnis Christi probandam abusi, Matth. XIV. 25. 29. Luc. XX. 36. Joh. XX. 19. 26. Luc. XXIV. 31. Act. VII. 55. 1. Cor. XV. 8. Apoc. I. 13. &c. prolixe a Wendelino, & nostris passim, vindicata. Ac de illatione ex Matth. XIV. 25. 29. nos Vindic. Bibl. lib. II. Loco XXIII. Et viderunt oculatiores, ex illa πανταχεσίᾳ Carnis, sequi Christum non minus praesentem in omnibus locis, lapidibus, lignis, (sic Joach. Westphalus Hamburgens.) quam in pane, nec minus ante Consecrationem quam post eam. Unde Brentii commentum, esse Corpus in solo pane consecrato, per dispensationem.
english: They read "he fills all things" (Ephesians 4:10) as if Christ's flesh itself fills every place.

Paul's point there is different: the flesh was raised by the ascension above the visible heavens, so that it is not that flesh which fills all things, but the exalted Christ who fills his whole Church with his gifts, Spirit, grace, and the rest.

Other abused proofs for the ubiquity, illocality, or invisibility of Christ's flesh — Matthew 14:25, 29; Luke 20:36; John 20:19, 26; Luke 24:31; Acts 7:55; 1 Corinthians 15:8; Revelation 1:13, and so on — we set aside; Wendelin and our side have already defended them at length.
For the inference from Matthew 14:25, 29, see our Biblical Vindications, Book II, Place XXIII.

Sharper eyes saw where that πανταχεσία of the flesh leads: Christ no less present in every place — in stones and wood, as Joachim Westphal of Hamburg put it — than in the bread, and no less before consecration than after it.
That is why Brentius fell back to this remark: the body is in the consecrated bread alone, by dispensation.

source_text: XII. De Baptismo. An S. Baptismi ea sit efficacia, ut quoquot Infantes aquâ baptizantur, hoc ipso internè regenerentur per Spiritum S. unde sequatur eos habere fidem actualem, quum Baptismus nihil profit fine fide? An sit adeò Baptismi lavacrum non solummodo medium externum divinitus ordinatum, in Sacramentum vel symbolum ac figillum nostrae Regenerationis, Tit. III.5. Act. XVI.22. ut & Instrumentum illius morale; sub conditione fidei vel praesentis in adultis, Marc. XVI.16. vel secuturae quoad victuros Infantes; habens hinc necessitatem hypotheticam & praecepti divini: Verum etiam an sit medium physicum, & efficientia interna, sine quo non fiat ordinariè Regeneratio; & quo omnino eadem efficiatur, habens hinc necessitatem absolutam & medii sine quo non? Ita ut sola privatio Baptismi in infantibus si non damnet, certe in damnationis periculo constituat, & huc faciant verba Christi de regeneratione ex aqua & spiritu, Joh. III.5. Unde in casu necessitatis, etiam privatis vulgo Laicis, imo & Mulieribus, non quidem & praedicare, 1. Cor. XIV.34.35. sed tamen baptizare liceat? Affirm. Luth. Negant Reform.
english: Controv. XII. On Baptism. Is holy Baptism so effective that every infant washed with water is by that very act inwardly regenerated by the Holy Spirit — and so must have actual faith, since baptism profits nothing without faith?

Is baptism's washing only an outward means God ordained, a sacrament or symbol and seal of our regeneration (Titus 3:5; Acts 16:22), and a moral instrument of it, under the condition of faith — faith already present in adults (Mark 16:16), or faith still to come in infants who will live — and so necessary only hypothetically, as a divine command?

Or is it also a physical means and an inward efficiency without which regeneration does not ordinarily happen, and by which that regeneration is altogether worked — and so absolutely necessary, a means without which it cannot be?

On that reading, mere lack of baptism in infants, if it does not damn them outright, at least puts them in danger of damnation; and Christ's words about being born of water and Spirit are pressed that way (John 3:5).
From this they ask whether, in necessity, private persons ordinarily called laypeople — and even women — may baptize, though they may not preach (1 Corinthians 14:34–35).
The Lutherans say yes; the Reformed say no.

source_text: Consensum Lutheranorum cum Reformatis, in eo quod essentiale est huic Sacramento, vidimus supra ex confessis, pag. 340. Quod reliquum est dissensionis, si aequa lance pendatur, vix tanti esse videbitur.
english: On what is essential to this sacrament, the Lutherans and the Reformed already agree; we saw that above from the confessed points (p. 340).
What is left of the quarrel, weighed fairly, will hardly seem worth so much.

source_text: Talis est Controversia, 1. Circa fidem actualem Infantum: Quos Reformati censent subjectum capax fidei, quoad hujus principium, semen, radicem, habitum, modo nobis ἀκαταλήπτῳ divinitus infusum; Capaces adeo esse gratiae alicujus, etiam internae, uti sunt gratiae foederalis, scil. cum parentibus assumpti in Foedus, & participes promissionis, Act. II.39. Sic capaces sanctificationis Sacramentalis, uti per Circumcisionem, Rom. IV.11. ita per Baptismum 1. Cor. VII.14. Col. II.14. Denique capaces remissionis peccati Original. & gratiae justificantis. 2. Talis quoque Controversia, circa gradum quendam necessitatis S. Baptismi; Unde secundum illos, ex sola privatione, citra neglectum ullum voluntarium, oriatur aut privatio salutis, aut periculum saltem hujus. 3. Talis & circa efficaciae modum; Ut Ceremoniae Baptismi sit alligata gratia Regenerationis, vel (ut loquuntur) Baptismo fluminis alligatus Baptismus flaminis, tanquam illius effectus, sed (ut addunt) ordinariè; neque tamen ex opere operato Pontificiorum, sed operatione Spiritus S.
english: The leftover controversy runs like this. First, about infants' actual faith. The Reformed take them as able to receive faith in its principle, seed, root, and habit — poured in by God in a way we cannot grasp — and so able to receive some grace, even inward grace: federal grace, as children taken with their parents into the covenant and sharers of the promise (Acts 2:39).

So they are capable of sacramental sanctification, as by circumcision (Romans 4:11), so by baptism (1 Corinthians 7:14; Colossians 2:14); and finally capable of the remission of original sin and of justifying grace.
Second, about how far holy baptism is necessary. On their side, bare lack of it — with no willful neglect — already works either loss of salvation, or at least danger of that loss.

Third, about the mode of efficacy: that regenerating grace is bound to the baptismal ceremony, or (in their phrase) the baptism of the Spirit is bound to the baptism of water as its effect — ordinarily, they add — yet not by the Papists' opus operatum, but by the Holy Spirit's own working.

source_text: 4. Talis tandem Controv. circa administrum Laicum, in casu necessitatis, qua in re non ita scrupulosa fuit Antiquitas, ut ex Tertulliano visum, accedentibus Grotio, Salmasio, aliis; supra pag. 311. 312. Mulieribus tamen ab ejus administratione constanter exclusis, non uno apud Tertull. loco, de Baptismo, de Velandis Virginib. de Praescriptione Haeretic. citatis G. J. Vossio, Disp. XI. Sed & in Canonibus Africanis, Concil. Carthag. IV. Can. c. Tomo II. Conc. Mulier baptizare non praesumat, quod absurde nonnulli ita limitant, praesentibus Sacerdotibus.
english: Fourth and last: controversy about a layperson administering baptism in a case of necessity. On that point antiquity was not so scrupulous, as Tertullian shows, and Grotius, Salmasius, and others agree (above, pp. 311–312).

Women, however, are constantly shut out from administering it — and not in one Tertullian passage only: On Baptism, On the Veiling of Virgins, and On the Prescription of Heretics, as G. J. Vossius cites them in Disputation XI.
So also in the African canons, Council of Carthage IV, canon c (Councils, tom. II): A woman must not presume to baptize — which some absurdly restrict to times when priests are present.

source_text: HYPOTHESES precariæ sunt, 1. Reformatos non censere neglectum Baptismi damnosum; Qui censent omnino, sed damnosum negligentibus, contra mandatum Christi. 2. Non tribuere nos omnem Baptismo virtutem, quam tribuit Christus, Marc. XVI.16. vel Paulus Tit. III.5. quasi alliget ille salutem, hic regenerationem S. Baptismo. Quum tamen nihil Christus, de Infantibus per Baptismum regenerandis; Sed de fide praevia, adeoque & praevia regenerationis gratia, in Adultis per Apostolos baptizandis; Suspensa etiam salute, non a Bapt. sed ab actu credentis; qui non crediderit, damnabitur. Paulo etiam Baptismus λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας, opposite ad lotiones Judaicas, quae nec obsignativae Regenerat. nec medium morale sub Novo T. illi inchoandae in Infantibus, continuandae in Adultis.
english: The precarious supporting claims are these. First: that the Reformed do not count neglect of baptism as harmful. They do count it harmful — harmful to those who neglect it against Christ's command.
Second: that we deny baptism the full virtue Christ gives it (Mark 16:16) or Paul gives it (Titus 3:5), as if Christ binds salvation to holy baptism and Paul binds regeneration to it.

But Christ says nothing there about infants being regenerated by baptism. He speaks of prior faith — and so of prior regenerating grace — in adults the apostles were to baptize. Salvation hangs not on baptism but on the believer's act: whoever has not believed will be condemned.

For Paul too baptism is the washing of regeneration, set against Jewish washings — which neither seal regeneration nor serve as a moral means, under the New Testament, for beginning that regeneration in infants and carrying it on in adults.

source_text: 3. Sic supponunt, parem esse necessitatem fidei & baptismi, in negotio salutis: Quum nusquam dixerit Christus, ut liquet, qui non baptizatus fuerit, damnabitur. Ac possit esse fides sine Baptismo, ut in Latrone converso, in Eunucho, Saule, Cornelio, nondum baptizatis; quemadmodum & Baptismus sine fide, ex. gr. in Simone Mago, id est ablutio externa, sine interna 1. Pet. III.21. uti Circumcisio carnis, sine illa cordis, Rom. II.28.29. 4. Sic precaria Hypothesis, locum Joh. III.5. agere de Baptismo aquae corporeo, externo, proprie dicto, nondum tunc instituto, sed demum Matth. XXVIII. Non verius agere, de necessitate rei significatae, ablutionis per Spiritum S. de quo unice Christus verbis sequentibus; quae & unice necessaria erat Nicodemo pridem circumciso, jam vero ad novam vitam excitando. Adde, si vel de Baptismo, non potuisse Verba Christi respicere nisi adultos, qui possent uti hoc Regenerationis instrumento, & nollent.
english: Third: they assume that faith and baptism are equally necessary for salvation. But Christ nowhere said — it is plain — that whoever has not been baptized will be damned.

Faith can stand without baptism: the converted thief, the Ethiopian eunuch, Saul, Cornelius, all before they were baptized. Baptism can also stand without faith: Simon Magus, for example — an outward washing without the inward (1 Peter 3:21), as fleshly circumcision without circumcision of the heart (Romans 2:28–29).
Fourth precarious claim: that John 3:5 is about baptism in bodily, outward water properly so called — a rite not yet instituted then, but only later (Matthew 28).

More truly it concerns the necessity of the thing signified: washing by the Holy Spirit, of which alone Christ speaks in the words that follow — and which alone Nicodemus needed, already circumcised long before, and now to be raised into a new life.
Add this: even if the text were about baptism, Christ's words could aim only at adults who could use this instrument of regeneration and refused to.

source_text: XIII. De Ritibus quibusdam inter Lutheranos, non plane Adiaphoris. I. An Usus Imaginum Sacrarum in Templis, quatenus is censetur non mere Civilis aut Politicus ad Templorum splendorem & ornatum, sed etiam sacer & religiosus, faciens videlicet ad commemorationem historicam, per picturas historicas Christi, Sanctorum, Martyrum, pro rudioribus; tum ad Instructionem moralem, εἰκονοπαιδείαν vocant, & Libros τῶν ἀγραμμάτων; tandem ad majorem reverentiam loci, & ad distinctionem Templorum Christianorum, à Judaicis ac Mahumedanis; An talis usus, non sit licitus modo & permissus, ut res in se ἀδιάφορος, nusquam prohibitus sub Novo T. cessante scil. inter Christianos causâ prohibitionis, qualis fuit Idololatriae olim periculum, in Gente Judaica, Exod. XX.4. Verum etiam sit primevus, jam à primis Christianae Ecclesiae Seculis, puta, ab aevo Tertulliani, idemque utiliter ac necessariè retinendus? Affirm. utrumque Luther. quidam, Contra Reform.
english: Controv. XIII. On certain rites among the Lutherans that are not plainly indifferent.

First: may sacred images stand in churches not only as a civil or political decoration for temple splendor and ornament, but as a sacred and religious use — for historical remembrance through pictures of Christ, the saints, and the martyrs, for the less learned; for moral instruction (what they call image-teaching, and books for the unlettered); and at last for greater reverence of the place, and to mark Christian temples off from Jewish and Muslim ones?

Is that use only lawful and permitted, as something indifferent in itself, nowhere forbidden under the New Testament once the old ground of the ban has ceased among Christians — the danger of idolatry that once hung over the Jewish nation (Exodus 20:4)?
Or is it even primeval, already from the first ages of the Christian church — say from Tertullian's day — and usefully, even necessarily, to be kept?
Some Lutherans affirm both; the Reformed deny.

source_text: NULLA de summotis inter Reformatos Imaginibus, lis mota à Lipsiacis, vel Rintelensibus nec cordatioribus aliis inter Lutheranos. Nullae etiam apparent in plurimis eorum Ecclesiis. Utilius etiam esse, nullas in Altaribus aut Templis collocari, pridem Lutherus statuit, quicquid impetuosos Iconoclastas inductu primo Carolostadii, nulla auctoritate Magistratus, improbaret: Alias, ego (inquit) Imagines non admodum amo, & vellem in Templo non statui, Annot. in Deuter. T. III. Jen. Lat. fol. 99. Idem senserunt Theologi Wittenbergenses, Giessenses, Nic. Palladius Hafniensis Theologus, Dav. Chytraeus, Mart. Chemnitius, &c. Testimonia videsis apud Christoph. Massonium, Anat. Universalis German. contra Matth. Hoë, P. III. à pag. 404.
english: No quarrel worth the name has been raised by the Leipzigers, the Rinteln men, or other more sober Lutherans over the images the Reformed have taken down. In most of those churches none appear either.
Luther himself long ago judged it more useful that none stand on altars or in temples — whatever he blamed in the hotheaded iconoclasts first led on by Karlstadt without the magistrate's authority.
"Otherwise," he says, "I do not greatly love images, and I would rather they were not set up in the temple" (Annotations on Deuteronomy, Jena Latin, vol. III, fol. 99).

Wittenberg and Giessen theologians, Nic. Palladius of Copenhagen, David Chytraeus, Martin Chemnitz, and others felt the same. Massonius gathers the testimonies against Matth. Hoe (Universal Anatomy of Germany, Part III, from p. 404).

source_text: PRECARIAE Hypotheses prolixè à Theologis discussae, ex gr. De Praecepti II. naturâ, in prohibitione Imaginum, quod ut de re in se ἀδιαφόρῳ, ita sit per Christianam Libertatem sublatum: Sic de praxi priorum Christianorum, quum tamen Chemnitius & alii fassi sint, ante tempora Hieronymi nullas in Templis collocatas Imagines: Sic de Imaginibus ut Libris imperitorum, eodem Chemnitio ad Concil. Trident. P. IV. hunc obtentum confutante, etiam exemplo Christi, Apostolorum, qui nec per Imagines, aut statuas docuerint, nec adhibuerint usquam, contenti doctrinam traditam in Scripturas retulisse, &c. Vide de priorum Seculorum praxi, & de Canone Eliberat. XXXVI, nostram Hist. Imag. Sect. I.
english: Theologians have long sifted precarious supporting claims here.
One: that the Second Commandment's ban on images concerns something indifferent in itself, and so Christian liberty has lifted it.
Another: early Christian practice — though Chemnitz and others admit that before Jerome's day no images stood in temples.

Another: that images are books for the unlearned. Chemnitz, answering Trent (Part IV), cuts that pretext down, and points to Christ and the apostles, who neither taught by images or statues nor ever used them, content to set the handed-down doctrine in the Scriptures.
On the practice of the earlier ages, and on Elvira canon 36, see our History of Images, Section I.

source_text: XIV. II. An Exorcismi Ceremonia in Baptismi administratione, quâ Minister baptizaturus Infantem, 1. Quaerit an credat, an abrenunciet seculo, &c. 2. Imperat Satanae, ut ab infante baptizando, non corporaliter quidem, sed spiritualiter à Daemone possesso, exeat, detque locum Spiritui S. 3. Adhibito Crucis signo, & certâ verborum formula; An sit ille ritus vel etiam utiliter retentus in Ecclesia Christiana, vel etiam necessarius, & omninò retinendus? Affirm. alterutrum Luther. quidam; Negant cum Reform. eorum plurimi. VIDE consensum Cassellanum, circa Exorcismum, suprâ p. 340. Ac fassi etiam Saxonici, & reliqui, Ritum nec essentialem esse Baptismo, nec imperatum à Christo vel Apostolis, nec vis alicujus spiritualis, nec nisi σημαντικὸν nasci Infantes irae filios, & sub Satanae potestate, extrà Christum, constitutos.
english: Second question under the rites head: the ceremony of exorcism in baptism.

The minister about to baptize an infant (1) asks whether the child believes, whether he renounces the world, and the like; (2) commands Satan to leave the infant — possessed by the demon not bodily, but spiritually — and give place to the Holy Spirit; (3) using the sign of the cross and a fixed form of words.
Is that rite usefully kept in the Christian church — or even necessary, and to be kept without fail? Some Lutherans affirm one or the other; most of them, with the Reformed, deny.
