See the Cassel consensus on exorcism (above, p. 340). Saxons and the rest also grant that the rite is not essential to baptism, not commanded by Christ or the apostles, not a spiritual power in itself — only a sign that infants are born children of wrath and stand under Satan's power outside Christ.

source_text: VERA autem ejus origo est, 1. Ab antiquo ritu circa adultos baptizandos, pro tempore ut praevia fuit Baptismo exutio vestium, aut calceorum, praevia solemnis abrenunciatio, conversio ad Orientem, unctio totius Corporis, ita φύσημα, ἐμφύσησις, exsufflatio seu fugatio Daemonis, voce humanâ, virtute divinâ, ut primis hujus ritûs meminit Cyprianus, ad salutarem aquam Baptismi, Epist. LXXVI. ad Magnum. Ipso etiam baptizato exsufflante seu exspuente quasi Daemonem, id est, improbos affectus, ex pectore suo. 2. Ab antiquo ritu κατηχήσεων, quo Catechumeni exsufflabantur, fugato scilicet Daemone ignorantiae, malitiae, de quo ad Canonem Laod. XXVI. Balsamo, & alii. Unde ἐξορκισταὶ, ἐφορκισταὶ, iidem qui κατηχηταί, ut in Ecclesiae Hist. nos pluribus. Et ita Catechizationum ritus in Baptismalem abiit. 3. Ab exorcismo Energumenorum δαιμονιώντων, qui solus obtinuit primâ & secundâ Aetate, extrà usum Baptismi, & quidem vi promissionis, Marc. XVI.17. Supponendis deinceps Energumenis iis omnibus, seu à Daemone quodammodo possessis, quotquot extrà Christum essent.
english: Its true origin is threefold.

First: the old rite around adults about to be baptized. For a time baptism was preceded by putting off clothes or shoes, solemn renunciation, turning east, anointing the whole body, and a human breath with divine power driving the demon out — φύσημα / ἐμφύσησις — as Cyprian first notes at the saving water of baptism (Epistle 76 to Magnus). The baptized person himself also blew out or spat as if casting the demon — that is, wicked affections — from his own breast.

Second: the old catechetical rite, in which catechumens were breathed upon to drive off the demon of ignorance and malice (Balsamon and others on Laodicea canon 26). So exorcists and catechists were the same office, as we show more fully in the Church History — and catechizing passed over into the baptismal rite.

Third: the exorcism of energumens, the demon-possessed, which alone stood in the first and second ages outside baptism, and by force of the promise (Mark 16:17). Later every person outside Christ was treated as somehow demon-possessed.

source_text: III. An Fractio panis cibarii in Sacra Coena, (quocunque modo fregerint primitus, sive digitis, sive cultro, sive ipsi Consecrantes, sive à Consecratione frangendum aliis ac discerpendum in μερίδας reliquerint) fractique panis distributio in manus communicantium, ad manducationem Sacramentalem sit Ritus non modo pius aut utilis, ut fatentur, sed etiam necessarius ex praecepto institutione Christi, quâ jussit nos hoc facere, quod ipse met fecit; Faciens idem non simpliciter ad essentiam Sacramenti, sed tamen ad integritatem illius, quod indè vocatum ἐξοχῶς fuit, Fractio panis? An verò sit Ritus simpliciter ἀδιάφορος, liberè intermissus; ut loco Panis cibarii vel usualis, rectè substituantur Hostiolæ, seu placentulae orbiculares, in os communicantium à Ministro ingestæ? Prius negant, Posterius affirm. Luth. nec omnes tamen, sed nec ex Luthero; Contra Reform.
english: Third: the breaking of ordinary table bread in the Holy Supper.

However they first broke it — by fingers or knife, by the consecrators themselves or left after consecration for others to break and tear into portions — and however the broken bread is put into communicants' hands for sacramental eating: is that rite only pious or useful, as they grant, or also necessary by Christ's institution, when He told us to do what He Himself did?
Not as if breaking belonged to the bare essence of the sacrament, yet as belonging to its integrity — which is why the supper was called, preeminently, the breaking of bread.
Or is the rite simply indifferent, freely dropped — so that little hosts or round wafers, placed by the minister in the communicants' mouths, may rightly replace ordinary bread?
Lutherans deny the first and affirm the second — yet not all of them, and not from Luther. The Reformed take the other side.

source_text: DISSENSUM non esse fundamentalem, post declarationem factam à Rintelensibus, suprâ pag. 336. agnoverunt Cassellani. SUPPONUNT autem Fratres, 1. Idem esse in Verbis Instit. fregit, quod distribuit, quomodo פרס & שבר Hebraeis sit frangere & quoque distribuere: Quasi verò aut Christus his vocibus usus sit, quae etiam praecipuè frangendi & dividendi significatu veniunt; aut non duplex actio Christi memoretur ἔκλασε καὶ ἐδίδου, etiam apud Syrum interpretem; aut τὸ κλάσαι, vel κλᾶσθαι, aliter de pane usurpetur, quam sensu frangendi obviis locis Novi Test. 2. Rem non esse necessariam, fractionem, quia fortè nescitur modus quô Christus fregerit; Quo ipso nec necessarium εὐλογῆσαι, εὐχαριστῆσαι, &c. quia non exprimitur modus, re expressissimâ. 3. Mandatum non exstare in Verbis, Hoc facite, scil. quod feci: Quae tamen ad panis fractionem retulit ipse Lutherus, cujus verba ex Tomo II. Oper. Jen. p. 25. habes apud Massonium, Anatom. P. IV. p. 253. & Wendelinum Exercit. Theologicar. contrà Gerhardum, P. I. Exercit. XVII. Vide & Consensum Chemnitii, Mentzeri, Giessensium, apud eundem Massonium, loco cit.
english: After the Rinteln declaration (above, p. 336), the Cassel men grant that this dissent is not fundamental.

Yet the brethren lean on precarious props. First: that in the words of institution "he broke" means only "he distributed," as Hebrew words for breaking can also mean distributing — as if Christ had used those Hebrew words; as if a double act were not recorded, "he broke and he gave" (ἔκλασε καὶ ἐδίδου), even in the Syriac; as if "to break" of bread meant anything else in the plain New Testament places.

Second: that breaking is unnecessary because we may not know how Christ broke — which would also make blessing and giving thanks unnecessary, since the manner is not spelled out, though the act itself is stated as plainly as can be.

Third: that "Do this" carries no command to do what He did — though Luther himself tied those words to the breaking of bread (Jena Works II.25; Massonius Anatomy IV.253; Wendelin against Gerhard, Exercises I.XVII).
See also Chemnitz, Mentzer, and the Giessen consensus in Massonius at the same place. Here Controv. XIII on rites closes before the mutual-tolerance head and before the Hexades.

source_text: XV. De Tolerantia mutua inter Evangelicos. An Reformati, ex canone charitatis, secùs sentientes in superioribus Capitibus Lutheranos, (nihil obstantibus istorum Capitum gravioribus consequentüs, sed ab his non agnitis, imò rejectis; tùm ob levius in aliis Capitibus momentum, si status Controversiae ritè explicetur, ut in Capite de S. Canâ, &c. tùm etiam ob retentum fidei principium ac fundamentum, Protestantibus commune, rejectamque Idololatriam, ac doctrinam Papalem) tolerare parati sint tanquam Fratres, & consortes ejusdem fidei ac salutis, ac membra verae Ecclesiae, sanctâ confederatione animorum, studiorumque?
english: Controv. XV. On mutual tolerance among Evangelicals.

By the rule of charity, should the Reformed — though they differ from the Lutherans on the chapters above — be ready to bear with them as brethren, sharers of the same faith and salvation, and members of the true church, in a holy bond of hearts and studies?

The graver consequences of those chapters need not block the way: the Lutherans neither own those consequences nor accept them. Other heads weigh less once the real state of the quarrel is set out fairly — as in the chapter on the Holy Supper. And both sides still keep the common Protestant principle and foundation of the faith, having rejected idolatry and papal doctrine.

source_text: Et an vicissìm Lutherani Reformatos habere debeant pro fratribus, quin pro sociis Augustanae Confessionis, ut à Melanchthone recognita est, quoad substantiam credendorum & faciendorum; adeóque nobiscum pacem ac mutuam correspondentiam colere, venireque in mutua adversùs Antichristum Romanum foedera? Procul scilicet damnandi temeritate, ut factum olim in Libro Concordiae, ac deinceps, vel exagitandi ac lacerandi libidine, invidiosissimis appellationibus Nestorianorum, Manichaeorum, Praedestinatianorum, Sacramentariorum, &c. idque in Concionibus, & Scriptis; Quo magis invidiosissimas Consequentias, de Deo Immiseracorde, Auctore peccati, &c. toto pectore Reformati detestantur?
english: And should the Lutherans, for their part, count the Reformed as brethren — even as partners of the Augsburg Confession in Melanchthon's revised form — as to the substance of what must be believed and done?
Should they keep peace and mutual correspondence with us, and join mutual leagues against the Roman Antichrist?

Not with the old rashness of damning, as in the Book of Concord and what followed; not with the appetite for baiting and tearing that brands men Nestorians, Manichaeans, Predestinarians, Sacramentarians, and the rest — in pulpits and in print.
All the more so because the Reformed themselves, with their whole heart, abhor the ugly consequences painted onto them: an unmerciful God, God as author of sin, and the like.

source_text: Affirmamus utrumque; Negarunt autem posterius Ubiquit. plerique, luctuosâ experientiâ; exceptis quos in Protheoria Catallacticâ laudavimus, à pag. 334. 335. 343. 344. &c.
english: We affirm both.
Yet most Ubiquitarians have refused the second half — that Lutherans ought to receive the Reformed as brethren and partners — as sorrowful experience shows.
The exceptions are those we have already praised in the Catallactic Protheoria (pp. 334–335, 343–344, and following).

source_text: QUANQUAM sunt haec quaedam vota, sed vota tantùm, omniaque hactenus eam in rem studia, dicta, factaque. Ventos irrita ferre ad nebulas aërias, ac malè perire, tristis experientia comprobavit: Quod de triplici aquarum genere dictum, qualis quae influit in mare, quae Vino affusa, aut quae in Judaeum effusa tingendum Christiano ritu.
english: And yet these are only wishes — wishes, nothing more — and so have been all the study, speech, and labor spent on that end till now.

Sad experience has shown that the work carries empty wind up to the airy clouds, and dies badly — like the old saying about three kinds of water: the stream that runs into the sea, the water mixed into wine, and the water poured on a Jew for Christian baptism.

source_text: Docet historia Aevi superioris, quo nihil magis Curia Papalis, Caesarea, Hispanica, & Clerus Gallicanus tempore Catharinae Medicae, formidavit, quàm sacram Confederationem Protestantium. Sed quanti tùm fuerint Heshusianis, Brentianis, Flaccianis, Bergensibus, Hunnianis, animorum motus; quae in suavissimum Melanchthonem (ne nostros dicam) hinc in Peucerum ejus generum, decennali carcere maceratum, in Strigelium, & alios, efferbuerint odia; quos illi passim despumarint irarum propemodùm fluctus, etiam in optimos moderatissimosque Principes; quin nostro seculo in Stregnensem Episcopum, in Calixtinos, Dreieranos, Rintelenses, & quotquot in Viris fratribus, de meliore luto formatis, aeterna dissidia noluerunt, reponere hoc in loco supervacuum foret.
english: The history of the last age shows what Rome's curia, the Imperial court, Spain, and the French clergy under Catherine de' Medici feared most: a sacred confederation of Protestants.

How fierce, then, were the passions of the Heshusians, Brentians, Flacians, Formula men of Bergen, and Hunnians? What hatred boiled against gentle Melanchthon — not to name our own — and then against Peucer, his son-in-law, wasted by ten years in prison, against Strigel, and the rest?

They skimmed off waves of rage almost everywhere, even against the best and most moderate princes; and in our own century against the Bishop of Strängnäs, the Calixtines, Dreier's men, the Rinteln theologians, and every brother formed of better clay who would not make the schism everlasting.
To rehearse that here would be needless.

source_text: Nec est quod nostras nobis dissensiones, aut contentiosas ἐπωνυμίας, quas inviti patimur, non ultrò à Magistris, quasi Theandris, mutuamur, invidiosius exprobrent. Viderint illi manticae quod in tergo est, ac meminerint ἐπωνυμιῶν inter suos ac scriptionum verè στηλιτευτικῶν, in causis, de Coena Domini, post emendatam Confessionem, de Praedestinatione, de Ubiquitate, de Formula Concordiae, de Communicatione Idiomatum, de Modo Conversionis, aut Justificationis illo, de Operum necessitate, de Adiaphoris & Libro Interim, &c. Undè obvia inter illos Nomina, tot quandoque telis transfixa, aut anathematis percussa, Ex gr. Philippistarum, Synergistarum, Flaccianorum, Brentio-Flaccianorum, Heshusianorum, Formulistarum, Hoffmannianorum, Osiandristarum, Majoristarum, Adiaphoristarum, Hasso-Calvinistarum vel Zwinglianorum, Variatae vel Invariatae Confessioni adhaerentium, &c.
english: Nor may they cast our quarrels — or the contentious nicknames we suffer against our will and do not freely borrow from masters as if those men were demigods — more bitterly in our teeth.

Let them mind the knapsack on their own back. Let them remember the party names among themselves, and the writings that truly brand men in public, in the fights over the Lord's Supper after the Confession was amended, over predestination, ubiquity, the Formula of Concord, the communication of properties, that mode of conversion or justification, the necessity of works, the adiaphora, and the Interim — and the rest.

Hence the names common among them, so often run through with shafts or struck by anathema: Philippists, Synergists, Flacians, Brentio-Flacians, Heshusians, Formulists, Hoffmannians, Osiandrists, Majorists, Adiaphorists, Hessian-Calvinists or Zwinglians, adherents of the Variata or of the Invariata Confession, and so on.
Here Controv. XV on mutual tolerance closes before the Hexades Annotationum on Spanheim's Protheoria.

source_text:
HEXAS ANNOTATIONUM AD B. SPANHEMII PROTHEORIAM HISTORICAM ET CATALLACTICAM PRAECIPUARUM CONTROVERSIARUM CUM AUGUSTANAE CONFESSIONIS, UT VOCANTUR, THEOLOGIS.

Prooemium.
H. I.

Seculum decimum quintum, Secundi Millennii, inde à Christo nato, ad Seculorum omnium consummationem, communiori Doctorum, Eliam quempiam Judaeum sequentium, opinione, expectandi Medium (ad quod tum Elenchi Auctoris, tum nostra, Protheoria Historico-Catallactica pertinet) num Reformatione Christianismi ipsâ, an Reformationis Necessitate, per cuncta adhuc secutura Secula, commemorandum magis sit, in ambiguo propemodùm positum arbitramur.
english: HEXAS OF ANNOTATIONS on the blessed Spanheim's historical and reconciling Protheoria of the chief controversies with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, as they are called.
Prooemium. H. I.

We judge it nearly an open question whether the middle stretch of the second millennium — from Christ's birth to the end of all ages — that learned men who follow some Jewish Elijah more commonly expect (the stretch to which both the Elenchus-writer's Protheoria and our own historical-reconciling Protheoria belong) is better remembered, through every age still to come, by Christianity's Reformation itself, or by the necessity of Reformation.

source_text: Necessitatem Reformationis in Capite Ecclesiae Christianae, (per insignem licèt abusum sic dictô) perinde atque in membris, uti istius temporis Status Christianorum omnes, tàm Spirituales, quàm Temporales, maximè ex Germanis & Gallis, & agnoverunt distinctè, & gravissimè doluerunt, quin profligatissimae Doctrinae pariter atque Vitae Papis, Juliis, Alexandris, Leonibus (post elusa ab his suique similibus elisaque, imò protrita planè ac conculcata Concilia saluberrima, Basiliense, Constantiense, Pisanum denique, Mediolani continuatum, Lugduni verò in Galliis confectum, idque per mille fraudes artesque malas, Concilia etiam opposita, mordaciter satis latrantia, i.e. Lateranensia potissimùm, aliaque lateritia à se habita) supplicibus passim de emendando precibus, partim acrioribus minis inculcarunt; ita hujus quoque aetatis, Viri per Orbem celeberrimi Reformationisque praeclarissimae, Dei gratiâ impetratae, participes, ex Reformatis in specie sic dictis ὁ πάνυ Hottingerus, tam in Historia Ecclesiastica, Parte V. & VI. quàm in Analectis Historico-Theologicis, Dissert. I. à pag. 1. ad 82. ex aliis Evangelicis, post Chytraeum & Celestinum, in Historiarum suarum Augustanae Confessionis Exordiis, etiam illustris Seckendorfius in Lutheranismo adversus Majemburgum defenso, Baclerus in Memoriali de rebus gestis Seculi XVI. p. 263. & seqq. & novissimè Celebris nominis Theologus Ulmensis, Dominus Elias Viel, peculiari Tractatu, pluribus expositum dederunt.
english: The necessity of reforming the Christian Church in her head (so named, though by a striking abuse) as well as in her members was something every Christian estate of that age — spiritual and temporal, Germans and French above all — both saw clearly and mourned with heavy grief.

They pressed for amendment by humble prayers everywhere, and partly by sharper threats, against the utterly wrecked teaching and life of Popes Julius, Alexander, and Leo — after those men and their like had dodged, crushed, and even trampled the most wholesome councils (Basel, Constance, and at last Pisa, continued at Milan and finished at Lyons in France) by a thousand frauds and foul arts, and after opposite councils that barked mordantly enough — the Lateran ones above all, and other brickish assemblies they claimed as their own.

So too the most famous men of our own age, sharers in that excellent Reformation won by God's grace, have laid the same necessity out at length: among those specially called Reformed, the great Hottinger (ὁ πάνυ), in Ecclesiastical History Parts V–VI and in the Historico-Theological Analecta, Dissertation I, pages 1–82; among other Evangelicals, after Chytraeus and Celestine in the openings of their Augsburg-Confession histories, the illustrious Seckendorf in Lutheranism defended against Maimbourg, Baclerus in the Memorial of sixteenth-century affairs (p. 263 ff.), and most recently the celebrated Ulm divine Elias Viel in a special treatise.

source_text: Reformationem verò ipsam, multis jam retrò Seculis occultiùs inchoatam fotamque (quô de multi multa, ex professo Auctor Catalogi Testium Veritatis & Magnus Usserius Armachanus in aureo de Successione Ecclesiarum Libello) apertiùs, Deo duce, aggressi sunt in superiori alter, alter in inferiori Germania, Ulricus Zwinglius, & Martinus Lutherus; iste publicè docendô & contra papales doctrinas detonandô prior; hic easdem & scriptis & factis publicis variis prior impetendô impugnandóque; uterque, per impudentissimam cumprimis Indulgentiarum Papalium nundinationem, cui isthìc Samsonius quispiam, hic famosus Tezelius obstetricabantur, ad id pertractus, vid. Gerhard. Theod. Mejerum, Hist. Relig. Cap. V. §. 29. p. m. 253. 254.
english: Yet the Reformation itself had already been growing in secret for many ages — Flacius's Catalog of Witnesses of the Truth and James Ussher of Armagh in his golden booklet on church succession have said much about that hidden work.
Under God's lead it broke into the open in upper and lower Germany through Ulrich Zwingli and Martin Luther.
Zwingli led first by public teaching and by thundering against papal doctrine; Luther led first by striking the same targets with public writings and deeds of many kinds.

What chiefly dragged both men into the fight was the shameless papal indulgence-market, midwifed in one place by a certain Samsonius and in the other by infamous Tetzel (Gerhard Theodor Mejer, History of Religion, ch. V, §29, pp. 253–254).

source_text:
§. II.
Tezelius quò efferatiùs, in hac ipsâ Viadrinâ nostrâ, sub umbone primi Academiae Rectoris Conradi Wimpinae, merces suas & venùm exponebat, & expositas commendabat, (absolutionem unicuique à scelere quovis pollicitus, qui vel decem solidos solvisset, & animarum ex Purgatorio Liberationem, simul ac contributio in Cistam conjiceretur, quin veniae impetrationem, etiamsi, per impossibilia, ipsam Dei Matrem violasset, referente Luthero in Epist. ad Archiepiscopum Moguntinum Albertum Brandenburgicum, Tom. I. Jenen. Latino, fol. 2.;) Eò animosiùs Luthero oppugnabatur, Wittenbergae ad valvas Templi, Theses suas contra foedam Indulgentiarum nundinationem affigendas curante.
english: §. II. Tetzel grew wilder still in our own Viadrina, selling under Conrad Wimpina's shield — Wimpina being the Academy's first Rector.

He hawked his wares and praised them once laid out: pay even ten shillings and receive absolution from any crime; drop a coin in the chest and souls leave Purgatory at once; buy pardon even if, by impossibles, you had violated God's Mother (Luther's Letter to Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg of Mainz, Jena Latin Tom. I, fol. 2).
That fury only hardened Luther's counterblow: at Wittenberg he had his Theses against the foul trade nailed to the church doors.

source_text: etiam Papae Leoni, sibi post plures, licèt humillimas factas deprecationes & protestationes (Tomo. I. Jen. Lat. fol. 69. in fine, & fol. 192. 210. in fine, fol. denique 435. legendas,) iniquiori ac leoninis prorsùs dentibus infestanti, tandem nunciùm mittente, combustâ Papali Bullâ condemnatoriâ, factâque ad Caesarem Carolum V. provocatione, Tom. II. Wittenb. Lat. fol. 44. & 45.
english: Pope Leo answered Luther's several most humble apologies and protests (Jena Latin Tom. I, fol. 69 end; fol. 192 and 210 end; finally fol. 435) with still harsher injustice and with teeth worthy of his name.
When that leonine message came, Luther burned the condemning Bull and lodged his appeal with Emperor Charles V (Wittenberg Latin Tom. II, fol. 44–45).

source_text:
§. III.
Ea propter Caesaris hujus Auctoritate, initiò quidem Lutherus, Wormatiam, Anno 1521. fide publicâ evocatus est, ut palinodiam cantaret; at postremò, cùm citra praeviam errorum suorum ab adversariis, ex Scripturis Sacris, factam demonstrationem, Lutherus se recantaturum constantissimè abnuisset, Saxoniae quoque Dux & Elector, Divus Fridericus, cum aliis nonnullis Imperii Romano-Germanici Statibus, Doctrinae Lutheri propiùs accessisset, ab eodem Caesare Comitia Augustana ista ipsâ indicta, ac Anno 1530. Mense Julio (Luthero intereà Coburgi, ob periculi metum, commorante, uti refert Sleidanus Lib. VII.) celebrata sunt, à quibus Auctori nostro B. Spanhemio, in Elencho suo, praecipuae quaedam Controversiae cum Augustanae Confessionis, ut vocantur, Theologis, i.e. Controversiae a nobis pertractandae, inscribuntur.
english: §. III. That clash brought imperial summons: in 1521 Charles V called Luther to Worms under safe-conduct and demanded a retractation.
Luther would not recant without first hearing his errors proved from Holy Scripture — and he held that line without wavering.

Meanwhile Frederick the Wise, Duke and Elector of Saxony, together with some other Romano-German estates, had drawn nearer to Luther's teaching. The same Emperor then set the Augsburg Diet for July 1530; Luther waited out the danger at Coburg, as Sleidan tells in Book VII.
From that Diet the blessed Spanheim, in his Elenchus, takes the title for certain chief Controversies with the so-called Augsburg-Confession theologians — the very Controversies we are to treat here.
Here the Hexades Prooemium ends; Annotatio I on the Augsburg Confession and its theologians follows.

source_text:
ANNOTATIO I.
De Augustana Confessione hujusque Theologis ac Sociis, ad haec Rubricae Auctoris verba:
Praecipuae Controversiae cum Augustanae Confessionis, ut vocantur, Theologis.
§. I.
Rubrica Auctoris nostri celeberrimi, quâ Controversias Protestanticas inscribit, Tria admodum nos inquirere jubet distinctiùsve determinare [I.] Quid & qua sit Augustana Confessio. [II.] Quinam Confessionis istius tam Theologi, quam Confessores seu Socii promiscuè? [III.] Quô Sensu nonnulli, prae aliis, Confessionis Augustanae Theologi vocitentur, vel se potiùs ipsos, non sine stomacho, vocitare consueverint & hodienum consuescant.
english: ANNOTATION I. On the Augsburg Confession and its theologians and associates — keyed to these words of the Author's rubric:
Chief Controversies with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, as they are called.
§. I. That rubric of our celebrated Author, by which he titles the Protestant Controversies, bids us press three inquiries, or settle them more sharply:
[I.] What the Augsburg Confession is, and of what kind.
[II.] Who count as its theologians, and who as its confessors or associates at large?
[III.] In what sense some men, ahead of others, are called Augsburg-Confession theologians — or rather have grown used, not without spleen, to calling themselves so, and still do.

source_text:
§. II.
Augustanam Confessionem, nulli affectui quicquam indulturi, necesse habent dicere, Christianae Fidei, quà praecipua hujus capita, Complexum, à Theologis Inferioris Germaniae praecipuis, delineante Lutherô, adornante autem inque Formam, quâ gaudet, tùm verbalem, tùm realem, digerente Melanchthone, Ordinum Imperii Romano-Germanici, in Germania Inferiori praecipuorum nomine, tàm congestum quam subsignatum, sicque Augustae Vindelicorum, Imperatori Carolo V., ceu Pontificiae cumprimis Heterodoxiae oppositum, Anno 1530. exhibitum; non quidem in Statuum omnium Confessu, in Imperatoris tamen Palatio, publicè praelectum, & licèt à dicto Imperatore, solenni Decreto rejectum, communi interim Statuum istorum consensu defensum, confirmatum, tandemque Anno insequente 1531. Wittenbergae primò omnium, publica Auctoritate, in lucem publicam editum.
english: §. II. If we give no play to party feeling, we must say this: the Augsburg Confession is a complex of the Christian faith in its chief heads.
Luther sketched it; Melanchthon dressed it and ordered it into the verbal and real form it now enjoys.

It was gathered and signed in the name of the chief estates of the Romano-German Empire in Lower Germany by the leading theologians of that region, then exhibited at Augsburg to Emperor Charles V in 1530 as a stand chiefly against papal heterodoxy.

It was not read in a full assembly of all the estates, but it was read publicly in the Emperor's palace. Charles rejected it by solemn decree; those estates nonetheless defended and confirmed it together; and in 1531 it was first issued into public light at Wittenberg by public authority.

source_text:
§. III.
Descriptionem hanc Augustanae Confessionis veram agnoverint cuicunque etiam Sectae addicti, Historiaeque Augustanae Confessionis gnari Christiani: Nam Articulorum Fidei Christianae praecipuorum Complexum, Augustanam Confessionem esse, ipsamet loquitur, per Articulos suos XXI. Partis suae prioris, cum Scriptura Sacra, fidei principio adaequato, collatos; idque non minus, ac Complexum hunc Pontificiis cumprimis oppositum esse, eadem, per Abusuum Partis suae posterioris Capita 7., clarissimè edisserit, si Capita haec cum Pontificiis Confessionibus & Catechismis comparentur. À Luthero verò Complexum illum delineatum primò, Articulisque XVII. rudius conceptum, ac postmodum à Melanchthone diligentius elaboratum distinctiùs consignatum, quanquam & sic quoque à Luthero pariter atque aliis nonnullis Theologis, Brentio, Jona, Snepfio, Spalatino approbatum, nomine Statuum dictorum, memoratis locô, tempore, modoque (postquam ab his subsignatus manibus esset) Caesari exhibitum, ab hoc publico Decreto explosum, ab istis tamen defensum, confirmatum, quin & in publicam lucem, lingvâ tàm Latinâ, quàm Germanicâ, in quibus exhibitus fuerat, Anno sequenti, editum esse, uno omnes ore & consentientibus undequaque calamis afferunt, quotquot Augustanae Confessionis Historiam adornare, resque has facti exponere aggressi sunt, quorum numerum, etsi nondum omnino plenum, Baclerus init, Lib. Memoriali de rebus Seculi XVI. p. m. 405. & 406.
english: §. III. Christians of every party, and anyone who knows the history of the Augsburg Confession, will own this description as true.
The Confession itself says it is a complex of the chief articles of Christian faith — through the twenty-one articles of its first part, set beside Holy Scripture, the adequate principle of faith.

No less clearly, through the seven heads of Abuses in its second part, it shows that this complex stands chiefly against the papal side, once those heads are compared with papal confessions and catechisms.

Luther first sketched that complex more roughly in seventeen articles; Melanchthon then worked it out more carefully and signed it more distinctly. Even in that shape Luther approved it, as did Brenz, Jonas, Schnepf, and Spalatin among other theologians.

In the name of those estates, at the place, time, and manner remembered — after their hands had signed it — it was shown to the Emperor, blasted by his public decree, yet defended and confirmed by them, and the next year published in both the Latin and the German in which it had been exhibited.

So say with one mouth, and with pens agreed from every side, all who have set out to write the Confession's history and narrate these facts — a company Baclerus begins to number, though the list is not yet full, in his Memorial of sixteenth-century affairs, pages 405–406.

source_text:
§. IV.
Caeterùm ex hoc verissimâ omnibusque admissâ Confessionis Augustanae Descriptione, in ipso statim limine, luce meridiana clariora sequentia innotescunt:
[1.] Confessionem illam, etiamsi quoad Substantiam & res suas, seu Fidei Articulos, Scripturae Sacrae Effatis consentientes, tam Universalis, quam θεόπνευσος Confessio, sensu scil. dici possit diminuto, [per eum scil. modum, quô omnis, unius etiam hominis Confessio, e.g. Confessio Divi Johannis Sigismundi, Electoris quondam Brandenburgici, gloriosissimae memoriae, quatenus cum Scriptura Sacra, Universaliter Christianis recepta, convenit, Confessio Universalis & Scriptum Dictumque quodcunque cum Scriptura Sacra exactè congruens, quatenus & quia ita congruit, θεόπνευσον (non tamen citra catachresin) appellari potest]; tamen, tùm quà Formam suam, seu verborum aequè atque Articulorum suorum Cohaerentiam; tùm quà Auctores, Subsignatores & Approbatores; tùm denique quà Usum, Confessionem [1.] Particularem audire, non Universalem; secus ac Confessiones Oecumenicorum Conciliorum omnes ac singulae: Hae enim, quanquam & ipsae propriis sibi formis accidentalibus gaudent; tamen eo ipsô quòd Oecumenicorum Conciliorum Confessiones sunt, non unius Regionis Christianae, sed Universarum, in Oriente pariter atque Occidente, Theologis Orthodoxis Auctoribus debentur, nec Germanicae solius, vel Partis rectiùs Germanicae, sed Universae, quaquà patet, Ecclesiae Christianae approbatione agnitae atque receptae, eoque Universales sunt. Certè non magis Universalis Confessio appellari poterit Augustana, quàm vel Anglicana, vel Batavica, vel Helvetica, vel quaevis alia, uni vel Regioni, vel Nationi & destinata, & recepta. Consentit Mentzerus, Exeges. August. Confess. Prolegom. n. 11. p. m. 9. & n. 15. in fine pag. 13. Calovii adhuc nascendum tum Criticum, in pagellis suis 17. & 18., per se etiam ipsas contradictoriis, praeveniendo emendaturus.
english: §. IV. From this most true description of the Augsburg Confession, admitted on all sides, these points stand out at the very threshold, clearer than noon:

[1.] Even where its substance and articles of faith agree with Holy Scripture, one may call it a universal or θεόπνευσος confession only in a weakened sense — the same way any single person's confession (for example that of blessed John Sigismund, once Elector of Brandenburg) can be called universal insofar as it matches Scripture received by Christians everywhere, and any writing exactly congruent with Scripture can be called θεόπνευσον, yet not without catachresis.

But as to its form — the coherence of its words and articles — as to its authors, subscribers, and approvers, and as to its use, it must be heard as a particular confession, not a universal one, unlike every confession of the ecumenical councils.

Those council confessions, though they too have their own accidental forms, belong as ecumenical to orthodox authors of the churches universal in East and West alike, and they are received by the whole Christian Church wherever it reaches — not by Germany alone, or even by a German part. Hence they are universal.
The Augsburg Confession can no more be called universal than the Anglican, Dutch, Helvetic, or any other confession meant for one region or nation and received there.

Mentzer agrees (Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, Prolegomena n. 11, p. 9; n. 15 at the end of p. 13), already correcting in advance Calov's Criticum, then still unborn, on its self-contradictory little pages 17–18.

source_text:
[2.] Humanam, non divinam, divinitate scil. seu θεοπνευσίᾳ formaliter proprièque sic dictâ, isti soli confessioni ac Scripto tribuendâ, quae tùm quà res, tùm quà verba, tùm quà utrorumque Seriem & Cohaerentiam, ab immediata Spiritûs Sancti inspiratione profluxerunt, Matth. 16. 17. 2. Petr. 1. 21. collat. cum 2. Tim. 3. 16. adstipulante Calovio, & emolliente Hutterianam in Expl. Form. Concord. p. 1. ab ipso tamen Huttero l. c. mox emolliendam, adscriptam θεοπνευσίαν.
Hincque porrò innotescit, ex una quidem parte, Augustanae Confessioni per omnia non adstipulato licèt, haud protinus Haereseos notam inurendam esse, sicuti contra inuritur jure iis, qui Oecumenicis Confessionibus Fidem derogant, vid. Hospinianus Concord. Discord. Cap. 18. p. m. 163., Rationes hujus Consectarii Theologorum Neostadianorum quam plurimas easque solidissimas adducens, cap. 40. p. m. 352. in fine. Ex altera verò parte, Augustanam Confessionem non esse infallibilem, infallibilitate scil. propriè sic dicta seu Originali, licèt impropriè sic dicta & Originata esse possit, quâ infallibile tam illud omne dicitur, quòd absolutè verum, etiamsi purum putumque philosophicum sit, quàm quod ex S.S. desumptum deductumque est; hôc ipso interim, quod humana fallibilisque opera intercessit, infallibilitate diminutâ duntaxat gaudens & ad infallibile absolutè infallibile Verbum DEI exigendum ac expendendum, sicque infallibilitatem suam diminutam, tùm quatenus, tùm quia cum Verbo Dei consentit, hôc unicô pacto acquisituram.
english: [2.] It is a human writing, not a divine one. Formal, proper θεοπνευσία belongs only to that confession and writing which, in matter, in words, and in the order and coherence of both, flowed from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 16:17; 2 Pet. 1:21 with 2 Tim. 3:16).
Calov agrees; and he softens the θεοπνευσία Hutter had ascribed in his Explanation of the Formula of Concord, page 1 — which Hutter himself was soon to soften in the same place.

From this two things follow. First: even if one does not assent to the Augsburg Confession in every point, the brand of heresy is not at once to be burned onto him — as it rightly is onto those who strip faith from the ecumenical confessions (see Hospinian, Concordia Discors, ch. 18, p. 163, gathering the many solid reasons of the Neustadt theologians' corollary, ch. 40, p. 352 at the end).

Second: the Augsburg Confession is not infallible with original, properly so-called infallibility — though one may call it infallible in an improper, derived sense, the sense in which anything absolutely true (even bare philosophy) or anything drawn from Holy Scripture is called infallible.

Yet because fallible human work came between, it enjoys only a diminished infallibility, and must be weighed against the absolutely infallible Word of God. It gains that lesser infallibility only insofar as, and because, it agrees with that Word.

source_text: II. Philippi Melanchthonis, non minus atque Lutheri, uti in adornanda & conscribenda, ita in explicanda & interpretanda Augustana Confessione, autoritatem, reverenter habendam esse; nec Lutheri magis, atque Philippi Melanchthonis interpretationem, publici juris valorisque quicquam in Germaniae inferioris Ecclesia obtinere posse, quam quatenus alterutra ab illis Statibus Ecclesiae Germanicae, quorum nomine Confessio Augustana fabricata, oblata atque defensa est, alteri praelata seu antehabita intelligitur; maximè, cùm & Apologia Confess. August. [totidem partibus & Articulis cum ista constans] etiam imperii Ordinum Protestantium nomine, non à Luthero, sed à Melanchthone composita sit, Chytraeo, loco citato, p. 326. multum prolixèque laudata, quanquam Chytraeus distinguat inter Apologiam priorem brevioremque Melanchthonis, Anno 1530, & inter posteriorem ac fusiorem Anno 1531. confectam, quarum ista quidem Statuum Consensu adornata fuerit, non item haec, quippe in Articulo X. in Bulgaro, seu Vulgario, allegata quaedam continens, quae Transubstantiationi Pontificiae nimiùm favent, vid. Joh. Museum in Praelect. ad Formulam Concord. p. 34. & Sohnium l. c. p. 6. circa finem.
english: II. Philip Melanchthon's authority — no less than Luther's — in framing and writing the Augsburg Confession, and in explaining and interpreting it, is to be held with reverence.

Luther's reading can claim no more public right or force in the church of Lower Germany than Melanchthon's, except insofar as those German estates in whose name the Confession was made, offered, and defended prefer one reading to the other.

That matters all the more because the Apology of the Augsburg Confession — matching it part for part and article for article — was also composed in the name of the Empire's Protestant estates not by Luther but by Melanchthon. Chytraeus praises it at length in the place cited (p. 326).

Yet Chytraeus distinguishes Melanchthon's shorter earlier Apology of 1530 from the later, fuller one finished in 1531. The first was dressed with the estates' consent; the second was not — for in Article X it cites certain things from Bulgarus (or Vulgarius) that lean too far toward papal transubstantiation (see Johannes Museus, Lectures on the Formula of Concord, p. 34; Sohnius in the same place, p. 6 near the end).

source_text:
III. Augustanam Confessionem per id, quòd Caesari praelecta in palatio est, nihil quicquam Auctoritatis, prae alia ejusdem aetatis, in Superiori Germania conscripta, ac vulgò Tetrapolitana appellata, Caesari etiam non minùs, atque ista, exhibita, etsi eidem haud praelecta, acquirere, quòd nihilominus utramque, unô etiam eodemque Decreto Imperiali proscriptam eliminatamque esse constat, narrante Chytraeo, Hist. August. Confess. edit. Francof. Anni 1578. p. 389. 393. collat. cum p. 379. & Caelestino Tom. III. p. 137. & Tom. IV. p. 120.
Interim IV. Autoritatem August. Confess. quà fidei Dogmata praecipua, esse magnam atque eximiam, quin, ut multarum Confessionum particularium, ita & Formulae Concordiae Autoritatem, multum praevalentem, agnoscente id etiam celeberr. Wittenbergens. Theologo, Philippo Ludov. Hannekenio, Declarat. Theol. de vera Aug. Conf. aestimatione, Quest. praelimin. 8. pag. 28. & Quest. 9. pag. 32. si alioquin mentem ejus obscuriùs paulò expositam, rectè assequor. DICO [1.] quà praecipua fidei Christ. Dogmata: Neque enim ad omnia sese porrigit, ut proinde perperam de ea Hutterus affirmet, in universum omni haeresi praesentissimum efficacissimumque eam opponere antidoton, Expl. Form. Conc. p. m. 22. DICO [2.] Autoritatem comparatè magnam eximiamque, non tamen absolutam Augustanae Confessioni competere; quô nomine Neostadienses perquam sobriè innuunt, se Doctrinae suae Confirmationem non (puta principaliter) ponere in Consensu seu patrocinio illius, ut istius praetextu eam hominibus venditent seu obtrudant: Dei enim beneficio melioribus fundamentis niti suam Fidem & Confessionem, quàm ut hominum testimoniis, aut praesidiis, nedum assimilatâ cum illis consensione, indigant; itaque non esse sibi anxiè laborandum, an Augustana Confessio à suis partibus stet, nec ne, dummodo certi sint, à se stare Confessionem Prophetarum & Apostolorum, cum hac si consentiant, liberum sibi esse ab Augustana & omnium hominum Confessionibus dissentire. Cap. 5. pag. 154. Postquam scil. Cap. praecedente 4to, pag. 116. protestati fuerant, suum non esse Consilium, ut August. Confessionem velint improbare, aut convellere, sed potiùs convenientem illi autoritatem asserere, ne, [sicut faciunt immodici illius praecones,] injustam ei autoritatem tribuentes, etiam justam adimant.
english: III. That the Confession was read to the Emperor in the palace wins it no authority beyond another confession of the same age written in Upper Germany and commonly called the Tetrapolitan — likewise shown to Charles, though not read aloud to him.

Both were struck down and cast out by one and the same imperial decree, as Chytraeus narrates (History of the Augsburg Confession, Frankfurt edition 1578, pp. 389 and 393, with p. 379; and Celestine, Tom. III p. 137 and Tom. IV p. 120).

IV. Meanwhile its authority on the chief dogmas of faith is great and outstanding — even much outweighing the authority of many particular confessions and of the Formula of Concord. The celebrated Wittenberg divine Philipp Ludwig Hanneken owns as much in his Theological Declaration on the true estimation of the Augsburg Confession (preliminary qq. 8–9, pp. 28 and 32), if I rightly catch a mind set out a little darkly.

I say, first: as to the chief Christian dogmas. The Confession does not reach to everything; so Hutter is wrong to claim it as the most ready and powerful antidote against every heresy whatever (Explanation of the Formula of Concord, p. 22).

I say, second: a comparatively great and outstanding authority belongs to it, yet not an absolute one. Under that name the Neustadt theologians hint very soberly that they do not (at least principally) rest the confirmation of their doctrine on its consent or patronage, as if under that cover they might sell or force it on others.

By God's gift their faith and confession stand on better ground than to need men's testimonies or props, still less a borrowed agreement with them. So they need not fret whether the Augsburg Confession stands with them or not, provided they are sure the confession of the Prophets and Apostles does — and if they agree with that, they are free to dissent from Augsburg and from every human confession (ch. 5, p. 154).

They had already protested in the preceding fourth chapter (p. 116) that they did not mean to reject or tear apart the Augsburg Confession, but rather to keep for it a fitting authority — lest, like its immoderate heralds, by giving it an unjust authority they strip away even the just one.
Here Annotatio I §.IV closes before §.V on the varied editions and the fights over autograph, apograph, and print.

source_text:
§. V.
QUID sit Augustana Confessio, indubia quâdam Descriptione elucidavimus; QUAE autem sit, ut inquiramus, variae ejus variataeque Editiones, & ingentes de his ipsis subortae altercationes ac digladiationes efflagitant. Namque VEL Αὐτόγραφον est, seu Ἀρχέτυπον, i. e. illud ipsum Exemplar, quod Caesari exhibitum fuit; idque sive Latinum tantum, eóque unicum, à Chytraeo memoratum, Hist. August. Confess. p. 81. sive Latinum potiùs & Germanicum simul, eóque binum, Caelestino descriptum utrumque Tom. II. pag. 151. & p. 169. Ambo Exemplaria, post praelectionem Exemplaris Germanici per Cancellarium Saxonicum Christianum Pontanum factam, Caesaris manu apprehensa sunt, Germanicum Secretario Imperatoris Alexandro Sveis, Electori Moguntino offerendum, à Caesare datum, Caelest. Tom. I. p. 141. & Tom. III. p. 190. & ad Moguntinum Archivum deinceps relatum; Latinum à Caesare retentum, tandemque ad Bruxellense archivum depositum est. Utrumque in dictis archivis, multis annis latuit, teste Bellarmino, Judicio de Libro Concordiae Tom. II. Controv. p. 485.; Quin paulò post alterum [Germanicum auguror] è Tomo Actorum publicorum, in Comitiis Augustanis tum collectorum, excisum esse adserit Dorscherius, Dissert. de Providentia Divina circa August. Confess. Ao. 1555. Rostochii habitâ; ut adeò Genuinum non-variatae augustanae Confessionis Exemplum hodie, non ampliùs exstet, rectè sic inferente Baclero, Memoriali sup. cit. p. m. 406. in fine. [Nota: Justus Jonas Luthero scribit, apud Chytraeum pag. 74. in med. Caesarem sibi fecisse Confessionem Augustanam Italicâ & Gallicâ linguâ reddi, hoc verò in linguas has transferri interpretor.]
english: §. V. What the Augsburg Confession is, we have already set out in a clear description.
Of what kind it is — that inquiry is forced on us by its many and altered editions, and by the huge quarrels and pitched fights that have grown up around them.
Either it is an αὐτόγραφον, or ἀρχέτυπον: the very copy shown to the Emperor.
Chytraeus remembers that copy as Latin only, and therefore unique (History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 81).
Celestine rather describes both a Latin and a German together — a pair (Tom. II, pp. 151 and 169).
After the Saxon chancellor Christian Pontanus had read the German aloud, Charles took both copies into his own hand.
He gave the German to his secretary Alexander Schweiß to offer to the Elector of Mainz; it later went into the Mainz archive (Celestine, Tom. I p. 141 and Tom. III p. 190).
He kept the Latin himself and at last lodged it in the Brussels archive.
Both lay hidden for many years in those archives, as Bellarmine notes (Judgment on the Book of Concord, Tom. II, Controversies, p. 485).

Dorsche adds that soon afterward one of them — I guess the German — was cut out of the volume of public acts gathered at the Augsburg Diet (Dissertation on Divine Providence concerning the Augsburg Confession, Rostock 1555).
So a genuine exemplar of the unvaried Confession no longer survives — Bacler rightly draws that conclusion (Memorial cited above, p. 406 at the end).
[Note: Justus Jonas writes Luther, in Chytraeus p. 74 mid-page, that the Emperor had the Confession put into Italian and French for himself; I take that to mean translated into those tongues.]

source_text: VEL Ἀπόγραφον seu ἔκτυπον, i. e. justum, de verbo ad verbum juxta Originale, calamo intellige conceptum Exemplar, quale tempore comitiorum Augustanorum non facilè negaverim exstitisse, cùm probabile haut fiat, nec Theologos, inter hos Concinnatorem augustanae Confessionis praecipuum, Melanchthonem, nec Status Imperii, quorum nomine Confessio adornata fuit, Exemplaris, Caesari exhibendi exhibitique, exactam omnino Copiam, imò plures à singulis Statibus procuratas, habuisse, sibiique in varios perquam casus retinuisse servasseque, alioquin, & si secus fecissent, ad unum omnes, si minus supinae negligentiae, certè stupidae cujusdam improvisionis, coarguendi; VEL denique, τυπόγραφον seu Ἔκτυπον, praelô, i. e. juxta Exemplar apographum, calamo factum, typis exscripta, idque vel privato ausu, qualis eodem anno Vratislaviae, vernacula lingva in 4to, typis Adami Dyonis, prodiit, de qua Chytraeus Hist. August. pag. 47. pronunciat, ad Originalem Confessionem in Moguntino servatam Archivo, fuisse formatam, quamque idem Chytraeus ipsemet haud rarò sequitur, vid. auctor. der ausführlichen Behauptung pag. 6. in fine; Vel publica auctoritate, quales anno sequenti Wittenbergae plures, tam Germanicae, quàm Latinae, & in 4to, & in 8vo excusae sunt, primas tamen inter omnes obtinente Latinâ in quarto, etiam Vratislaviensem in praefatione sua, ceu spuriam arguente, uti observat Calovii Critic. Sacr. pag. m. 82.
english: Or it is an ἀπόγραφον — an ἔκτυπον: a fair pen copy, word for word from the original.
I would not easily deny that such copies stood ready at the Augsburg Diet.

It is hardly likely that neither the theologians — Melanchthon chief among the framers — nor the imperial Estates in whose name the Confession was dressed, kept an exact copy of what was shown to Charles, and even several copies procured estate by estate, held back against every sort of chance.
Had they done otherwise, they would one and all stand convicted — if not of lazy neglect, then of a stupid want of foresight.
Or last, a τυπόγραφον — an ἔκτυπον from the press: type set from a pen apograph.

That could be by private venture: the same year a vernacular quarto came out at Breslau from Adam Dyon types. Chytraeus says it was shaped to the original Confession kept in the Mainz archive (History, p. 47), and he himself often follows it (see the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, p. 6 at the end).
Or it could be by public authority: the next year Wittenberg printed several, German and Latin, quarto and octavo.
Among them the Latin quarto took first place, and in its preface even branded the Breslau print a spurious one — as Calov notes (Critica Sacra, p. 82).

source_text: De his omnibus, praelô scil. annis duobus primis, commissis, certum est, tùm inter se, tùm ab Autographo haud rarò verbis differre: Probant enim discrimen verborum prius, non Exemplaria tantùm Wittenbergensia cum Vratislaviensi, sed & Wittenbergensia inter se, Latinum scil. in 4to, cum Germanico ejusdem formae, collata, potissimum quod ad Articulum X. attinet, etiamsi utrumque Exemplar Wittenbergense eundem Typographum Georgium Rhauium expertum sit, vid. Calovii Critic. p. à 86. ad 98. Idem probant Exemplaria Augustanae Confessionis, tam Latina, quàm Germanica, à Chytraeo & Coelestino Historiis suis illata; etiam utriusvis Auctoris Latina cum Germanicis comparata. E.g. tàm Caelestini, quàm Chytraei Germanica, Articulum X. his verbis efferunt: Vom Abendmahl wird also gelehret, daß wahrer Leib und Blut Christi wahrhaftiglich unter der Gestalt des Brods und Weins im Abendmahl gegenwärtig sey, und da ausgetheilet und genommen wird, derhalben auch die Gegenlehre verworffen wird. Tom. II. p. 53. b.; At Latina eorundem Autorum, articulum X. sic formatum habent, ut Speciei Panis & Vini nulla prorsus mentio injiciatur: De Coena Domini docent, quòd Corpus & Sanguis Domini verè adsint, & distribuantur vescentibus in Coena Domini, & improbant secus docentes. Tom. eod. pag. 172. b. Similes Discrepantias reperias circa Articulum XIII. & XVIII. in Exemplaribus Latinis Chytraei & Coelestini, se inter comparatis, utpote quorum prius, Chytraeanum scil. multa adjecta habet, quae in Coelestiniano haud inveniuntur. Ut proinde mirùm non sit, cùm Pontificios, tùm Protestantium nonnullos, de discrepantia Exemplarium conquestos subinde fuisse, nec à vero abludat Bellarminus, quando loco retrò citatô scribit, singulis propè annis, alia atque alia Exemplaria prodiisse, quae licèt omnia Confessionis augustanae titulum prae se ferrent, tamen & verbis & sententiis, tum inter se, tùm ab illa prima Confessione, Caesari exhibita, plurimum dissenserint; Quin potiùs quali quali verborum Bellarmini veritate convictus Joh. Schmidius, solius hyperboles dictionem Bellarmini infimulet, ita respondens: Quod de mutatione, singulis prope annis factâ, scribit Bellarminus, est hyperbolicon; mutatam fuisse Augustanam Confessionem non negamus, sed quoad verba tantùm, non quoad res ipsas & Sententias; Initio mutationem esse factam concedimus, quô pactô ipsi Confessionis essentiae nihil accessit vel decessit: Certum enim est, August. Confess. Anno 31. Wittenbergae editam, ratione Substantialium & Doctrinalium, ab Exemplari Augustae exhibito, nequaquam dissensisse, licèt quoad Phraseon & Dictionum additiones cum prototypo non planè congrueret. Causas mutationum variarum require apud Calovium in Crit. & pag. 85. Posterius verborum Discrimen multiplex, scil. typis expressorum exemplarium Imprimis ejus, quod Formulae Concordiae insertum ab Autographo, accurata collatione delineavit Illustriss. Princeps Ernestus Fridericus Marchio Badenensis, im Christl. Bedenck. und Motiven, die Sr. Fürstl. Gnaden von der Subscription der F. C. abgehalten. à pag. 1. ad 98. gedruckt auf dem Schloß Staffort anno 1599.
english: Of all these first-two-years press copies it is certain: they often differ in wording both from one another and from the autograph.

The earlier verbal split shows not only when Wittenberg copies are set beside the Breslau one, but when Wittenberg copies are set beside each other — the Latin quarto against the German of the same size — above all on Article X, though both Wittenberg runs used the same printer, Georg Rhau (Calov, Critica, pp. 86–98).
The same is proved by the Latin and German exemplars Chytraeus and Celestine put into their histories, and by matching either author's Latin with his German.

Celestine's and Chytraeus's German both cast Article X thus: they teach of the Supper that Christ's true body and blood are truly present under the form of bread and wine, are distributed and received there, and that the contrary teaching is rejected (Tom. II, p. 53b).

But their Latin forms Article X so that the species of bread and wine are never named: they teach concerning the Lord's Supper that the body and blood of the Lord are truly present and are distributed to those who eat, and they reject those who teach otherwise (same Tom., p. 172b).
Like gaps turn up around Articles XIII and XVIII when Chytraeus's and Celestine's Latin copies are compared: Chytraeus has many additions Celestine lacks.
No wonder, then, that Papists and some Protestants have complained of discrepant copies.

Bellarmine is not far from the truth when he writes (in the place already cited) that almost every year new exemplars appeared which, though all wore the Augsburg title, differed much in words and sentences both among themselves and from the first Confession shown to Charles.

Johann Schmid, pressed by whatever truth sits in those words, answers that Bellarmine's yearly-change talk is hyperbole alone: we do not deny verbal change, but we deny change of the things and sentences; an early change we grant, yet by that pact nothing was added to or taken from the Confession's essence.

The Wittenberg edition of 1531, he says, did not dissent from the Augsburg-exhibited exemplar in substance or doctrine, though its added phrases and diction did not wholly match the prototype. For the causes of the various changes, see Calov, Critica, and p. 85.

Later, the many verbal differences among printed copies — above all the Formula of Concord insert set against the autograph — were carefully collated by the most illustrious prince Ernest Frederick, Margrave of Baden, in the Christian Reflections and Motives that kept His Princely Grace from subscribing the Formula (pp. 1–98, printed at Castle Staffort, 1599).

source_text:
§. VI.
Typis exscripta Augustanae Confessionis Exemplaria succedentibus annis plura alia insecuta sunt, donec Melanchthon Anno 37. & 38. vivo adhuc Luthero aliisque Augustanae Confessionis exhibitoribus, cum varietatem exemplorum plurium observasset, de edenda expolitiori & correctiori consilium & cepit, & nemine contradicente executus est, quod e pluribus Theologi in colloquio Altenburgico pag. 404, probaturi hoc pacto istud, quod Calovius nullo documento constare scribit, Critic. pag. 202. Videatur etiam Auctor der ausführlichen Behauptung. pag. 27. in fine & pag. 28. Idem Anno 1540. & 1542. repetere instituit Melanchthon; quin Anno 1551. repetitionem tertia vice, sed prolixiorem paulò, idque jussu multorum Statuum Protestantiorum confecit, in Corpore Doctrinae Melanchthonis legendam, Scriptum utile & lectu dignum, a Joh. Museo appellatum, in quô Doctrina Augustanae Confessionis perspicue & eleganter declarata sit. Praelect. in Epitom. Formul. Concord. pag. 35. Et quamvis priores duae Editiones Melanchthonianae, Approbationem publicam Antecedentem haud habuerint, habuerunt tamen Consequentem, tàm aliorum Theologorum, Chytraei, Selnecceri, Brentii, Theologorum Altenburgicorum, hosque inter Pauli Eberi, Misnicorum, Grypswaldensium, ipsius quoque Lutheri, Tomo Germanico Jenensi 7. fol. 447. collat. cum fol. 448. b. quam Statuum Imperii in Conventibus, Wormatiensi, Ratisbonensi, Francofurtensi & Nauenburgico, approbationem suam sequentibus verbis declarantium: Neque verò animus nobis est, quòd per hanc repetitionem & renovatam Subscriptionem primum excusae Confessionis, discedere ab ea quae Anno 40. exhibita, vel in minimo velimus. Cum enim illa aliquot Colloquiis, & Disputationibus cum Adversariis institutis, in aliquibus Articulis ideo copiosius explicata sit, ut Caelestis Veritas eò magis illucesceret, & fiducia in meritum Redemtoris nostri J. C. absque humanis traditionibus pura & incorrupta conservaretur & ad posteritatem transmitteretur, perinde illam sicut & aliam, deserere non possumus, praesertim cum locupletata ista, Anno 40. & 42. typis evulgata Confessio multorum nunc in manibus & magna ex parte Ecclesiis & Scholis nostris in usu sit.
english: §. VI. In the years that followed, many other printed copies of the Augsburg Confession came after the first.

Then in 1537 and 1538 — Luther and the other original exhibitors still alive — Melanchthon, seeing how the many copies varied, took counsel to issue a more polished and corrected edition, and carried it out with no one contradicting.
Many theologians at the Altenburg colloquy (p. 404) thus prove the very point Calov says no document establishes (Critica, p. 202). See also the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, pp. 27–28.
Melanchthon undertook the same again in 1540 and 1542.

In 1551, by order of many Protestant Estates, he finished a third and somewhat longer repeat, to be read in his Body of Doctrine — a useful writing worth reading, says Johannes Museus, in which Augsburg doctrine is set out clearly and with elegance (Lectures on the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, p. 35).
The earlier two Melanchthon editions lacked a public approval beforehand; they still won approval afterward.

Other theologians owned them — Chytraeus, Selneccer, Brenz, the Altenburg men, among them Paul Eber, the Meissen and Greifswald faculties — and Luther himself (Jena German Tom. 7, fol. 447 with 448b).
So did the imperial Estates in the diets at Worms, Regensburg, Frankfurt, and Naumburg, declaring in these words:
Nor is it our mind, by this repetition and renewed subscription of the Confession first printed, to depart even in the least from that shown in the year 40.

For in some colloquies and disputations with adversaries that later text was explained more fully in certain articles, so that heavenly truth might shine the more, and trust in the merit of our Redeemer Jesus Christ might be kept pure and uncorrupted without human traditions and handed on to posterity.
We cannot desert that enriched Confession any more than the other — especially since the 1540 and 1542 print now sits in many hands and is largely in use in our churches and schools.

source_text: Omnia haec prolixius prosecuti sunt nostates, Hospinianus, Georgius Pauli, Sohnius, Ursinus aliique, etiam hôc locô praecipuè commemorandi tum Auctor der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 27. & 57; etiam in appendice, oder dem Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 25. ad 36. tùm Venerandus Becmannus noster, sub nomine Orthuini Gratii contra Liebhardum Cap. III. §. 2. integrô à pag. 73. ad 74. qui etiam variandae Confessionis Augustanae causas haud negligendas in medium adducit, à pag. 69. & exceptiones, Approbationi subsequenti variatae Confess. intentari solitas, nervose retundit l. cit. à pag. 73. ad 81. Crocium secutus, Comment. de Aug. Conf. Societate Cap. 54. 55. 56. cum quo etiam Cavillationes, tàm Vetustiores seu Hutterianas, in Concordia Concordi, p. m. 344. & 418. ac seqq., nec non in Anti-Peucero à pag. 7., quàm recentiores & Calovianas Crit. Sacr. à pag. 203. ad 228. enervat eluditque. Nobis hic suffecerit annotasse, etiam Balth. Mentzerum, Variatae Confessionis Oppugnatorem satis strenuum, approbationem hujus subsequentem publicam, pro qua nunc disputamus, ingenuè agnovisse, quando in Prolegom. ad August. Confess. p. m. 21. ita scribit: Qui mutatam Confessionem admiserunt, publicè testati sunt, hactenus & non aliter à se recipi, quatenus in ipsis rebus planè conveniat cum Prototypo, sicuti patet ex Hist. Conventus Navenburgici pag. 61. Hactenus Mentzerus; quod ipsum quomodo intellexerint Status Imperii, vidimus paulò ante ex Epistola eorum ad Ferdinandum primum scripta. Praeterquam quòd, vel ex adductis è Mentzero verbis, apparet, Variatam Confessionem Augustanam in ipsis rebus planè cum Prototypo convenientem habitam fuisse.
english: Our own writers have chased all this out at more length — Hospinian, Georg Pauli, Sohn, Ursinus, and the rest.

Here I mark especially the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung (pp. 27 and 57; and the Anhang, pp. 25–36), and our own venerable Becmann under the name Orthuinus Gratius against Liebhard (ch. III §2, pp. 73–74 entire).

Becmann also brings forward causes for varying the Augsburg Confession that deserve a hearing (from p. 69), and he beats back hard the stock objections aimed at the Variata's later approval (pp. 73–81), following Crocius on Augsburg fellowship (chs. 54–56).
With Crocius he also drains and turns aside both the older Hutterian cavils (Concordia Concordi, pp. 344 and 418ff.; Anti-Peucer from p. 7) and the newer Calovian ones (Critica Sacra, pp. 203–228).
For us it is enough to note this: even Balthasar Mentzer, a sturdy enough foe of the Variata, candidly owns the later public approval for which we now argue.

In his Prolegomena to the Augsburg Confession (p. 21) he writes: those who admitted the changed Confession have publicly testified that they receive it thus far and no otherwise — insofar as in the things themselves it plainly agrees with the prototype, as the History of the Naumburg Convention shows (p. 61).
So Mentzer. How the imperial Estates themselves took that point, we saw a little earlier in their letter to Ferdinand I.
And even Mentzer's own words make plain that the Varied Augsburg Confession was held to agree with the prototype in the things themselves.

source_text:
§. VII.
Ut proinde tam in Augustanam Confessionem ipsam, quàm in ejus praecipuum propemodum ex Theologis Auctorem, Theologorum pariter atque omnium Eruditorum Germanorum suô tempore Phoenicem faciléque Principem, optimum Melanchthonem, injurii sint qui Variatam Editionem, ceu corruptam & depravatam, cum August. Confess. primigenia haudquaquam eandem, sed ab hac prorsus aliam, clamitant. Nam Variatio isthaec vel Essentialis est, & in Fidei Fundamentum impingere dicitur, & tùm Philippus, unà cum Confessione mutata, Haereseos infimulatur; vel Accidentalis, & tùm cum primigenia in ipsis rebus planè congruit, ut loquitur Mentzerus, eóque cum ista eadem. Quâ ratione huc quadrat responsio Joh. Schmidii, Bellarmino regesta, & §. V. à nobis allata, cui adjicimus, quae idem Auctor subnectit: Quodsi, inquit, Verborum, Dictionum & Phrasium Mutatio & Variatio ipsam Confessionem tolleret, jam dudum de Symbolo Apostolico actum fuisset, quòd aliâ atque aliâ verborum serie ab aliis Ecclesiae Doctoribus propositum fuisse, monumenta testantur pag. 77. in fine & pag. 88. Praesertim, quandô ipsi Status Imperii inter duas dictas Confessiones neutiquam discriminarunt, sed utramque unam eandemque reputarunt, vid. Der Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung à p. 43. ad 52. Inepti verò habendi, qui Variatam, proptereà Augustanam esse negant, quod Augustae exhibita non fuit, porismatizante sic Mentzero: Quae Confessio Augusta exhibita non fuit, Augustanam eam dici non deberi. Proleg. n. 9. p. m. 8. etiam asseclas híc nactô, quàm plurimos, Schmidium, locô citatô pag. 12. Calovium, l. c. p. 8. aliosque. Quasi verò, nihil, quòd Augustae exhibitum non est, Augustanum dici non possit; Vel Augustana Confessio, locum Civitatemque magis, in qua facta est, quam res & Articulos, ex quibus constat, denotet respiciatve; (Dico, Confessionem August. non MAGIS Civitatem in qua facta est, quàm Articulos, ex quibus constat, denotare atque respicere, ut non negem, à Civitate ista denominari potuisse, etiam denominandam in posterum fore, licèt forte contingat, ut [quod fieri coepisse gravissimè dolemus] civitas haec Imperialis ad pagi cujusdam formam redigatur.); Vel Wittenbergae Anno 1531. in lucem edita Confessio aliaeque haud paucae mutatae, mutationemque variam, omnium Confessione, passae, non iis ipsis ampliùs Augustanae sint, qui à Philippo variatam aspernantur ac aversantur, eò, quòd Augustae non exhibitae sunt.
english: §. VII. Those who cry that the Variata is corrupt and depraved — not the same as the original Augsburg Confession, but utterly another — do injury both to the Confession itself and to Melanchthon, its near-chief theological author, in his day the phoenix and easy prince of Germany's theologians and learned men.

For that variation is either essential, and is said to strike the foundation of faith — and then Philip, together with the changed Confession, is charged with heresy — or it is only accidental, and then it plainly agrees with the original in the things themselves, as Mentzer puts it, and is therefore the same confession.
Johann Schmid's answer to Bellarmine, which we already cited in §. V., fits here; and we add what he subjoins:

If change of words, diction, and phrases took away the Confession itself, the Apostles' Creed would long ago have been done for — the monuments show church doctors set it out in one wording and another (pp. 77 end and 88).
Above all, the imperial Estates themselves drew no line between the two Confessions, but counted both one and the same (Anhang of the Ausführliche Behauptung, pp. 43–52).

Inept, too, are those who deny the Variata the name Augsburg because it was not shown at Augsburg — Mentzer's corollary (Prolegomena n. 9, p. 8), with a crowd of followers: Schmid (p. 12), Calov (p. 8), and others.
As if nothing not exhibited at Augsburg could bear an Augustan name; or as if the Augsburg Confession pointed more to the city where it was made than to the matters and articles of which it consists.

(I say it does not mark the city MORE than the articles — without denying it could take its name from that city and should still do so hereafter, even if, as we most heavily grieve has begun, that imperial city should shrink toward the shape of a village.)

Or as if the Confession published at Wittenberg in 1531, and not a few other altered prints that everyone owns suffered various change, ceased to be Augsburg even for those who scorn Philip's Variata — merely because they were not shown at Augsburg.

source_text: Denique sibi ipsis adversi & tantum non αὐτοκατάκριτοι deprehenduntur, qui vel (1.) Confessionem Augustanam invariatam hujusque Sensum adeò ampliatum eunt, ut etiam soli Formulae Concordiae domesticas Doctrinas, e.g. de Orali Corporis Christi Manducatione, de Ubiquitate seu Omnipraesentia Corporis Christi, similesque, (de quibus ne somniavit quidem Augustana Confessio) quin totam Concordiae Formulam illacomprehenfam ajunt, expunctâ tamen variante in nonnullis, Philippicâ Confessione, Brentianis sic interpretationibus & Consequentibus locum facturi, prohibitis exclusisque Melanchthonianis. Quorsum digitum intendit doctissimus alioquin Lutheranorum Theologorum & non nisi cum veneratione mihi nominandus, Joh. Georg. Dorscheus, Disp. Seculari de Consequentibus Augustanae Confessionis insignioribus, quippe has inter alias, Conclusiones formans: Interpretatio Augustanae Confessionis admittit, quicquid ex ea per legitimam Consequentiam deductum est. Item: Religio August. Confess. non ita interpretando coangustanda est, ut totaliter & secundum omnes suos Articulos, in August. Confess. expressa esse dicenda sit, Cap. 2. pag. m. 182. & 200. Scilicet: Quicquid Formulistae vel jam commenti sunt, vel in posterum comminiscentur, istud August. Confess. invariatae Doctrina fuerit, quippe per legitimam consequentiam, (uti ipsis videtur,) ex ea deductum; Quicquid ex adverso, vel Philippus, declarandae ergo Augustanae Confess. à se ipso olim confectae (cujusque proinde interpres, ceu verborum suorum, optimus, videri potest) vel addidit, vel immutavit, Philipistae quoque Pezelius, Sohnius, Crocius, Georgius Pauli, Hoffmannus, Helmstadienses aliique commentantur in Augustanam Confessionem, perque legitimas sibi visas Consequentias inde deducunt, illud ab Augustana Conf. invariata quàm alienissimum habendum. Vel (2.) cum eodem Dorscheo, capite sequenti tertiô, Canones ejusmodi cudunt, qui, ceu à vero haud abludentes, indeque admissi, Variatam Confessionem Philippicam, omnibus aequâ istam lance expendentibus, omnino genuinam ostendunt, & nonnisi odiose, etiam à Dorscheo exagitatam. Variatio, inquit Dorscheus, Augustanae Confessionis quacunque, etiam Substantialis, non debuit alicui transitum ad aliam religionem suadere. Canon. 2. Ergò qui Philippicae adhaeret Confessioni, licèt substantialiter, juxta Dorscheum, variatae, adhuc dum Religioni illi adhaeret, quam Augustana Confessio invariata profitetur, nec Confessio Philippica ad aliam huic Religionem transitum suadet, nedum eundem alteri Religioni addicit. Iterum: Variatio, ait Dorscheus, in Substantiam Veritatis, Articulis Augustanae Confessionis expositae mutationem nullam inferens, non debet odiose exagitari aut causa esse aliquem extra pacem Religionis constituendi. Canon. 3. Item: Variatio, quae suum locum Originalibus exemplaribus relinquit, sinceritati Augustanae Confessionis, non obstat, p. m. 216. 217. 218. Subsumo ego: de Variata Philippica: Non infert haec mutationem in Substantiam Veritatis, [testante Mentzero] relinquit verò locum suum Originalibus Exemplaribus, si quae alicubi supersunt. Ergò.
english: Finally these opponents are caught at odds with themselves — all but αὐτοκατάκριτοι.

(1.) They stretch the unvaried Augsburg Confession and its sense so wide that they even fold into it the Formula of Concord's household doctrines — oral manducation of Christ's body, ubiquity or omnipresence of Christ's body, and the like — of which the Augsburg Confession never so much as dreamed — yes, the whole Formula, they say, is packed inside it.
Yet they strike out the Philippica Confession where it varies in some points, so as to make room for Brentian readings and consequences while Melanchthon's are barred and shut out.

Where the finger of Johann Georg Dorsche points — otherwise among the most learned Lutheran divines, and a name I speak only with reverence — in his Secular Disputation on the more noted consequences of the Augsburg Confession, forming among others these conclusions:
Interpretation of the Augsburg Confession admits whatever is drawn from it by legitimate consequence.
Also: Augsburg religion is not to be so narrowed by interpreting that it must be said to be expressed wholly, and in all its articles, inside the Augsburg Confession itself (ch. 2, pp. 182 and 200).
In plain: whatever the Formulists have already spun, or will invent later, is to count as unvaried Augsburg doctrine — because deduced, as they see it, by legitimate consequence.

But whatever Philip added or changed in declaring the Confession he himself once framed — and he may well seem its best interpreter, as of his own words — and whatever Philippists (Pezel, Sohn, Crocius, Georg Pauli, Hoffmann, the Helmstedt men, and others) comment and draw by consequences that seem legitimate to them, that is to be held most alien from the unvaried Confession.

(2.) Or with the same Dorsche in the next, third chapter they mint canons which, if admitted as not far from the truth, show the Variata Philippica altogether genuine to anyone who weighs it with an even hand — and only odiously harassed, even by Dorsche.
Variation of the Augsburg Confession of whatever kind, says Dorsche, even substantial, ought not to have talked anyone into crossing to another religion (Canon 2).

Therefore he who holds to the Philippica, though Dorsche calls it substantially varied, still holds to the religion the unvaried Augsburg Confession professes; the Philippica does not urge a crossing to another religion, still less binds a man to one.
Again: variation that brings no change into the substance of truth set out in the Augsburg articles ought not to be odiously harassed or used to push anyone outside the peace of religion (Canon 3).
Also: variation that leaves the original exemplars their place does not block the sincerity of the Augsburg Confession (pp. 216–218).
I subsume for the Variata Philippica: it brings no change into the substance of truth — Mentzer is witness — and it leaves the original exemplars their place, if any still survive. Therefore.

source_text:
§. VIII.
Equidem videri hic possum Dorschaanis, etiam modestioribus, Principium petere, cum Joh. Museo, Confess. Philippicam ita comparatam pronunciaturis, ut plerique quidem Articuli inibi fusius deducti & uberius declarati sint, multaque etiam utilia in ista Editione reperiantur; interim, ut quaedam etiam inserta fuerint, quae postea in controversiam vocarunt Augustanae Confessionis Theologi inter se, v. g. An Evangelium sit concio poenitentiae? Cumprimis verò, ut Articulus decimus de Coena Domini in gratiam Calvinianorum depravatus fuerit. Nam in Articulo X. primae Editionis haec haberi verba: De Coena Domini docent, quod Caro & Sanguis Christi verè adsit & distribuatur vescentibus, & improbant secus docentes. In altera verò Editione verba (Verè adsunt & distribuuntur) omissa esse, substitui autem haec: Quòd Corpus & Sanguis verè exhibentur &c. At verò formulam hanc loquendi, etiam concessisse Calvinianos; sed dixisse, quod spiritualiter exhibeantur. Deinde verba: Et improbant secus docentes, in Editione Philippica omissa esse, Atque hinc Controversiam de auctoritate hujus Confessionis ortam fuisse, Hactenus Museus Praelect. in Epitom. Formul. Concord. p. m. 32.
english: §. VIII. Here I may seem, even to the more modest Dorscheans, to beg the question — standing with Johann Museus, who will weigh the Philippica Confession like this:
Most of its articles, they grant, are drawn out more fully and declared more richly, and many useful things appear in that edition.
Yet some insertions later set Augsburg-Confession theologians quarreling among themselves — for example, whether the Gospel is a sermon of repentance.
Above all, they say, Article X on the Lord's Supper was corrupted to favor the Calvinists.

In Article X of the first edition the words run: Concerning the Lord's Supper they teach that the flesh and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed to those who eat, and they reject those who teach otherwise.
In the other edition, Museus reports, the words are truly present and are distributed drop out, and this is put in their place: that the body and blood are truly exhibited, and so on.
The Calvinists, he adds, even conceded that formula of speech — yet said the exhibition is spiritual.
Then the clause And they reject those who teach otherwise is omitted in the Philippica edition; and from that, he says, the controversy over this Confession's authority arose.
So far Museus, Lectures on the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, page 32.

source_text: Quibus Dorschaeanis modestioribus & Museanis respondemus (1.) Accipiendo quae de Confessione Philippi honorificè satis edisserunt, quaeque omnino urgent, non odiose eam exagitandam esse. (2.) advertendo, Confessioni Philippicae inserta ea, quae postea in controversiam vocarunt Aug. Conf. Theologi inter se (v. g. Num Evangelium sit Concio poenitentiae &c.) non talia fuisse, quae in Substantiam Veritatis, Articulis Augustanae Confessionis expositae, mutationem aliquam intulerunt, alioquin non talia fuissent, quae Augustanae Confess. Theologi, se inter, in controversiam vocassent. (3.) Contestando, articuli Xmi Mutationem duplicem, quae oppugnantibus eam maxima in oculis sudes est, (quasi in gratiam Calvinianorum facta, quae explodendae Pontificiae Transubstantiationi instituta unicè fuerat) nec Mutationem Substantialem inferre, nec Calvinianae, quam ajunt, Sententiae ulla ex parte magis favere, quam ipse Articulus X. invariatus ei favet.
english: To those more modest Dorscheans and Museans we answer:
First, we take what they have said honorably enough of Philip's Confession — and what presses hardest of all: it is not to be odiously harassed.

Second, the insertions later fought over among Augsburg-Confession theologians for example whether the Gospel is a sermon of repentance did not change the substance of the truth set out in the Augsburg articles. Had they done so, those same theologians would not have been fighting the points among themselves.

Third, we contend that Article X's twin mutation — the chief sweat in the attackers' eyes, as if Melanchthon had altered it for the Calvinists, though the article was framed solely to explode pontifical transubstantiation — neither introduces a substantial change, nor favors the so-called Calvinian sense in any part more than the unvaried Article X itself already does.

source_text: PRIUS patet ex verbis Articuli Xmi utriusque Confessionis inter se collatis, quae in Variata Anni 1531., communiter Invariata dicta, ita se habent: De Coena Domini docent, quod Corpus & Sanguis Christi verè adsint & distribuantur vescentibus in Coena Domini, & improbant secus docentes; In Variata autem vulgò dicta, sic sonant: De Coena Domini docent, quod Corpus & Sanguis Christi verè exhibeantur vescentibus in Coena Domini. Ubi meritò ad cujusvis Sensum & Intellectum provoco: Num duae dictae propositiones substantialiter inter se differant, praesertim quando posterior non tantum priorem supponit: (Corpus enim & Sanguis Christi dicta verè exhiberi in Coena, eô ipsô necesse est dici verè in Coena adesse & distribui); sed & posterior priori plus dicit: Nam adesse in Coena Corpus & Sanguis Christi verè possunt, nec non a ministro verè distribui, ut tamen non verè, communicantibus, certè non omnibus, exhibeantur; at, quandocunque in S. Coena à Ministro Corpus & Sanguis Christi communicantibus, verè exhibentur, necesse est & ea adesse, & ea distribui.
english: The first point is plain once you set the two forms of Article X side by side.

In the 1531 Variata — commonly called the Invariata — it runs: Concerning the Lord's Supper they teach that the body and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed to those who eat in the Lord's Supper, and they reject those who teach otherwise.
In the Variata commonly so named it sounds: Concerning the Lord's Supper they teach that the body and blood of Christ are truly exhibited to those who eat in the Lord's Supper.
I appeal to anyone's sense: do these two propositions differ in substance?

The later wording not only presupposes the earlier — for if Christ's body and blood are truly exhibited in the Supper, then by that very fact they must be said to be truly present there and distributed — but also says more.
Body and blood can truly be present in the Supper, and truly distributed by the minister, and yet not truly exhibited to the communicants — certainly not to all.
But whenever in the holy Supper the minister truly exhibits Christ's body and blood to the communicants, they must both be present and be distributed.

source_text: Ad mutationem verò alteram quod attinet, seu potius omissionem Verborum horum in Variata: Et improbant secus docentes, etsi verba sic expressa inibi haud legi fateamur, in Confessionis tamen cujuscunque Articulis singulis subintelligi vel eadem, vel similia, videri necessariò debent: Qui enim positivè aliquid in Confessione fatetur, ille id semper, quod secus se habet, diffitetur ac improbat; Ut proinde omissio verborum istorum, Tautologiae duntaxat evitatio habenda sit, certè Substantialem mutationem nullam inducere queat. Taceo, quod ad priorem mutationem attinet, in prototypo Exemplari Invariatae Confessionis (prout id Germanica disertè ostendit) Articulum ita fuisse expressum, (non diffitente Dorscheo, cit. pag. 183.) De Coena Domini &c. fatentur, Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, sub specie panis & Vini, verè adesse; id quod Transubstantiationem Pontificiam per se, istô praesertim tempore, redoluisse, nulli facilè dubium esse potest.
